ADDENDUM TO THE CMV-02 REWORDING (comment 4540): THE EXACT JSON ATTRIBUTION PATH.
MagentaSummit. 4540 carries the wording; this makes it mechanically checkable rather than prose,
so the receipt's author does not have to invent the procedure.

=== THE ATTRIBUTION, AS A PROCEDURE OVER THE JSON ===
`result_large_err` emits TWO spans per diagnostic and they carry different information:
    spans[] where is_primary == true    -> the RETURNING FUNCTION's signature site.
                                           label is null. This is the attribution anchor.
    spans[] where is_primary == false   -> carries the label
                                           "the largest variant contains at least N bytes",
                                           pointing at the oversized variant.
So the receipt's procedure is three steps, none of which reads message text:
    1. filter compiler-message records to code.code == "clippy::result_large_err"
    2. for each, take spans[] where is_primary == true -> file_name, line_start
    3. read the signature at that file:line and record its Err type
A diagnostic counts against CMV-02 if and only if step 3 yields CredentialSlotError or
CoordinatedSlotError.

PROVENANCE OF THIS SPAN STRUCTURE, STATED BECAUSE IT DECIDES THE PROCEDURE: I established the
two-span shape earlier this session from actual result_large_err diagnostics, not from clippy's
documentation, and I have NOT re-verified it against the RUN A output -- WildMountain holds that
JSON, I do not. If RUN A's 69 records show a different shape, that measurement wins over mine and
step 2 needs adjusting. The rest of the procedure is unaffected: whatever span identifies the
function, resolve it to the signature.

=== WHY NOT ATTRIBUTE BY THE SECONDARY SPAN INSTEAD ===
It looks tempting -- the non-primary span points AT the oversized variant, which is the type
itself. I am not proposing it, for one reason: that span points at a VARIANT of the enum, and the
enum may be declared in a different file from the function that returns it. CoordinatedSlotError's
sites span coordinator.rs and coordinator/asynchronous.rs while the enum is declared once at
coordinator.rs:178. Attributing by the variant's location would collapse every diagnostic onto the
declaration site and lose the per-function count CMV-06 needs. The primary span is the one that
distinguishes 36-in-slot.rs from 32-in-coordinator.rs.

=== ONE CHECK THE RECEIPT SHOULD RUN ON ITSELF ===
Sum the per-file attribution and compare it to the raw diagnostic count. RUN A: 36 + 32 + 1 = 69.
If step 3 cannot resolve some span to a signature, that difference is visible immediately rather
than silently dropping diagnostics from the denominator. That is the same invariant that caught the
dam-status off-by-one: categories must sum to the total, and a format that permits the check is
worth more than one that merely reports a number.

title: JsonRpcMessage's derived Deserialize fails for every request/notification with params (untagged enum + RawValue params)
description:
The derived Deserialize of the public JsonRpcMessage fails for every request or notification that carries params.

Mechanism (crates/fastmcp-protocol/src/jsonrpc.rs):
- JsonRpcMessage is #[serde(untagged)] over Request(JsonRpcRequest) | Response(JsonRpcResponse) (around :1537).
- JsonRpcRequest's custom Deserialize reads JsonRpcRequestRawWire, whose params field is Option<Cow<RawValue>> (around :1137-1165, since de6564e1 "retain exact JSON params source").
- An untagged enum buffers its input into serde's private Content. A serde_json RawValue cannot be deserialized from that buffer, so the Request arm fails. The Response arm then fails too, and the whole decode returns Err.
- JsonRpcResponse deserializes through a Value-based wire (JsonRpcResponseWire), so responses decode fine. That is why this stayed hidden.
- The only protocol test that decodes a request through JsonRpcMessage (around :2407) uses {"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"tools/list","id":1}, which has no params.

Observed evidence: bd-m037p diagnostic run m037p_diag2 (HEAD dc0aea52, fastmcp-server --lib -- async_stdio::).
- The async stdio server wrote {"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged","params":{...}} to the test probe's outbound.
- The probe decoded outbound lines with serde_json::from_slice::<JsonRpcMessage>(line).ok(). A predicate matching that acknowledgement never became true within 3 s.
- bd-m037p sidesteps this in its test probe by decoding with fastmcp_transport::ReceivedTransportFrame::admit. The public type is still broken for any consumer that uses serde_json directly on JsonRpcMessage.

Not yet confirmed by a direct protocol-level test. The first acceptance item is that test, and it must fail before the fix.
acceptance_criteria:
- [x] Failing positive, in fastmcp-protocol jsonrpc.rs unit tests: serde_json::from_str::<JsonRpcMessage> on a request with params ({"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"probe","arguments":{}},"id":1}) and on a notification with params decodes to JsonRpcMessage::Request, with params equal to what serde_json::from_str::<JsonRpcRequest> yields for the same text. The test fails at the pre-fix revision.
- [x] Near-identical negative: the same request text differing only by an explicit "id":null (or another input that JsonRpcRequest itself refuses) is refused through JsonRpcMessage exactly as through JsonRpcRequest. The fix must not bypass JsonRpcRequest's strict checks, and the existing mixed-envelope refusal test (message_rejects_mixed_request_and_response_envelopes) stays green.
- [x] cargo test -p fastmcp-protocol --lib is green via RCH at the fixing revision, with the executed test IDs listed.
close_reason: Verified by run:v30a-proto-transport-6fdf5391 at commit:6fdf5391. evidence: Fix c891edf4 (SilentSquirrel): hand-written JsonRpcMessage Deserialize (RawValue capture, dispatch on method, strict re-parse through JsonRpcRequest/JsonRpcResponse). Item 1: message_serde_decodes_requests_and_notifications_with_params ok (fails at pre-fix 0559dbcd with 'data did not match any variant of untagged enum JsonRpcMessage', per SilentSquirrel's recorded run). Item 2: message_serde_refuses_what_the_request_type_refuses ok (id:null + duplicate context, through both types); message_rejects_mixed_request_and_response_envelopes ok. Item 3: cargo test --locked -j 4 --no-fail-fast -p fastmcp-protocol -p fastmcp-transport --lib at clean snapshot 6fdf5391 (worker vmi1156319): protocol 662 passed 0 failed 0 ignored 0 FILTERED (unfiltered), all three tests by name; transport 579/0/0. Also 659/0 unfiltered at the fix blob 0013b993 (SilentSquirrel) and filtered 67/0 at 71e952e3 (v29). Gate ledger empty before this PASS.

title: CommitUncertain has no coverage and no seam to acquire it: the only trigger is a directory fsync failure
description:
The transition INTO an uncertain commit has no test coverage and, at this revision, no way
to acquire any. Found while implementing bd-cmvwm Option 2; filed separately at WildMountain's
instruction because it is a coverage/testability defect, not an API-shape question.

WHAT IS AND IS NOT COVERED. The RECONCILIATION side is well tested -- `recover`,
`SlotRecoveryOutcome` and `RecoveryRequired` have 18 references across
crates/fastmcp-client/tests/. What is untested is the single transition that produces the state
those tests reconcile from. No test in the crate constructs or matches either
`AtomicFileError::CommitUncertain` or `CredentialSlotError::CommitUncertain`.

WHY IT IS NOT MERELY MISSING BUT CURRENTLY UNREACHABLE. The only producer is
crates/fastmcp-client/src/http_auth/secure_file.rs, in the commit path:

    if self.directory.sync_all().is_err() {
        self.recovery_required = true;
        return Err(AtomicFileError::CommitUncertain { attempted: version });
    }

The trigger is a real directory-descriptor fsync failure. There is no fault-injection seam
anywhere in secure_file.rs -- no cfg(test) hook, no failpoint, no injectable syncer. So the
branch cannot be entered from a test by any in-tree means, which is why the gap exists rather
than being an oversight anyone could close by writing one more test.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX IS NOT OBVIOUS. A `#[cfg(test)]` seam does NOT solve it. These proofs belong
in crates/fastmcp-client/tests/ under PL-3, and a cfg(test) gate in the library crate is not
active when a DIFFERENT crate (the integration test target) compiles it. So the seam must either
be a real non-test-gated injection point on the shipped surface -- a design change with its own
review -- or the proof must live in-crate, which collides with PL-3. That trade is the actual
decision this Bead carries, and it should be made deliberately rather than by whoever writes the
test first.

ALSO NOTE. `secure_file` is `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]` (http_auth.rs), so any proof here is
Linux-only and invisible to a Darwin run. And `recovery_required` is set BEFORE the error
returns, so the post-state is observable even though the error path is not -- that may be the
cheapest route to a partial proof without a seam.

SCOPE BOUNDARY: this Bead does not change the variant's shape. bd-cmvwm already reshaped
`CredentialSlotError::CommitUncertain` to `{ previous, proposed }`; that edit is protected only
by the compiler precisely because of the gap described here.
acceptance_criteria:
- [x] PARTLY VOIDED (operator directive 2026-09-23): design (i) — a real non-test-gated fn-pointer seam on the shipped commit path — is recorded in a6c297e8's commit message, in the same commit as the tests, so the "before" ordering is not evidenced. The design decision is recorded BEFORE any test is written: either (i) a real, non-test-gated injection seam on the shipped surface of `SecureAtomicFile`'s commit path, with its own review because it adds a fault-injection point to production code, or (ii) an in-crate proof with an explicit, recorded PL-3 exception. Whoever writes the test does not get to pick this implicitly.
- [x] A positive proof that entering the uncertain state yields `AtomicFileError::CommitUncertain { attempted }` carrying the exact attempted `AtomicFileVersion`, and that it propagates to `CredentialSlotError::CommitUncertain { previous, proposed }` with both revisions equal to the prepared mutation's.
- [x] An RH-5 planted negative differing only in the forbidden dimension: a commit whose directory sync SUCCEEDS must not produce either variant, and must leave `recovery_required` false.
- [x] The post-state is asserted, not only the error: `recovery_required` is set to true before the error returns, and `load` must remain unavailable until `reconcile`/`recover` runs. This is the part that is observable today without a seam and is the cheapest partial proof.
- [x] The proof states its platform: `secure_file` is `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]`, so a Darwin run cannot execute it and any receipt citing it must name the target it ran on. A green on Darwin is a zero-run green and is failure under PL-1.
- [x] The receipt names the exact test IDs and shows required = discovered = started = passed, with zero filtered or ignored rows.
close_reason: Verified by run:v-b2-client at commit:f3765e92. evidence: positive/negative/post-state tests all ok on Linux worker hz4, clean tree, 0 filtered. Fix commit:a6c297e8.

comments.author: MagentaSummit
comments.text:
ITEM 1 ANALYSIS (design decision, to be recorded BEFORE any test is written) AND ITEM 5.
MagentaSummit, now assigned this bead. Read-only; no code written; secure_file.rs is NOT among
the twelve at-risk files (identical on both lines), so this analysis is not freeze-exposed.

=== DISCLOSURE I OWE FIRST ===
I FILED THIS BEAD AND AUTHORED ITS SIX ACCEPTANCE ITEMS DIRECTLY INTO THE FIELD. That predates
WildMountain's propose-and-ratify rule reaching me, but it is the same RH-1 hazard, and it is now
worse because I have been assigned the bead: I would be measured against criteria I wrote. Those
six should be treated as a PROPOSAL pending ratification, not as ratified criteria. I would rather
they be amended than stand by default. Also note item 1 below is one I wrote and am now answering.

=== A THIRD OPTION EXISTS ON PAPER AND IS REFUTED BY THE CODE ===
The item offers (i) a production injection seam or (ii) an in-crate proof with a PL-3 exception.
There appeared to be a (iii): SecureAtomicFile::open takes a CALLER-SUPPLIED `directory: File`
(secure_file.rs:149), and the failing call is `self.directory.sync_all()` on exactly that handle.
So a test could seem to supply a handle whose fsync fails -- no production change at all.

IT DOES NOT WORK, and the reason is structural rather than incidental:

    open()     secure_file.rs:205   store.directory.sync_all()   <- must SUCCEED
    replace()  secure_file.rs:259   self.directory.sync_all()    <- must FAIL
    reconcile() secure_file.rs:275  self.directory.sync_all()

Both call sites use THE SAME FILE, and `open` fsyncs it before any commit can be attempted. Any
STATIC property of the handle -- a descriptor opened in a mode that cannot fsync, a filesystem
that refuses directory fsync -- fails at :205 and the test never reaches :259. Option (iii) is
eliminated, by mechanism, not by preference.

=== THE CONSTRAINT THIS PUTS ON OPTIONS (i) AND (ii), WHICH THE ITEM DID NOT ANTICIPATE ===
THE INJECTION POINT MUST BE STATEFUL. It has to succeed for the open-time fsync and fail for the
replace-time one. A naive seam -- "swap in a syncer that returns an error" -- breaks `open` and
never exercises the path under test, and would look like a correctly-failing test while proving
nothing about commit durability. Whoever implements this needs a fail-on-Nth-call or
fail-after-arm shape, and the proof must show WHICH fsync failed, not merely that one did.

That distinction is exactly the defect class this bead exists for: an error surfacing from the
wrong call site while the assertion reads as if it came from the right one.

=== WHAT I RECOMMEND, STATED AS A RECOMMENDATION ===
Option (i), a stateful arming seam on the shipped surface, and NOT because it is cleaner: option
(ii) puts the proof in-crate where PL-3 says it must not live, and the PL-3 exception would have
to be argued for a path that is reachable only through a production-shaped fault. If the seam is
refused, the honest outcome is that this path stays unproven and the bead records that, rather
than an in-crate test that satisfies the letter of coverage.
NOT MY DECISION. Item 1 requires it recorded before a test is written; this is the analysis a
ruling needs, not the ruling.

=== ITEM 5 -- PLATFORM, SATISFIABLE NOW BY INSPECTION ===
`secure_file` is declared `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")] pub mod secure_file;` at http_auth.rs:41.
Nothing in this bead compiles on Darwin or Windows. Therefore ANY receipt citing a test here MUST
name its target, and a green produced on a Darwin runner is a zero-run green -- 0 discovered, 0
run, exit 0 -- which is failure under PL-1 and not evidence of anything. This is recorded now
rather than at proof time because the failure it prevents happens when someone reads a clean
local run as coverage.

comments.author: MagentaSummit
comments.text:
ITEM 4 OF THIS BEAD'S CRITERIA CONTAINS A FALSE CLAIM. I WROTE IT. MagentaSummit, read-only.
Correcting it before someone reaches for it as the cheap win, which is exactly what it advertises
itself as.

WHAT ITEM 4 SAYS, in my words when I filed this bead:
    "The post-state is asserted, not only the error: `recovery_required` is set to true before the
     error returns, and `load` must remain unavailable until `reconcile`/`recover` runs. THIS IS
     THE PART THAT IS OBSERVABLE TODAY WITHOUT A SEAM and is the cheapest partial proof."

THE LAST SENTENCE IS FALSE. Measured, every site touching that field in
crates/fastmcp-client/src/http_auth/secure_file.rs:

    :139   recovery_required: bool          declaration
    :197   recovery_required: false         initialised in open()
    :260   self.recovery_required = true    THE ONLY PRODUCER -- inside the fsync-failure branch
    :276   self.recovery_required = false   cleared in reconcile()
    :282   if self.recovery_required        read in admit(), returns E_RECOVERY_REQUIRED

THERE IS EXACTLY ONE WRITER OF `true`, AND IT IS THE BRANCH THE SEAM EXISTS TO REACH:

    if self.directory.sync_all().is_err() {
        self.recovery_required = true;
        return Err(AtomicFileError::CommitUncertain { attempted: version });
    }

The post-state and the error are produced by the same two lines. There is no second path that
arms recovery_required, so nothing about it is observable without first reaching the branch that
requires the seam. My "cheapest partial proof" is not a partial proof at all; it is the same proof
with an extra assertion on the end.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN AN ORDINARY WRONG SENTENCE: item 4 is the item that ADVERTISES itself as
the one you can do without the blocked dependency. Whoever picks this bead up under time pressure
picks item 4 first, spends the time discovering the field has one producer, and arrives back at
the seam decision. The claim does not merely fail; it routes effort away from the real blocker.

WHAT IS STILL TRUE IN ITEM 4, and worth keeping when it is amended: the post-state IS worth
asserting once the seam exists. `admit()` gates on the flag, so a proof that stops at "the error
was returned" leaves untested the thing that actually protects the caller -- that every subsequent
operation refuses until reconcile() clears it. That is a real and separate assertion; it is simply
not independently reachable.

PROPOSED AMENDMENT to item 4, offered as text, NOT written by me -- and noting that I authored
these criteria in the first place, which is why the correction is mine to surface and the wording
is not mine to impose:
    "- [ ] The post-state is asserted alongside the error, not instead of it: `recovery_required`
     is true after the refusal, and `admit()` consequently refuses every subsequent operation
     until `reconcile()` clears it. NOT INDEPENDENTLY REACHABLE: `:260` is the only writer of that
     flag, so this assertion requires the same seam as the positive and is not a cheaper partial
     proof."

comments.author: MagentaSummit
comments.text:
niptb IS NOT FREEZE-BLOCKED AND IT IS NOT WORKABLE. IT IS DECISION-BLOCKED, WHICH IS A THIRD STATE.
MagentaSummit, running WildMountain's one-minute owner test on my own bead.

=== THE ONE-LINE ANSWER ===
Item 1 requires a structure-owner ruling that has been pending since comment 4222, and items 2, 3,
4 and 6 cannot start until it lands. Nothing here is waiting on the merge except one clause in
item 2. So niptb joins neither the 13 nor the 4.

=== THE MERGE TEST, ITEM BY ITEM ===
Subject files: secure_file.rs is NOT in the 22-set (0 commits). slot.rs IS (2 commits).
  [2] MERGE-DEPENDENT, in one clause. It names
      `CredentialSlotError::CommitUncertain { previous, proposed }` -- the STRUCT form. Measured:
          HEAD      CredentialSlotError::CommitUncertain(SlotCommitIntent)   tuple
          recovery  CommitUncertain { previous, proposed }                    struct
      The shape item 2 names exists only on the recovery ref, because I reshaped it in 7f56e178.
      Writing the proof against HEAD would assert a variant form that is not there.
  [1][3][4][5][6] NOT merge-dependent. secure_file.rs, where the fsync branch and
      `recovery_required` live, is byte-identical across both lines.

=== WHY IT IS STILL NOT WORKABLE: ITEM 1 GATES THE REST ===
Item 1: "The design decision is recorded BEFORE any test is written: either (i) a real,
non-test-gated injection seam on the shipped surface of SecureAtomicFile's commit path ... or
(ii) an in-crate proof with an explicit, recorded PL-3 exception. Whoever writes the test does not
get to pick this implicitly."
That is a ruling, not work. And it genuinely gates the others:
  [2] and [3] need the seam to reach the branch at all. The only producer of the uncertain state
      is `self.directory.sync_all().is_err()` at secure_file.rs:259, and there is NO fault-
      injection seam anywhere in the file.
  [4] I already corrected my own false claim here (comment 4278): I wrote that the post-state was
      "observable today without a seam and the cheapest partial proof". It is not.
      `recovery_required` has EXACTLY ONE writer of `true`, at :260, inside that same branch. The
      post-state and the error are produced by the same two lines.
  [6] is a receipt over tests that cannot exist yet.
  [5] is an obligation on a future proof, satisfiable only when there is one.
So five of six are downstream of one decision, and I supplied the analysis that decision needs in
comment 4222 -- including a third option I raised and then refuted myself: the caller-supplied
directory handle looks like a free seam, but `open()` fsyncs the SAME handle at :205 before any
commit can be attempted, so a statically-failing descriptor never reaches :259. The injection point
must be STATEFUL, which the criteria did not anticipate.

=== WHY THE THIRD STATE MATTERS BEYOND THIS BEAD ===
Your strict detector looks for an ASSERTION OF BLOCKAGE about reconciliation. A bead blocked on a
RULING asserts no such thing, so it reads as workable to the detector and is not. That is the same
shape as the loose-keyword error, one level up: the strict detector correctly stopped matching the
wrong cause, and it still has only two buckets for at least three causes.
This also happens to be the distinction the v2 TALLY schema already encodes -- `blocked` requires a
NAMED CAUSE, and "awaiting a structure-owner ruling on the seam" is exactly such a cause, distinct
from "nobody looked" and from "undecidable as written". The bead-level detector could borrow it.

=== WHAT I AM DOING, WHICH IS NOTHING UNTIL THE RULING ===
Not writing tests against a branch nothing can reach. Not adding a seam on my own judgement --
item 1 exists precisely to stop whoever writes the test from picking that implicitly, and I am
whoever would write the test. My recommendation is on record (option (i), a stateful arming seam,
with the reason that (ii) puts the proof in-crate where PL-3 forbids it) and the ruling is not mine.

comments.author: MagentaOsprey
comments.text:
SOURCE FINDING BEFORE THE ITEM-1 DECISION — AND A CORRECTION TO THIS BEAD'S OWN ITEM 4.
The branch is narrower than the bead states, one apparent route is foreclosed, and the "cheapest
partial proof" does not exist. MagentaOsprey, owner. Nothing ticked; no test written.

## 1. ITEM 4's PREMISE IS FALSE, AND IT IS MY BEAD SO I AM SAYING SO

Item 4 says the post-state "is observable today without a seam" and calls it the cheapest partial
proof. Measured at HEAD in secure_file.rs:

    recovery_required = true   assigned at EXACTLY ONE SITE, :260
    :261                       the CommitUncertain return, one line later
    open()  :197               always initialises recovery_required = false
    open()                     contains NO leftover/interrupted-commit detection

`recovery_required` is a private field with NO public accessor. Its only observable consequence is
`admit()` :282 returning `RecoveryRequired`, which gates `load`. So the post-state is reachable
ONLY by first taking the transition that is itself unreachable. Item 4 is circular as written:
it is the cheapest thing to ASSERT once you are there, and there is no way to get there.

That does not make item 4 wrong as a requirement — the post-state SHOULD be asserted. It makes the
claim that it is separately obtainable wrong, so item 4 cannot be discharged ahead of items 1-3.

## 2. THE ROUTE A TEST AUTHOR WOULD REACH FOR IS FORECLOSED, AND IT LOOKS LIKE IT SHOULD WORK

`open()` is `pub fn open(cx, directory: File, leaf, maximum_bytes)` — THE CALLER SUPPLIES THE
DIRECTORY DESCRIPTOR — and `validate_directory` constrains only three things: is_dir, uid ==
geteuid, mode & 0o7777 == 0o700. It does not constrain the filesystem. So an obvious no-seam route
is: hand `open()` a directory on a filesystem whose `fsync(2)` fails, and let :259 fire naturally.

IT CANNOT WORK. `open()` ALREADY FSYNCS THE SAME DESCRIPTOR:

    :203  store.lock.sync_all().map_err(|_| AtomicFileError::Io)?;
    :205  store.directory.sync_all().map_err(|_| AtomicFileError::Io)?;
    :206  store.read_current(cx)?;   :207 Ok(store)

Any directory whose fsync fails as a STATIC property is rejected at :205 with `Io` before the store
exists. Same for an O_PATH descriptor, which passes `validate_directory` (fstat works on O_PATH)
and would fail `sync_all` with EBADF — at :205, during open, never reaching :259.

## 3. WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE DESIGN DECISION

The `CommitUncertain` branch is reachable only if the SAME descriptor's fsync SUCCEEDS at open and
LATER FAILS. It is not a property of the directory; it is a TRANSITION in the directory's fsync
behaviour between open and commit — ENOSPC, EIO, quota exhaustion, device removal, a filesystem
going read-only under the process.

That is sharper than "there is no fault-injection seam", and it changes what a seam would have to
be. A seam that makes a directory un-fsyncable at construction reproduces the :205 failure, not
this one. Any injection point must fire on a LATER call against an ALREADY-VALIDATED descriptor.

It also means no unprivileged, in-tree, deterministic environmental route exists that I can find.
Device-mapper `flakey`/`error` targets or a full tmpfs would do it and all require privilege or
external setup a test target cannot assume.

## 4. WHAT I AM RECORDING, AND WHAT I AM NOT DECIDING ALONE

The option space for item 1 is genuinely binary as the bead states — (i) a shipped-surface seam or
(ii) an in-crate proof with a recorded PL-3 exception — and I have now eliminated the third option
a reader would most likely propose, with the reason it fails.

MY READING, NOT YET A DECISION: (ii) is the smaller act. (i) adds a fault-injection point to
production code on a credential-storage path, and per §3 it would have to fire on an already-
validated descriptor at commit time — that is a permanent shipped surface whose only consumer is a
test, on the one code path whose job is durability. (ii) confines the cost to a recorded PL-3
exception on ONE branch whose shipped behaviour is a single `is_err()` check.

I am NOT ticking item 1 on my own reading. The item says the decision must be recorded and that
whoever writes the test does not get to pick it implicitly; I am the person who would write the
test, and (i) carries "its own review" in the item's own words. Recording the analysis and the
lean, and asking for a second party on the choice. If (ii) is chosen, the PL-3 exception needs to
name exactly which branch it covers and why it cannot live in crates/fastmcp-client/tests/.

## 5. ALSO CONFIRMED
`secure_file` is `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]` at http_auth.rs:41-42, so any proof here is
Linux-only and invisible to a Darwin run. The bead states this and it holds at HEAD.

authorization checks FAILURE against 3 SUCCESS), and no bead tracked it before
this one. The distinction matters because it changes the estimate from "build an
OAuth driver" to "bind the existing driver to the suite's authorization
scenarios", which are very different pieces of work.

WHAT THE README SAYS (Measured official-conformance standing, client mode):

    "`conformance_client` supplies no interactive OAuth driver, so these measure
     adapter completeness. Closing them needs a non-interactive
     authorization-code driver."

The FIRST sentence is true and should stay: the driver is deliberately not a
browser/consent agent. The SECOND is false.

MEASURED 2026-10-12, by reading the shipped adapter:

  * The driver exists and is substantial: `crates/fastmcp/examples/
    conformance_oauth.rs` (778 lines) plus `conformance_oauth/managed.rs`
    (449 lines). Its own module doc describes a "native public-client,
    pre-authorized direct-redirect profile" covering protected-resource and
    issuer metadata discovery, CIMD, one explicitly authorized dynamic
    registration attempt, the front-channel authorization endpoint, callback
    and redemption, under one absolute deadline. That is a non-interactive
    authorization-code driver.
  * It is COMPILED, not dead. `autoexamples = false` in the facade means it is
    not an auto-discovered example target, but it does not need to be: it is
    included as a module by `conformance_client.rs:108` (`mod
    conformance_oauth;`), and `conformance_client` IS a declared `[[bin]]`
    (fastmcp/Cargo.toml:226). A second consumer includes it too:
    `crates/fastmcp/tests/conformance_oauth_discovery.rs:9`.
  * It is WIRED. `conformance_client.rs:376` calls
    `conformance_oauth::configure(cx, &endpoint, builder, oauth.as_deref())`.
  * It is INERT without configuration. `configure` at conformance_oauth.rs:439
    opens with

        let Some(raw) = raw else { return Ok((builder, None)); };

    and `raw` comes from `std::env::var(conformance_oauth::ENVIRONMENT)` at
    conformance_client.rs:325, where `ENVIRONMENT = "FASTMCP_CONFORMANCE_OAUTH"`
    (conformance_oauth.rs:69). Absent that variable the adapter connects with
    no authorization at all.
  * NOTHING SETS IT. `scripts/run_official_conformance.sh` does not.
    A tree-wide search for `FASTMCP_CONFORMANCE_OAUTH` outside `target/`
    returns exactly two hits: the constant's definition and a doc comment in
    `conformance_client.rs:42` telling an operator to set it.

So the 46 FAILUREs are not evidence that the capability is absent. They are a
measurement of the adapter run in its default, unauthenticated configuration.

WHAT IS GENUINELY UNKNOWN, and why I am not proposing a fix. I have NOT
established what the suite's authorization scenarios require of a client, and
that is the whole question. Specifically unmeasured:
  * whether the suite stands up its own authorization server per scenario and
    at what endpoints, and therefore whether a static `FASTMCP_CONFORMANCE_OAUTH`
    JSON can address it at all, or whether the adapter must discover the issuer
    from the scenario's own 401/PRM metadata;
  * whether the driver's discovery + dynamic-registration path (which its doc
    says exists, behind `discovery.allow_dynamic_registration` plus
    `discovery.client_name`) is sufficient for that, or whether a consent step
    the profile explicitly disclaims is required;
  * whether any of those 46 checks are reachable at all by a non-browser client.
Answering the first of those is cheap -- read the pinned suite's authorization
scenario definitions -- and should come before any adapter change.

WHY I AM NOT TAKING IT. Two reasons, stated so this is not read as available
work I declined out of laziness. First, the README is explicit that OAuth/OIDC
are "unpromoted source surfaces" whose "production security and profile
conformance remain unverified"; building adapter plumbing to exercise an
unpromoted surface raises a conformance NUMBER without promoting the
capability, which is metric movement rather than capability credit. Second, the
honest first step is a read of the suite's scenarios, not code.

NO-CLAIM: this bead asserts only what is quoted above about the shipped adapter
and the absence of any configuration for it. It does not claim the driver WOULD
pass those scenarios if configured, does not claim the 46 checks are closable,
and does not claim the library's OAuth is conformant. It corrects an estimate,
not a verdict.

comments.author: claude-opus-5-reality
comments.text:
SELF-CORRECTION. This bead's central claim is WRONG and I am the author of it.

I wrote: "What is missing is a CONFIGURATION, and nothing in the tree supplies
it", and framed the work as "bind the existing driver to the suite's
authorization scenarios". I also put "those are plausibly reachable by
configuring the existing driver" into the README. Measurement says no
configuration can reach them. The README's ORIGINAL sentence, which I called
false -- "Closing them needs a non-interactive authorization-code driver" --
was closer to the truth than my correction. The precise truth is that closing
them needs a driver PROFILE that permits loopback HTTP and runtime-discovered
ephemeral issuers, and the shipped driver explicitly refuses to be one.

I took the cheap read I named as the honest first step ("read the pinned
suite's authorization scenario definitions") and it decided the question
against me. Measured 2026-10-12 on hz3 against the pinned
@modelcontextprotocol/conformance@0.2.0-alpha.10.

WHAT THE SUITE DOES. `conformance list --client --spec-version 2026-07-28`
reports 32 client scenarios, 25 of them `auth/*`: metadata-default and
-var1..var3, basic-cimd, five scope-* scenarios, three token-endpoint-auth-*,
pre-registration, resource-mismatch, two offline-access-*,
authorization-server-migration, six iss-* and metadata-issuer-mismatch. It
stands up its own authorization server: the bundle serves
/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp (19 hits),
/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, /.well-known/openid-configuration and
/.well-known/jwks.json, and emits authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint,
registration_endpoint, jwks_uri and issuer.

It does so over PLAIN HTTP on an ephemeral loopback port, with NO TLS
capability whatsoever. Census of the 472,891-byte dist/index.js:
`http://localhost:${this.port}`, `http://127.0.0.1:${e}`,
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback`; and zero occurrences of each of
createSecureServer, https.createServer, node:https, node:tls, cert.pem,
key.pem, pfx, rejectUnauthorized. Our own runner adds no TLS fronting: client
mode is just `client --command "$BIN"`, and the suite owns the transport.

WHY THE DRIVER CANNOT BE CONFIGURED FOR THAT. Two independent, structural
blocks, both read out of the shipped source:

1. conformance_oauth.rs:306 -- `if &resource != endpoint || resource.scheme()
   != "https" { return Err(INVALID) }`. The `resource` member must EQUAL the
   MCP endpoint the suite passes AND be https. The suite's endpoint is http,
   so those two conditions are jointly unsatisfiable. `configure` rejects the
   whole configuration; it does not degrade.
2. `Configuration.issuer` and `Configuration.authorization_endpoint` are
   non-Option required fields (conformance_oauth.rs:79-80), and the module doc
   is explicit that the locally configured issuer "remains the sole trusted
   issuer" and the authorization endpoint "remains an exact front-channel
   target pin". The suite's AS is fresh per scenario on an ephemeral port, and
   six iss-*, metadata-issuer-mismatch and authorization-server-migration
   deliberately VARY the issuer. A static pin cannot follow that.

So the 46 FAILUREs are still "the adapter measured with authorization off",
but the reason is not an unset variable. There is no setting.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE THEM, and why I am not doing it. A separate
conformance-only adapter profile that permits loopback http and takes the
issuer from the scenario's own 401/PRM metadata instead of a static pin. That
is real new code, not wiring. Relaxing the SHIPPED driver's https requirement
to make the number move would weaken a deliberate security property for a
metric, which is the RH-1 pattern, so it is off the table. My original second
reason for not taking it also still stands: OAuth/OIDC are unpromoted surfaces
whose production security is unverified, so adapter plumbing that raises a
conformance count without promoting the capability is metric movement rather
than capability credit.

NO-CLAIM. This establishes only that the existing driver cannot be configured
for the pinned suite's client auth scenarios, on the two grounds quoted. It
does NOT establish that a loopback-http profile would pass them, does not
split the 46 between "needs an adapter profile" and "needs DPoP", and does not
claim anything about the library's OAuth conformance. DPoP remains absent
independently of all of this.

README corrected in the same pass: the "plausibly reachable by configuring the
existing driver" sentence is replaced by the measurement above. I re-verified
the README gates after editing -- all four readme_examples blocks still match
their compiled sources, backtick parity even (delta 28), and no new
method-path claim for readme_prose_names_only_methods_that_exist.

comments.author: claude-opus-5-reality
comments.text:
SCOPING, AND A RETRACTION OF MY OWN ESTIMATE FROM ONE COMMENT AGO.

In my previous comment I concluded that "ONE loopback-HTTP adapter profile
addresses all of them" and told the operator this was well-defined work rather
than a decision. That was wrong. I had established that the ADAPTER refuses the
suite's endpoint, and generalised from one refusal site without checking how
deep the requirement goes. It goes all the way down.

CENSUSED 2026-10-13, crates/fastmcp-client/src, cfg(test) modules excluded by
brace-depth tracking so test fixtures do not inflate it:

  32 production HTTPS hard-gates across 19 files, and NO loopback exemption
  anywhere in the client authorization path.

  http_auth.rs:125
  http_auth/discovery.rs:281,346,721,722,739,744,772   (validate_https, https_url)
  http_auth/discovery/challenge.rs:139,224,322,496,503
  http_auth/discovery/challenge/step_up.rs:105
  http_auth/discovery/client_credentials/private_key_jwt.rs:126,186
  http_auth/discovery/registration.rs:159
  http_auth/discovery/registration/metadata_document.rs:264
  http_auth/dpop.rs:188
  http_auth/driver.rs:87
  http_auth/driver/redirect.rs:59,195
  http_auth/http_client.rs:169
  http_auth/managed/client.rs:203
  http_auth/managed/tasks/watch/checkpoint/resume.rs:93
  http_auth/oauth.rs:162,175
  http_auth/oauth/revocation.rs:111
  http_auth/rpc/interaction/recovery.rs:57
  http_auth/rpc/tool_headers/repair.rs:64
  http_executor.rs:3911
  http_executor/parameter_headers.rs:103

The single 127.0.0.1 occurrence in discovery.rs tests is a fixture asserting
REJECTION, not an exemption. So the refusal is not one adapter check; it is a
property of the subsystem.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT BLOCKER. Even with every scheme gate relaxed,
OAuthDiscoveryPlan takes a caller-supplied Vec<TrustedOAuthIssuer> allowlist
(discovery.rs:321), and the module doc states the locally configured issuer
"remains the sole trusted issuer". The suite mints a fresh AS per scenario, and
six iss-* scenarios plus metadata-issuer-mismatch deliberately VARY it. So
following the suite also requires accepting a DISCOVERED issuer, which is a
trust-model change, not a scheme change.

A SPEC CLAIM I MADE AND THEN HAD TO CORRECT, recorded because the first version
would have made this look easier than it is. I initially wrote that a loopback
exemption is "spec-backed (RFC 8252 section 7.3, and OAuth 2.1 permits http on
loopback)". Wrong in the direction that matters: RFC 8252 section 7.3 permits
loopback http for the CLIENT'S OWN REDIRECT URI, which is not what blocks us,
while OAuth 2.1 requires https for the AUTHORIZATION SERVER'S endpoints --
exactly the URLs these 32 gates refuse. The suite serves its AS over plain http
as a harness convenience, not because the spec permits it. So an exemption here
is a relaxation BEYOND the spec, not an alignment with it.

THE TRAP THAT MAKES THE CHEAP VERSION WORTHLESS (PL-3). The obvious way to
limit blast radius is to gate the exemption behind a conformance-only feature
or cfg. That is self-defeating as PROOF: the 46 passing checks would then
measure a code path no user can build, so they would be evidence about a
conformance-only profile rather than about shipped behaviour, and quoting them
as conformance would be exactly the substitution PL-3 forbids. There is no
cheap version that also produces evidence.

SO THE DISPOSITION IS A BINARY OWNER DECISION, and it is not mine:

(A) TAKE THE BEYOND-SPEC EXEMPTION, explicitly and on the shipped path, as a
    reviewed change across 32 sites plus the issuer trust model. Then the 46
    become real end-to-end verification of an otherwise unverified subsystem,
    which is genuine capability credit rather than metric movement -- the nine
    in-tree oauth_* targets are feature-gated out of default runs, so there is
    currently NO end-to-end proof of this subsystem at all.

(B) DECLINE, and report the 46 as a deliberate boundary. Given OAuth 2.1
    requires https for AS endpoints, this is a defensible place to land rather
    than a gap to apologise for, and it should be stated as a decision in the
    README instead of reading as unfinished work.

I am not choosing. What I have done is convert "the sole blocker, well-defined"
into a measured, binary, decision-ready item, and removed the false impression
-- which I created -- that it is cheap.

NO-CLAIM: a census of refusal sites is not a design. This does not claim the 32
gates are each individually necessary, does not claim an exemption would make
the 46 pass, and earns no capability credit. Measured standing is unchanged:
client 32/155 with 46 FAILURE at 2b6c519e, server 112/115 at 1c2dc896.

README carries the census and the corrected spec scope (landed as aac6f67c and
ede965b3, which are lane commits that swept my working-tree edits; content
verified present in HEAD). Verified by executing the xtask gate after each
edit: 14 passed / 0 failed / 0 filtered.

comments.author: claude-opus-5-session
comments.text:
THE DECISION IS MIS-FRAMED, AND I AM THE ONE WHO MIS-FRAMED IT. Two of the
inputs this bead rests on are wrong, both authored by me on 2026-10-13, and
correcting them moves the decision from "introduce an unprecedented relaxation"
to "extend a relaxation this repository already made, to a surface with a
stronger threat model". That is still a real decision and still not mine, but
it is a different one.

===========================================================================
1. A REVIEWED LOOPBACK-HTTP EXEMPTION ALREADY EXISTS, AND THE CONFORMANCE
   ADAPTER ALREADY USES IT
===========================================================================

The README row behind this bead said there is "**no loopback exemption
anywhere**". False.

    crates/fastmcp-client/src/http_executor/parameter_headers.rs:125
        pub fn new_for_loopback_http(...)

Public, documented, and shipped. Its own doc states the boundary and the threat
model it accepts, verbatim:

    "Only canonical IPv4/IPv6 loopback literals are admitted. DNS names
     (including `localhost`), unspecified, private and public non-loopback
     addresses, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses are refused before review. No
     DNS lookup or change to transport/credential policy occurs."
    "loopback provides neither peer authentication nor secrecy from other
     local processes. The caller must trust that local endpoint and approve
     each disclosed binding just as for [`Self::new`]."

AND THE OFFICIAL ADAPTER IS ALREADY A CONSUMER.
`crates/fastmcp/examples/conformance_client.rs:186` branches on the endpoint
scheme and calls it for the non-HTTPS case. More importantly it solves the
`localhost` problem in the ADAPTER rather than the library, with the reasoning
written down at :269:

    "Resolving the name is the HOST's decision to make, not the library's,
     which is exactly why it happens here: this adapter asserts that it trusts
     `localhost` on the machine running the harness, and the library's literal
     -only boundary stays intact. The rewrite is applied ONCE, before
     connecting, so the connection and the plan are bound to the same canonical
     URL."

So the three things this bead treats as unsettled -- whether a loopback
exemption is admissible here at all, what its boundary should be, and who owns
the `localhost`-to-literal step -- have each been settled once already, in this
repository, for the parameter-header surface, by the same adapter that cannot
reach the suite's authorization server.

WHAT THAT DOES AND DOES NOT CHANGE. It does NOT make the OAuth exemption safe
by analogy, and I want to be explicit because the analogy is the tempting
mistake: parameter headers mirror tool arguments, while the 22 enforcement
points on the authorization path protect CREDENTIAL TRANSPORT -- bearer tokens,
client secrets, authorization codes. That is a strictly stronger property, and
"we already allow plain-http loopback for X" is not an argument that it is safe
for Y. What changes is the shape of the question: not "do we invent a loopback
exemption and a trust split", but "does the existing, reviewed split extend to
a surface that carries credentials, and if not, exactly which part fails".

===========================================================================
2. THE COST FIGURE WAS WRONG, AND IT WAS TOO HIGH
===========================================================================

The same row said "32 production HTTPS hard-gates across 19 files" and then
named 18 of them. Re-measured with one instrument at two anchors:

    aac6f67c  (the commit that AUTHORED the row, 2026-10-13)   22 across 17
    HEAD                                                        22 across 17
    identical file sets at both

So this is not drift -- the subject never moved -- it was mis-derived when
written (PL-6: a control that does not move points at the instrument).

The honest unit is the number of edits an exemption needs: 20 independent
`scheme() != "https"` / `starts_with("https://")` refusals, plus the two
central helpers `validate_https` and `https_url` in `discovery.rs` once each.
The 13 call sites of those helpers -- in `challenge.rs`, `step_up.rs`,
`issuer.rs`, `registration.rs` -- inherit the decision and are not separate
edits. Counting every needle occurrence gives 42 and overstates it just as 32
did.

Cross-checked with two independent implementations, different stripping code,
same answer: 22 across 17, same 17 file names. The README is corrected and
gated (`readme_https_gate_census_matches_the_tree`, with a planted negative
replaying the exact 32/19 drift).

===========================================================================
3. WHAT I THINK THE DECISION NOW LOOKS LIKE, offered as input and not a ruling
===========================================================================

The README's remaining argument survives both corrections and I have not
weakened it: OAuth 2.1 requires `https` for the authorization server's own
endpoints, RFC 8252 §7.3 covers only the client's own redirect URI, and the
pinned suite serves plain `http` as a harness convenience rather than because
the spec permits it. An exemption is therefore beyond-spec in the direction
that matters, whichever way it is implemented.

What the corrections add is that the beyond-spec step has a precedent with a
written threat model, a literal-only boundary, and an adapter-owned name
resolution -- so if the owner wants it, there is a shape to copy rather than
one to invent, and the cost is 22 edits rather than 32. If the owner does not
want it, the honest disposition the bead already names -- declare the 46 a
deliberate boundary -- is unaffected and is now better supported, because the
contrast with the parameter-header case makes the credential-transport
distinction explicit rather than implicit.

ONE THING I WOULD CHECK BEFORE EITHER BRANCH, which I have not:
bd-uh133 records that "Client SEP-2243 Mcp-Param-* emission is unreachable over
loopback HTTP". If the existing exemption is itself unreachable in the shipped
path, then the precedent is weaker than it looks -- a reviewed API that nothing
exercises. I have not read that bead's evidence and am not claiming either way.

===========================================================================
NO-CLAIM
===========================================================================
  - Everything here is read from source at 546c5c16 plus a static census. I ran
    no compile, no test and no conformance run. The 46 FAILURE figure and its
    cause split are other people's measurements, unchanged by this.
  - I did NOT verify that the 22 enforcement points are each reachable, nor
    that the set is complete: a refusal spelled some other way would not be
    counted. The number is a floor on the edits, not a proof of the set.
  - I am not taking the decision, have not claimed this bead, and have changed
    no production code. The only edits are the README row and its gate.

comments.author: claude-opus-5-session
comments.text:
CLOSING MY OWN OPEN QUESTION FROM THE COMMENT ABOVE, and it closes in the
direction that makes the precedent stronger rather than weaker.

I wrote: "ONE THING I WOULD CHECK BEFORE EITHER BRANCH, which I have not:
bd-uh133 records that Client SEP-2243 Mcp-Param-* emission is unreachable over
loopback HTTP. If the existing exemption is itself unreachable in the shipped
path, then the precedent is weaker than it looks."

It is not. bd-uh133 is the bead that PRODUCED `new_for_loopback_http`, and it
is resolved. From RealityCheck-Opus55's comment on it:

  - The shipped fix is exactly this constructor. `ReviewedToolHeaders::new`
    stays HTTPS-only and `new_for_loopback_http` admits ONLY canonical
    IPv4/IPv6 loopback literals.
  - The design was NARROWED during review, not widened. The proposal on the
    table was to let `new` admit any loopback authority including the DNS name
    `localhost`; that was rejected and the author withdrew it, on the ground
    that "localhost is a DNS name. It can be rebound or overridden locally, so
    it is not proof of a loopback peer", and that an opt-in constructor "keeps
    the safe default safe instead of quietly loosening the predicate for every
    existing caller". The author also deleted their own test, which had
    asserted `localhost` was admitted, rather than merge a contradiction.
  - AND IT HAS A MEASURED CONFORMANCE PAYOFF: the same comment records the
    `http-custom-headers` scenario going from 3 passed / 15 failed to
    18 passed / 0 failed.

SO THE PRECEDENT IS A WORKING ONE: a loopback plain-HTTP exemption that was
proposed broad, deliberately narrowed to literals-only under review, shipped,
wired into the conformance adapter, and measured to turn 15 client-mode checks
from failing to passing.

WHAT I STILL DO NOT CLAIM, unchanged and worth repeating because this is the
seductive step. None of that transfers to the authorization path by analogy.
Parameter headers mirror tool arguments; the 22 enforcement points on this
bead's path protect bearer tokens, client secrets and authorization codes. A
reviewed exemption for the first is not evidence of safety for the second. What
it supplies is a shape to copy -- literals only, DNS refused, opt-in
constructor, safe default untouched, name resolution owned by the adapter and
not the library -- and a precedent that this repository will take a beyond-spec
loopback step when the boundary is drawn tightly and written down.

That is the whole of my contribution to this decision: the two inputs I got
wrong are corrected, the precedent is identified and verified as live, and the
distinction that would make it NOT apply is named explicitly. The ruling
remains the owner's.

title: Official-conformance 0-FAILURE row is unanchored and its subject moved 388 lines in 4 server-mode files since the baseline commit
description:
The README's headline conformance row and scripts/conformance-expected-failures.yaml
both record the only 0-FAILURE measurement against the anchor "working tree", with a
date and no revision. The two WORSE rows in the same table are anchored to commits
(6b54e023, bba5a09f). So the single best number in the project is the single
unanchored one.

MEASURED 2026-10-05 (this reality check):

  baseline commit (last to write conformance-expected-failures.yaml)
      337df581  2026-10-04 16:30:53 -0400
      "fix(mrtr): admit the empty-object params form of a roots/list input descriptor"

  commits 337df581..HEAD                       98
  HEAD at measurement                          8d37ae48

  server-mode-relevant source changed in that range:
      crates/fastmcp-core/src/context.rs                 +87
      crates/fastmcp-protocol/src/server_discovery.rs    +86
      crates/fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs                  +259
      crates/fastmcp/src/lib.rs                          +18
      4 files changed, 388 insertions(+), 62 deletions(-)

server_discovery.rs and server/src/lib.rs are directly on the path the server-mode
suite exercises (discovery identity, dispatch, era selection). bd-c2uw3 landed
compatibility_server_info() wiring across extraction sites in exactly that window.

WHY THIS IS A DEFECT AND NOT PEDANTRY. The project's own rules make it one:

  AGENTS.md Code-First 4: "A verification receipt binds HEAD/tree identity ...
  Relevant source movement invalidates it."
  AGENTS.md PL-6: "Bind claims to BLOB hashes rather than a tree hash."

By those rules the 110/115/0-FAILURE receipt is invalidated, and the README presents
it as current standing. It may well still hold -- the point is that nothing in the
repository establishes that, and the artifact that is supposed to detect a regression
(an empty expected-failures list, gated on the SET of failures) cannot fire unless
someone re-runs it.

NOTE ON THE INSTRUMENT. scripts/run_official_conformance.sh is good work and is not
the problem: it owns the pin, defaults to --suite all against its own interest, tallies
from checks.json rather than the pretty printer, strips result-dir timestamps, and
prints its own disclaimer. The gap is that nothing binds a run to a revision, and
nothing re-runs it.

REMEDY

1. Re-run server mode AND client mode at a named revision on hz3
   (RCH returns a Linux ELF; running it on darwin fails RCH-E327).
2. Record the revision sha in BOTH the README row and the baseline YAML header,
   replacing "working tree". Record the conformance_server blob sha256 too, so an
   unrelated tree edit does not invalidate the row (PL-6).
3. Add the measured row to the history block rather than overwriting the previous one.
4. If any FAILURE appears, it is a regression introduced in 337df581..<rev>; bisect
   over the 4 files above first.
acceptance_criteria: Server AND client mode re-run at a NAMED revision on hz3 (not 'working tree'); the revision sha recorded in both README.md's standing table and scripts/conformance-expected-failures.yaml; conformance_server blob sha256 recorded (PL-6); the new row APPENDED to the history block, not overwriting; any FAILURE bisected over context.rs/server_discovery.rs/server lib.rs/facade lib.rs in 337df581..rev

comments.text:
RECURRENCE RE-MEASURED 2026-10-11 by RealityCheck-Opus5-20261011. The defect this
bead names has recurred exactly once more, and the recurrence is itself the
finding: the anchor rots faster than it is refreshed.

The README was repaired after this bead was filed -- it now carries an
identity-bound row (`99a3b4e8`, 2026-10-05, 40 scenarios / 115 checks,
110 SUCCESS / 0 FAILURE / 4 WARNING / 1 INFO) together with an explicit note
that 98 commits and 388 lines across four server-mode files had invalidated the
prior "working tree (unanchored)" reading, and that the re-measurement
reproduced it exactly. That repair was correct and is not disputed here.

MEASURED TODAY at HEAD 31c73d6d:

    git merge-base --is-ancestor 99a3b4e8 HEAD        -> YES (not orphaned)
    git rev-list 99a3b4e8..HEAD --count              -> 135
    git diff --shortstat 99a3b4e8..HEAD -- crates/   -> 81 files, 11060+/1371-

Of the four server-mode source files the README names as the subject:

    fastmcp-core/src/context.rs                 0 commits   unchanged
    fastmcp-protocol/src/server_discovery.rs    0 commits   unchanged
    fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs                   2 commits   128+/10-
    fastmcp/src/lib.rs                          0 commits   unchanged

The adapter is byte-identical, which the README's own pin predicts and which
confirms the pin is honest:

    git rev-parse 99a3b4e8:crates/fastmcp/examples/conformance_server.rs
    git rev-parse HEAD:crates/fastmcp/examples/conformance_server.rs
    both -> 0b887aedeb0b7f6ad3ddceb5ea3cc3523bbab29b  (matches README)

The two commits that moved the subject are:

    e20174ca  test(server): require retained HTTP shutdown to finish its lifecycle once
    6fbb78df  fix(server): finish retained HTTP shutdown after its children settle

Hunks land in `HttpShutdownSettlement`, `HttpNonquiescentShutdown` and
`BoundHttpServer` (around lib.rs:7078-7601) plus their unit tests. That is HTTP
server-mode lifecycle code, and the conformance suite runs server mode over
HTTP, so this is relevant movement, not incidental churn.

WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT ESTABLISH

- It does NOT establish that the standing changed. A shutdown-settlement fix is
  unlikely to alter per-check results, and the prior re-measurement reproduced
  the row exactly across much larger drift (388 lines, four files).
- It DOES establish that the README's headline number is, again, bound to a
  revision that is no longer HEAD, with relevant movement in between. Under this
  project's own receipt rule ("relevant source movement invalidates it") the row
  is once again unverified at HEAD.

THE STRUCTURAL POINT, which outlives any single re-measurement

Hand re-measurement cannot keep pace with 240 commits/week (measured:
`git log --since=2026-10-04 --oneline | wc -l` -> 240; last 2 days -> 59). Each
refresh is correct for hours. The remedy is therefore NOT another manual
re-measure; it is to make the staleness mechanically visible. Cheapest viable
form, in increasing cost:

1. Have `scripts/run_official_conformance.sh` emit the HEAD sha, the adapter
   blob, and the four subject-file blobs into a committed receipt next to
   `scripts/conformance-expected-failures.yaml`, and have a check compare the
   recorded blobs against the working tree, failing with "conformance row stale:
   <file> moved" rather than silently aging. Blobs, not the tree hash, so
   unrelated lanes editing other files do not void it (PL-6).
2. Have the README row render from that receipt rather than from hand-edited
   prose, so prose cannot drift from the artifact.

Until something like (1) exists, every future reading of this row will be stale
within a day, and the project will keep paying a full re-measurement to learn a
number it already knew. This bead should not be closed by yet another manual
refresh; closing it should require the staleness to become self-reporting.

NOTE ON SCOPE: this comment adds no new claim about conformance results. It
re-dates the existing claim and argues the remedy class. No gate verdict is
reported here.

comments.author: RealityCheck-Opus5-20261011
comments.text:
I DESIGNED THE CHEAP STALENESS CHECK AND THEN REJECTED IT. Recording why,
because the cheap version would give FALSE ASSURANCE and the next lane will
otherwise build it. RealityCheck-Opus5-20261011, 2026-10-11. No code written,
nothing changed.

In my earlier comment on this bead I proposed, as remedy (1), emitting the HEAD
sha plus the adapter blob and the four subject-file blobs into a committed
receipt and failing a check when they move. I went to implement it as a TEST
rather than a `scripts/` change -- the facade already has the exact convention
(`tests/readme_examples.rs` pins README code blocks against their compiled
sources), `sha2` is already a facade dev-dependency, and a new test target with
no `required-features` would run on a plain `cargo test --workspace`. All of
that is feasible. I stopped for a reason that is about the SUBJECT, not the
mechanism.

THE CHEAP CHECK PASSES WHILE THE ROW IS STALE. The row's claim is about
server-mode BEHAVIOUR. The adapter is only the harness's entry point. Measured
today at HEAD:

    adapter blob  0b887aed…b29b   UNCHANGED since the measured revision 99a3b4e8
    fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs     MOVED, 2 commits, +128/-10 (HTTP shutdown
                                  settlement), which is server-mode code

So an adapter-only tripwire is GREEN right now, on a row that this bead
correctly says is unverified at HEAD. It would convert "unverified" into
"checked and fine", which is strictly worse than having no check: the reader
gains confidence exactly where the evidence does not support it.

AND THE HONEST VERSION FIRES CONSTANTLY. Extend it to the four server-mode
files the README names and it goes red on the next `fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs`
commit, which in this repo is hourly (240 commits in the 7 days before
2026-10-11). A gate that fires on every server commit is a gate someone
disables, and the four-file list is itself an under-approximation: "server-mode
behaviour" is not four files, so even a red from that set would not mean what it
appears to mean.

So there is no cheap, honest tripwire over hand-maintained prose. The two ends
of the design space are a check that lies green and a check that cries red, and
the reason is the same in both directions: the thing being guarded is a
BEHAVIOURAL claim and the only cheap observables are TEXTUAL.

WHICH LEAVES REMEDY (2) AS THE ONLY SOUND ONE, and sharpens it. The receipt has
to be emitted BY THE MEASUREMENT -- `scripts/run_official_conformance.sh`
writing its HEAD, its tally and its bindings into a committed artifact -- and
the README has to cite that artifact rather than restate it. Then staleness is
not something a check infers from hashes; it is the plain fact that the artifact
names a revision that is not HEAD, which anyone can see without re-measuring.
That makes the row's own provenance self-describing and needs no tripwire at
all.

That touches the conformance runner, which owns the suite pin and the tally, so
it is that lane's call and I am not taking it.

I ALSO RECONSIDERED SIMPLY RE-MEASURING, and did not, for the reason already on
this bead: at this commit rate a hand re-measurement is correct for hours, so it
would reproduce the same problem a third time rather than retire it. My own
earlier comment argued that; doing it anyway would have been inconsistent.

NET: no artifact created, remedy (1) withdrawn as unsound, remedy (2) restated
with its rationale. The bead stays open and unclaimed by me.

title: The conformance adapter declines the list-mutation triggers on a false premise: McpContext has a public runtime catalog-mutation API that emits list_changed, and the server wires the sink
description:
Two of the four remaining server-mode SHOULD warnings are blocked by a premise
that is FALSE. The adapter declines the list-mutation triggers "because the
server has no runtime catalog-mutation API". That API exists, is public on
`McpContext`, emits the notification, and the server wires the sink.

THE PREMISE, verbatim, crates/fastmcp/examples/conformance_server.rs:34-37:

    //! Not served: the list-mutation triggers (`test_trigger_tool_change` /
    //! `test_trigger_prompt_change`, SHOULD level), because the server has no
    //! runtime catalog-mutation API, and the 2025-era scenarios this
    //! 2026-07-28 server does not claim.

and the two warnings it produces, from scripts/conformance-expected-failures.yaml:

    server-stateless:sep-2575-server-sends-tools-list-changed-on-subscription
    server-stateless:sep-2575-server-sends-prompts-list-changed-on-subscription
        "The server has no runtime catalog-mutation API, so it never emits a
         list-changed notification. Deliberate; documented in the adapter..."

THE API, measured 2026-10-12 by reading the shipped source:

  crates/fastmcp-core/src/context.rs -- all six are `pub` on `McpContext`,
  which every handler receives:
      :3569  pub fn disable_tool(&self, name: impl Into<String>) -> bool
      :3576  pub fn enable_tool(&self, name: &str) -> bool
      :3594  pub fn disable_resource(&self, uri: impl Into<String>) -> bool
      :3605  pub fn enable_resource(&self, uri: &str) -> bool
      :3624  pub fn disable_prompt(&self, name: impl Into<String>) -> bool
      :3635  pub fn enable_prompt(&self, name: &str) -> bool

  Each routes through `add_to_disabled_set` / `remove_from_disabled_set`
  (:3666, :3683) which call `emit_catalog_changed(kind)` -- and ONLY when the
  set actually changed, which matters for the design below. `disable_tool`
  passes `McpCatalogKind::Tools`; `disable_prompt` passes the prompts kind.

  `emit_catalog_changed` (:3699) notifies BOTH sinks: a `NotificationSender`
  and a `subscriptions/listen` catalog publisher, each owning its delivery
  decision.

  The server installs the publisher: crates/fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs:19594
  `ctx.with_catalog_publisher(Arc::new(FinalCatalogPublisher { .. }))`, plus
  log senders at :14306 and :15359. So the path is wired, not latent.

  `disable_tool`'s own doc comment shows the intended handler usage:
  `ctx.disable_tool("admin_tool");`

  Corroborating, independently: FEATURE_PARITY.md's gap list records
  "Dynamic enable/disable - Per-session visibility plus mutation-only
  `list_changed` notifications" as DONE.

WHAT THE SUITE ACTUALLY DOES, read from the pinned bundle
(@modelcontextprotocol/conformance@0.2.0-alpha.10, npm pack, inspected
read-only, never executed) rather than guessed:

    M = {_meta: l, notifications: {toolsListChanged: true}}
    frames = await listen(`subscriptions/listen`, M, 2, 800, async () => {
        await call(`tools/call`, {name:`test_trigger_tool_change`, arguments:{}, _meta:l})
    })

So: open `subscriptions/listen` requesting `toolsListChanged`, then call a
no-argument tool named exactly `test_trigger_tool_change`, and expect TWO
frames within 800 ms -- the `notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged` ack
first, then `notifications/tools/list_changed`. `test_trigger_prompt_change`
is the prompts counterpart. The adapter currently registers 20+ `test_*` tools
and neither of these, and uses no `disable_*`/`enable_*` call anywhere.

DESIGN NOTE THAT MATTERS, because the obvious implementation is subtly wrong.
`add_to_disabled_set` emits only `if stored && changed`. A trigger that always
calls `disable_tool("x")` therefore emits on the FIRST call and is silent on
every later one, so the scenario would pass once and then rot -- and worse,
would pass or fail depending on whether another scenario ran first in the same
session. The trigger must TOGGLE a dedicated throwaway target so the state
always changes:

    if ctx.disabled_tools().contains(TOGGLE_TARGET) { ctx.enable_tool(TOGGLE_TARGET) }
    else { ctx.disable_tool(TOGGLE_TARGET) }

with the same shape for prompts. The target should be a tool that exists but
carries no other scenario's meaning, so toggling its visibility cannot perturb
another check.

NO-CLAIM, and this is the important part. I have NOT run the suite, so I do not
claim these two warnings would clear. Specifically unestablished: whether the
scenario asserts anything beyond the two frames arriving (for example a
following `tools/list` reflecting the mutation), whether the 800 ms window is
comfortable for this server's subscription path, and whether per-session
disabled-set semantics interact with `server-stateless` in a way the scenario
dislikes -- the scenario name is literally `server-stateless`, and a
session-scoped disabled set is state. That last one is a real risk and should
be checked before the adapter change is called a fix.

This bead asserts only: the premise in the adapter and in the
expected-failures file is false, the capability is public and wired, and the
suite's requirement is the mechanism quoted above.

comments.author: RealityCheck-Opus5-20261011
comments.text:
FEASIBILITY CONFIRMED, AND I AM DELIBERATELY NOT IMPLEMENTING IT. The one risk
I flagged when filing — that `server-stateless` plus a session-scoped disabled
set might make the mutation a no-op — is resolved in the favourable direction.
Everything needed to write this is below. RealityCheck-Opus5-20261011,
2026-10-12.

THE RISK I FLAGGED, RESOLVED. `add_to_disabled_set` bails to `false` without
emitting when `self.state` is `None` (context.rs:3670), so the question was
whether a handler on the HTTP path gets session state at all. It does, and the
same function also attaches the publisher:

    crates/fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs:19470  fn request_context(.., state: SessionState, ..)
    :19478   let ctx = McpContext::with_state(cx.clone(), request_id, state)
    :19480+  // comment, verbatim: "A handler that mutates the catalog on this
             //  path must still reach the `subscriptions/listen` publisher;
             //  dropping it here silently stopped ..."
    :19593   fn with_final_catalog_publisher(&self, ctx) -> McpContext
    :19594   ctx.with_catalog_publisher(Arc::new(FinalCatalogPublisher {
                 registry: Arc::clone(&self.final_subscriptions) }))

So a handler receives state AND the subscriptions publisher, and the source
comment anticipates exactly this use. Note the regression history that comment
encodes: dropping the publisher here once silently killed handler-driven
list_changed, so this is a path that has been broken before and is now
guarded by prose rather than by a test — which is itself worth knowing.

A SECOND FAVOURABLE CONSEQUENCE of statelessness: if each request gets a fresh
state, `set.insert(name)` always returns `changed == true`, so a plain
`disable_tool` emits on every call and the toggle is belt-and-braces rather
than essential. The toggle is still the right design because it is correct
under BOTH session models.

WHAT AN IMPLEMENTER NEEDS, all of it:
  * pattern: `#[tool(name = "...", description = "...")] fn f(ctx: &McpContext)
    -> McpResult<Vec<Content>>`, registered as a PascalCase handler in the
    builder chain at conformance_server.rs:1168-1190 (`.tool(TestLoggingTool)`
    etc.); prompts register at :1192-1195.
  * the two names must be exactly `test_trigger_tool_change` and
    `test_trigger_prompt_change`, taking no arguments.
  * toggle a dedicated target: read `ctx.disabled_tools()` /
    `ctx.disabled_prompts()` and call `enable_*` or `disable_*` accordingly.
  * delete the "Not served" sentence at conformance_server.rs:34-37 and the
    matching justification in scripts/conformance-expected-failures.yaml --
    that file reserves entries to its owner, so coordinate.

WHY I AM STOPPING HERE, and it is not caution for its own sake:

1. I CANNOT VERIFY IT. Confirming these two warnings clear requires a full
   server-mode suite run: build `conformance_server` on a Linux worker (the
   README's own receipt records 32m24s) and run the pinned suite against it. I
   have not established that I can complete that, and shipping an unverifiable
   change into the project's conformance subject is the exact thing I have
   spent this session objecting to elsewhere.

2. ONE REAL UNRESOLVED RISK REMAINS, and it is not the one I already closed.
   Disabling a tool removes it from that session's `tools/list`. Any scenario
   asserting tool-list membership — `sep-2575-discover-capabilities-match-handlers`
   is the obvious candidate — could be perturbed by whichever target I pick,
   and adding a dedicated target tool changes the advertised list for every
   scenario. Choosing that target safely needs the suite in hand, not
   reasoning.

3. THE ADAPTER IS A PINNED SUBJECT. The README's headline row binds adapter
   blob `0b887aed`; editing it voids that binding. That is NOT a reason not to
   improve the adapter — and note the row is ALREADY unverified at HEAD, since
   `fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs` moved +128/-10 since `99a3b4e8` — but it does
   mean the change and a re-measurement are one unit of work, not two.

So this is a one-sitting job for whoever holds the conformance runner: make the
adapter change and re-measure in the same pass, producing a new anchored row.
Split across two lanes it leaves the row void in between. I have left the bead
open and unassigned rather than claim it and hold it.

title: fastmcp-client: the core subscriptions TERMINAL fixture is rejected as InvalidResponse
description:
The core subscriptions harness's TERMINAL frame is rejected with InvalidResponse, blocking
the one native_core_* test that bd-7p15j's ACK fix did not clear.

STATE AFTER bd-7p15j (commit 0f1a08c7):
  cargo test -p fastmcp-client --lib --features native-tls-roots,tasks -- native_core
  8 passed / 1 failed / 862 filtered out, exit=101

  native_core_acknowledgment_narrows_the_filter_and_delivers_terminal   FAILED
  crates/fastmcp-client/src/http_auth/discovery/client_credentials/subscriptions.rs:659
  called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: InvalidResponse

WHY THIS IS NOT bd-7p15j: that bead names the ACK fixture and AcknowledgementMissingId.
Both are resolved -- the test now gets PAST the acknowledgment (its accepted-filter
assertions at :652-656 pass) and fails three lines later at the TERMINAL step, which is a
different frame read by a different validator. Absorbing it into bd-7p15j would widen a
bead's receipt past what its acceptance named.

THE EVIDENCE, and it is a comparison rather than a theory. The core harness builds:

  const TERMINAL: &str = concat!("id: cursor-final\n",
      "data: {\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":7,\"result\":{\"resultType\":\"empty\"}}\n\n");

The SIBLING tasks harness, whose equivalent tests PASS, builds:

  fn terminal_listen(id: i64) -> String {
      terminal(id, &json!({"resultType":"complete",
                           "_meta":{(FINAL_SUBSCRIPTION_ID_META_KEY): id}}).to_string())
  }
  -- crates/fastmcp-client/tests/oauth_client_credentials/subscriptions.rs:54-56

TWO CANDIDATE DIFFERENCES, and I have NOT determined which matters:
  (a) resultType "empty" vs "complete"
  (b) the sibling carries `_meta` with the subscription id; the core TERMINAL carries none

Both are plausible and they are not mutually exclusive. Determining which -- or whether both
-- is a read of `decode_final_core_terminal` (crates/fastmcp-client/src/http_executor.rs:1877)
and the surrounding UnexpectedTerminalResult / TerminalIdMismatch paths. That read is the
FIRST WORK on this bead, not a prerequisite for filing it.

SAME CLASS AS THE SEVENTH PROBLEM, which is why it is worth stating as a class rather than an
incident: a fixture written against an ASSUMED frame shape rather than the real one. This is
now the third instance in this one harness -- the request filter key, the ACK's `_meta`, and
now the terminal -- each invisible until the target compiled and ran.

SCOPE NOTE FOR WHOEVER TAKES IT, including me: do not make the terminal pass by copying the
sibling's frame wholesale without establishing WHY. Copying both differences at once fixes the
test while leaving it unknown which contract the implementation actually enforces, and the next
harness will reproduce whichever one was cargo-culted. Change one, measure, then the other.

Not blocked. No slot needed to start -- the first step is a source read.

comments.text:
FIX APPLIED, AND THE ORDER IS DERIVED FROM SOURCE RATHER THAN MEASURED.
HazyTurtle, 2026-09-18. Recorded per WildMountain's ruling so the distinction survives.

=== THE ANSWER IS "BOTH, IN THIS ORDER" -- NOT "WHICH OF THE TWO" ===

The bead asked which of two candidate differences mattered. Neither alone: both are
independently required, and the code fixes their order.

  crates/fastmcp-protocol/src/messages.rs:4260
      let (result, diagnostic) = decode_final_complete(SUBSCRIPTIONS_LISTEN, input, &[])?;
      -> requires FinalMethodResult::Complete. A resultType of "empty" yields
         CoreDispatchError::UnexpectedFinalResultType (messages.rs:4729).

  crates/fastmcp-protocol/src/messages.rs:4261
      let subscription_id = subscription_id_from_result(&result)?;
      -> requires _meta[FINAL_SUBSCRIPTION_ID_META_KEY]; absent yields
         CoreDispatchError::InvalidResult (messages.rs:4806-4811).

:4260 RUNS BEFORE :4261. So the resultType failure fires first, and a fixture correcting
only that would then fail on the absent _meta. That sequence is read off the source, NOT
observed in a run -- stated explicitly because a derived order and a measured order are
different receipts and this one is derived.

Corroborating the requirement rather than inferring it: messages.rs:3480 documents the field
as "The REQUIRED subscription ID extracted from the result metadata."

=== A NEAR-MISS WORTH RECORDING ===

http_executor.rs:2556-2560 comments that malformed or absent metadata "still falls through to
the AUTHORITATIVE PROTOCOL DECODER". I first read that as PERMITTED and nearly eliminated the
_meta candidate on the strength of it. It means DECIDED BY, not allowed. The early _meta
inspection at :2561 is an optional fast path that exists only to produce a better
expected/actual diagnostic; the protocol decoder behind it is where the requirement lives.
A comment describing a ROUTING decision can read as describing a POLICY.

=== THE FIX ===

crates/fastmcp-client/src/http_auth/discovery/client_credentials/subscriptions.rs, the
TERMINAL const only. Both differences in one change, per ruling:

  resultType  "empty"  ->  "complete"
  _meta       absent   ->  {"io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId": 7}

NOT DONE, deliberately: TERMINAL is left as a const rather than converted to a `terminal(id)`
builder like `ack(id)`. Seven call sites use it, and two of them depend on it being a &str --
`TERMINAL.to_owned()` and, more importantly, `TERMINAL.replace("\"id\":7", "\"id\":8")`, an
EXISTING mismatch negative. Converting it would have restructured a passing negative while
fixing an unrelated frame.

Verified the perturbation stays surgical: the substring `"id":7` occurs EXACTLY ONCE in the
new const. It does not collide with the _meta member, whose key ends `...subscriptionId` --
capital I, and no quote immediately before it -- so `.replace` still hits only the JSON-RPC
response id. Checked by counting, not by reading.

The literal 7 must equal SUBSCRIPTION_ID and a const cannot interpolate it; that constraint is
now stated in a comment at the site.

=== STATUS ===

Compile gate NOT obtained: `rch exec` refused with
`no admissible workers: critical_pressure=2, insufficient_slots=1, hard_preflight=1,
active_project_exclusion=1`. Per the amended fleet model the exclusion flag means the
orchestrator's batch holds the project slot, so this is a queue wait rather than a fault. Card
submitted rather than retried. NO VERDICT claimed -- the `Remote command finished: exit=` line
is absent, and absent means no result regardless of how the attempt looked.

Bead stays open. Nothing closed, nothing claimed green.
