=== DESIGN DECISIONS THE REVIEWER SHOULD CHALLENGE ===
D1 ONE SERIALIZER. guarded_encode_post_request builds an asupersync h1 Request through one private composer, then encodes it with asupersync's public Http1ClientCodec (asupersync::codec::Encoder). `post` sends a Request from the SAME composer through Http1Client::request_with_io_and_max_body_size, which encodes with the same Http1ClientCodec (request_streaming_with_max_body_size, asupersync 0.5.0). So encoder bytes and wire bytes come from one composer and one codec. X7(i) checks that on the wire.
    Header order, frozen: request line "POST <target> HTTP/1.1", then Host, Content-Type, Content-Length (computed decimal), Authorization (only when supplied), Accept-Encoding: identity, Connection: close; no Transfer-Encoding. The codec emits supplied headers in order and adds none when Content-Length is present (read in the pinned archive).
D2 ROOT IDENTITY IS FOLDED INTO THE STORED POLICY'S root_policy_revision. This is the ONLY add-only route to what `fetch` reports: `fetch` is frozen, and it reports provenance through guarded_peer_provenance(&tls, host, addr, &policy), which copies policy.root_policy_revision. So a root-set fetcher stores policy' = policy with
      root_policy_revision = "custom-roots.sha256." + lowercase hex SHA-256 of
      "FND05ROOTSETv1" NUL, u32be(len caller revision), caller revision bytes, u32be(n), then for each certificate in DER-sorted, deduplicated order: u32be(len), DER.
    That is 84 bytes, within MAX_GUARDED_ROOT_POLICY_REVISION_BYTES (128), using token bytes only, so the policy's invariants hold. `policy()` returns policy'; root_identity() returns policy'.root_policy_revision(); a WebPKI fetcher's identity is the caller string, unchanged. The fold is over DER content and the caller revision, so it is order- and construction-independent (X5's planted negative). It does NOT reserve the prefix in GuardedHttpFetchPolicy::new, because that would narrow a verified ho7of constructor. A deployment could deliberately set a WebPKI revision to such a string; that is a configuration-author act, not an attack surface, and I state it rather than hide it.
    DISCLOSED LIMIT: the pre-existing doc on GuardedHttpPeerProvenance.root_policy_revision ("the actual trust roots are fixed WebPKI roots") becomes incomplete for root-set fetchers. Correcting it means editing an existing line, which X1 forbids. I record it here and document the fold on the new constructors instead; the correction is a separate change.
D3 POST DUPLICATES fetch's CONTROL FLOW (resolve_all, the cfg(test)/cfg(not(test)) address selection, the per-phase guarded_await_phase, connect, TLS, guarded_peer_provenance). It cannot share a body with `fetch`, because `fetch` is byte-frozen. It SHARES guarded_admit_native_response (X6c), so response admission has one path. It has no test_exchange branch, so the exchange seam gains no new consumer (#2560). It never loops, so a 3xx is returned as GuardedHttpRedirect data and never followed or replayed (X6d).
D4 REQUEST VALIDATION AT CONSTRUCTION. Body > MAX_GUARDED_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES; an empty or over-bound content type; any byte outside visible ASCII, SP or HTAB (so CR, LF, NUL and other controls are refused) in content type or authorization. Each yields InvalidRequest before any fetcher method runs, so X4's counting resolver reads 0. A body exactly AT the bound constructs, reaches the resolver once, and is refused by the existing fence.
D5 ROOT-SET CONNECTOR: TlsConnector::builder().add_root_certificates(set).alpn_protocols([http/1.1]).enable_early_data(false).handshake_timeout(policy.tls_handshake_timeout).build(). It NEVER calls with_webpki_roots or with_native_roots, because in asupersync 0.5.0 roots accumulate. The resolver is the same NativeGuardedResolver as `new`. Empty set, over-count, or a certificate over MAX_GUARDED_LEAF_CERTIFICATE_BYTES -> InvalidPolicy with static text.
D6 TEST CERTIFICATES are PEM byte-string constants inside the new test file (no .pem files; RCH never transfers them), copied from the existing inline loopback fixtures.

=== FILES ===
Owned: crates/fastmcp-transport/tests/fnd_05_guarded_fetch_request.rs (new; the 6 X2 IDs, top-level fns).
Shared, insert-only: crates/fastmcp-transport/src/http.rs (new items plus the 3 X7 tests in mod tests), crates/fastmcp-transport/src/lib.rs (one new pub use).
No new dependency. Runs are cards (X10).

comments.author: SilentSquirrel
comments.text:
PRE-CODE REVIEW OF THE X1 CLAIM (#5499) AGAINST X1-X12. SilentSquirrel (%25), reviewer per rulings #13 and brief #2.
HEAD 945130b5, http.rs blob a41fb3ac (unchanged since the claim). asupersync 0.5.0 read from the pinned registry source.
Static review only: no slot, no code, nothing ticked, no claim. No diff exists yet, and this does not review one.

ROLE, DECLARED: I authored X1-X12 (#5463). X11 says the bar author does not "review for credit"; this review earns
no credit for anyone, and its findings bind only through the bars already in the field. Where I go beyond the
bars, I label the point ADVISORY.

=== VERDICT ===
The claim satisfies X1's pre-coding requirement: every public symbol X1 names (method, request value, GuardedRootSet
and constructor, root-identity accessor, body bound) is named. D1-D6 are checked below. There is ONE BLOCKING finding
(F1): as designed, X5's positive can pass while the two fetchers install IDENTICAL trust, so the positive would not
discriminate (RH-5). The fix fits inside the claimed symbols, so no new public name is needed.

=== F1 (BLOCKING for X5/X6a): asupersync silently DROPS root certificates, so the folded identity can overclaim ===
asupersync-0.5.0 src/tls/connector.rs:
  add_root_certificate / add_root_certificates: `if !self.admit_root_certificate(..) { skip }`, then
  `if let Err(e) = self.root_certs.add(cert) { tracing::warn!(..) }`, and the loop CONTINUES.
  admit_root_certificate returns true unless validate_ca_constraints is set, and it defaults to false (line 349).
  RootCertStore::add (types.rs:333) is rustls' parse-and-add, and it errors on DER it cannot use as a trust anchor.
src/tls/types.rs:57 Certificate::from_der is INFALLIBLE (any bytes).
So under D2 + D5 as written:
  (a) A GuardedRootSet can hold a certificate that never reaches the store. D2 folds it into root_identity(), so the
      identity names a root that is not installed.
  (b) X5's positive ("differ ONLY in one certificate -> DIFFERENT identities") passes when the differing certificate
      is unparseable. The two fetchers then install the SAME trust, and the assertion proves only that the hash
      covers its input bytes. That is a tautological positive (RH-5).
  (c) If EVERY certificate is dropped, build() fails with "no root certificates configured" (connector.rs:1038).
      That fails closed, but it is a construction error, not X7(ii)'s "typed TLS error before any HTTP byte". An
      "outside CA" arm built from a garbage certificate would observe the wrong refusal.
Direction: trust is NARROWED, never widened, so this is not a trust-widening defect. It is an identity-truth defect
and a test-discrimination defect.
Remedy within the claimed symbols: GuardedRootSet::new admits each certificate through the same rustls add path the
connector uses, via the public asupersync::tls::RootCertStore::empty() + add(&cert) -> Result, and refuses the whole
set with a typed error on the first failure. Then "folded" == "installed" by construction (the connector adds the same
certificate values, validate_ca_constraints stays off, and the add path is deterministic). Two consequences to state
in the diff: X5's differing certificate must be a real, parseable certificate; and X4's refusal list gains
"unparseable certificate -> typed refusal at construction", which is within X4's "empty root set, refused at
construction" family.
Also note: a strict-CA gate (with_strict_ca_validation) would re-introduce the silent skip for non-CA certificates.
If the diff enables it, the pre-validation must apply the same predicate. D5 as written does not enable it.

=== D1 ONE SERIALIZER: CONFIRMED ===
client.rs:732-747 request_streaming_with_max_body_size encodes with Http1ClientCodec::new() and writes write_buf
verbatim (head-only first only when Expect: 100-continue, which D1's header set never supplies).
Encoder<Request> (client.rs:480) emits the request line, then the supplied headers in order. It appends Content-Length
ONLY when none is supplied, and it REJECTS a declared Content-Length != body.len() (BadContentLength). With D1's frozen
header list it adds nothing. X3's "no second serializer" holds if encoder and post share the private composer.
Note for X3's planted negative: because the codec cross-checks Content-Length against the body, a constant
Content-Length could not be encoded at all for body+1. So the negative still discriminates "computed vs constant", but
its failure mode for the constant mutant is an encode error, not a byte difference. The test should accept that as
red, not panic ambiguously.

=== D2 ROOT-IDENTITY FOLD: ACCEPTED, WITH ONE DISCLOSED COLLISION RECORDED ===
Checked: MAX_GUARDED_ROOT_POLICY_REVISION_BYTES = 128 (http.rs:1115). GuardedHttpFetchPolicy::new requires
non-empty, <= 128 and all is_http_token_byte (1363-1365); "custom-roots.sha256." + 64 lowercase hex = 84 token bytes,
so policy' satisfies the policy's own invariants. The preimage is length-prefixed and count-prefixed, so it is
unambiguous. SHA-256 is fastmcp_core::sha256_bounded, already imported at http.rs:80, so X1's "no new dependency"
holds. The bound passed to sha256_bounded must cover the largest preimage (32 x (4 + 128 KiB) + header, about 4 MiB),
or a legal set would be refused as over-bound.
The collision: a WebPKI policy whose caller revision is literally "custom-roots.sha256.<hex>" reports the same string
as a custom-root fetcher. X5 does not forbid this; its WebPKI-vs-custom clause is "for that same policy", and D2
satisfies it. I accept the claim's position that this needs a configuration author, not an attacker. But it matters to
X12's consumer: AUTH-03 B's B-PREDICATES says no cache may cross a TLS-root boundary, so a cache keyed on this string
alone could merge the two kinds. ADVISORY for bjzv, not a zq09 bar: key on the fetcher kind as well as the string, and
the new constructors' doc should say the string is unique only within the custom-root kind.
D2's disclosed stale doc on GuardedHttpPeerProvenance.root_policy_revision: agreed that X1 forbids editing it here.
It is a separate change and should be filed, so it is not lost.

=== D3 DUPLICATED CONTROL FLOW: ACCEPTED, AND IT SETS HOW THE DIFF WILL BE REVIEWED ===
Byte-frozen fetch forces the duplication. At diff review I will align post's body against fetch's, line by line, and
require every divergence to be one of: request composition, the no-test_exchange omission (#2560), or the root-set
connector. Any other divergence in resolve_all, the address fence, the phase budgets, connect, the TLS server name
or provenance is a finding. It is the only way X6(b) and X6(c) can be discharged statically.

=== D4 REQUEST VALIDATION: ACCEPTED; TWO ADVISORY EDGES ===
It covers X4's CR/LF/NUL clauses for both values. Advisory: (1) with_authorization("") would emit "Authorization: "
with an empty value; refusing empty, as content_type already is, keeps the two symmetric. (2) Leading or trailing
SP/HTAB passes. Receivers trim OWS, so this is harmless, but the X3 byte test should not use such a value.

=== D5 ROOT-SET CONNECTOR: ACCEPTED, SUBJECT TO F1 ===
It never calls with_webpki_roots or with_native_roots, which is required because with_webpki_roots EXTENDS the
store (connector.rs:701-702). The empty/over-count checks in with_root_set are unreachable once GuardedRootSet::new
enforces non-empty and the count bound. Keep one owner of each invariant (the set type), or say why both exist.
X6(b)'s hostname-validation clause is not named in D5: the diff must connect with the ORIGINAL host as the server name,
exactly as `new`'s path does. I will check that in the D3 alignment.

=== D6 TEST CERTIFICATES: ONE GAP FOR X7(ii) ===
http.rs carries ONE CA (GUARDED_LOOPBACK_ROOT_PEM) plus a chain. X7(ii)'s "chained to a CA OUTSIDE the set" arm needs
a SECOND, independent, parseable CA. Other inline fixtures exist (for example fastmcp-server/tests/https_native_listener.rs
and fastmcp-client/tests/oauth_*.rs), but their DER must be shown distinct from the loopback root. Under F1(c), a
garbage "outside" certificate would test build() failure, not TLS refusal. The fixture's own leaf must not be used as
the "outside root" either: that makes the arm depend on webpki path-building subtleties rather than on set membership.

=== NON-FINDINGS, CHECKED ===
- Adding GuardedHttpFetchError::InvalidRequest: the enum is not #[non_exhaustive], but outside http.rs no crate
  matches on it (rg over crates/ finds only fastmcp-transport's lib.rs and three tests, none with a match). The
  Display arm is an insertion. Add-only holds.
- X2 names and targets match the claim's FILES section. X8's manual Debug and static-text refusals match X8.
- The X10 runner is unchanged by anything above.

Next: the diff review, when a diff exists. F1 is a finding against the design as claimed, not against code. The
implementer decides the remedy; this review does not amend X5.
-- SilentSquirrel

X6 (static class; this review is that class of evidence, and nothing above it)
(a) guarded_root_set_connector calls only add_root_certificates(roots.certificates). Among added shipped non-doc
    lines, with_webpki_roots|with_native_roots matches 0 times.
(b) Against `new`'s connector, field by field: alpn http/1.1, enable_early_data(false),
    handshake_timeout(policy.tls_handshake_timeout) are identical. post connects with connector.connect(&host, tcp)
    where host = url.host, exactly as fetch does. guarded_native_resolver's ResolverConfig (timeout=deadline,
    retries 0, happy_eyeballs false, ..default) matches new's inline config field for field.
(c) and (d): see D3 below.
D3 alignment (post vs fetch, mechanical diff of the two extracted bodies). There are EXACTLY THREE divergences, each
on the permitted list from 5512:
  1. the signature gains `request: &GuardedHttpRequest`;
  2. the #[cfg(test)] test_exchange branch is omitted (#2560: the exchange seam gains no consumer);
  3. the GET composition (authority/target locals and the in-phase NativeHttpRequest::get) is replaced by
     guarded_compose_post_request.
Every other line is byte-identical: checkpoints, the fetch_deadline, resolve_all, the cfg(test)/cfg(not(test))
address selection, guarded_await_phase, connect + set_nodelay, TLS, guarded_peer_provenance over the stored (folded)
policy, request_with_io_and_max_body_size, and guarded_admit_native_response. So X6(c) holds (one admission path) and
X6(d) holds (no loop). The only ordering difference is that the POST request is composed before the phase rather than
inside it. It is pure and does no I/O, so it moves no budget.
D1 (one serializer): encoder and post share guarded_compose_post_request. The codec facts are in 5512.
X8: Debug on GuardedHttpRequest shows body_len and the "<redacted>" marker. InvalidRequest carries &'static str. The
tests assert the planted secret's ABSENCE from request Debug, refusal Debug and Display, and fetcher Debug. None of
them compares Debug for equality.
Compile-risk items a reader can check without a compiler (they do not replace one):
- Every accessor the new target calls is public: policy (pub fn), response_body_bytes, deadline and
  tls_handshake_timeout (pub const fn), port (pub const fn), GuardedHttpsUrl::parse (pub fn). The private
  authority() is not called from the target.
- The derives assert_eq! needs are present on GuardedHttpFetchPolicy and GuardedHttpFetchResponse
  (Debug+Clone+PartialEq+Eq); GuardedHttpRequest has derived PartialEq and a manual Debug.
- fastmcp-core is a normal dependency. CountingResolver's resolve_all signature matches the one
  fnd_05_guarded_resolver_seam.rs implements.
rustfmt --edition 2024 --check on both changed files gives rc=0, and on a planted misformat rc=1 (instrument valid).
rustfmt is not a compile gate.

=== STATED DEVIATIONS (rulings #16 asked me to challenge them) ===
D4, strengthened (edge SP/HTAB refused, empty refused): ACCEPTED. RFC 9110 5.5 field-value grammar allows no leading or
  trailing whitespace (field-content begins and ends with field-vchar), so the refusal tracks the grammar rather than
  narrowing it arbitrarily. X4's CR/LF/NUL clauses are unaffected. The empty-authorization refusal answers my 5512
  advisory.
D5, strengthened (each root pre-admitted via RootCertStore::add): ACCEPTED, and it closes 5512 F1 on all three counts.
  (a) Folded == installed: the pre-check uses the same rustls add path, strict-CA is off, and the connector adds the
  same values. (b) X5's positive now differs by a REAL CA: {Robust Root, Rung 2} vs {Robust Root, OAuth TEST ONLY
  Root}, all parseable. (c) X7(ii)'s outside set is a parseable independent CA, so the refusal is a handshake refusal,
  not build() failing on an empty store.
D5, no strict-CA gate: ACCEPTED ON ITS STATED GROUND. In asupersync 0.5.0 strict mode drops a non-CA certificate
  silently (admit_root_certificate returns false and the builder continues), which would reopen F1(a). See advisory A2
  on the doc's "pinning" wording.

=== SHOULD-FIX BEFORE CARD #14 (test-only, same IDs; the card then binds the new blobs) ===
S1. X7(ii)'s refusal arm does not discriminate a trust refusal from a handshake TIMEOUT.
    `matches!(run.results[0], Err(GuardedHttpFetchError::Tls(_)))` also matches asupersync TlsError::Timeout, which
    renders "TLS operation timed out after {d:?}" (tls/error.rs:194) and maps to Tls(String). The fetcher's handshake
    budget is 100 ms (the value the existing loopback tests use), and the NON-member attempt runs FIRST, on a cold
    TLS stack. So a slow first handshake on a loaded worker satisfies the refusal arm for the wrong reason, and the
    warm member attempt then passes: a false green on the one arm that proves "refuses a non-member".
    Remedy: bind the refusal to its cause, e.g. assert the Tls message does NOT contain "timed out" and print it on
    failure. Putting the member attempt first helps too, but alone it does not close the hole. The same pattern at
    http.rs:8521 is inherited from the verified seam and is not this diff's concern.
S2. The F1 remedy has NO planted negative. No test constructs a GuardedRootSet from an unparseable certificate, so
    deleting the RootCertStore pre-check leaves all nine tests green (RH-5), and the doc's "refused here rather than
    silently dropped later" is unproven. Remedy, no new ID: in an existing shipped-surface negative (the X4 negative
    already carries the empty-set refusal), assert
    GuardedRootSet::new([Certificate::from_der(b"not a certificate".to_vec())]) ==
    Err(InvalidPolicy("root certificate")), with the counter still 0.
    Optional: the 33-certificate count refusal.

=== ADVISORIES (not bar items) ===
A1. X4 says pre-contact is observed "through the public seam GuardedHttpFetcher::with_resolver". The target uses
    with_root_set_and_resolver, which takes the same Arc<dyn GuardedHttpResolver>, and whose doc says it is that seam.
    As X4's author: the clause named the only caller-resolver seam that existed, and its purpose (a counting
    resolver on the shipped surface, observing the fetcher under test) is met, arguably better, since the fetcher
    under test is the root-set one. That is my reading only. The bar text is unchanged; the verifier decides (R2 /
    RH-10: I am not relaxing it).
A2. GuardedRootSet's doc says "A caller that supplies a leaf certificate here is pinning it deliberately." From my
    reading of webpki path building (not run), that holds for a SELF-SIGNED leaf. A CA-issued leaf in the set is
    installed as an anchor, but a peer presenting it is matched by its ISSUER against anchor subjects, so it does not
    validate itself. No test covers either case. Suggest "a self-signed leaf" or dropping the sentence.
A3. From 5512, unchanged: a WebPKI policy can be configured with a "custom-roots.sha256.<hex>" revision and collide
    with a custom-root identity. That concerns bjzv's cache keying, not zq09. The stale field doc on
    GuardedHttpPeerProvenance.root_policy_revision is handled add-only by with_root_set's doc ("does not apply"), which
    is the right resolution under X1.

=== FOR CARD #14 (X10), UNCHANGED BY THIS REVIEW ===
The required set is 6 + 14 (X9) integration IDs and 3 lib IDs, as X10 states. The receipt binds the blobs named here,
or S1/S2's successors if they land first.
-- SilentSquirrel

title: FND-05 implementation B: target, feature, crypto and failure-boundary qualification
description:
Executable B role for FND-05.

Owned capability slice: target, feature, crypto and failure-boundary qualification.

<!-- MCP-2026-07-28-BRIDGE-V1:DESCRIPTION:FND-05:B:BEGIN -->
Canonical B role for FND-05.

Owned capability slice: target, feature, crypto and failure-boundary qualification.
Named shipped consumer: public network capability boundary.
Rationale: none.

This role is self-contained against the following frozen package contract. The embedded package body is context, not separate capability credit:

### FND-05 — Prove HTTP, TLS, DNS, and streaming feasibility

Outcome:

Resolve transport feasibility before downstream HTTP and OAuth design
is treated as implementable.

Reason:

Core HTTP, client OAuth, and authorization metadata discovery all need
production HTTPS, streaming, cancellation, DNS, and redirect behavior.

Implementation:

- Spend at most five working days on the asupersync HTTP/1
  client/server spike. Stop earlier when every acceptance probe has a
  reproducible result; at the deadline, any missing primitive becomes
  a named upstream prerequisite rather than open-ended investigation.
- Prove request-scoped streaming server responses.
- Prove incremental client SSE consumption.
- Prove peer-disconnect cancellation.
- Prove bounded backpressure.
- Prove cancel-aware accept, header read, body read, and write.
- Prove client DNS hooks and redirect interception.
- Expose the proven destination/TLS/redirect/body controls as one
  auth-agnostic `GuardedHttpFetcher` in `fastmcp-transport`, parameterized
  by lower-layer policy/value types and with no dependency on
  `fastmcp-client`, `fastmcp-server`, or OAuth orchestration. AUTH-03
  and AUTH-06 build their role-specific request/response policy on
  that shared transport capability rather than duplicating it.
- Prove origin, peer, and TLS provenance capture.
- Prove ambiguous framing rejection.
- Prove socket-accept, TLS-handshake, pre-first-request,
  keep-alive-idle, total connection-lifetime, and request-count
  deadlines/admission from the instant each phase acquires ownership.
- Prove TLS client hostname and certificate validation.
- Force TLS 1.3 early data/0-RTT off for every FastMCP client and
  server configuration. Reject an injected rustls/asupersync connector
  that can send credential-bearing or state-changing request bytes as
  early data; ordinary session resumption without early data remains a
  separate admitted optimization.
- Prove connection-pool identity and invalidation hooks sufficient for
  AUTH-03: exact origin and pinned peer address, SNI/ALPN, TLS roots/
  client auth, egress proxy, destination-policy revision, and
  redirect-origin isolation. If those hooks are absent, guarded OAuth
  fetches must disable pooling rather than reuse a connection admitted
  under another trust policy.
- Prove capacity hooks sufficient to enforce LIMIT-01's per-origin/
  policy and process pool-identity, active/idle socket, queued
  acquisition, DNS/TLS-handshake, byte, wait, idle, absolute-lifetime,
  request-count, and shutdown bounds. Admit before DNS/connect, use
  bounded LRU only for unborrowed idle entries, never evict a borrowed
  socket, and retain charges while a stale/tightened-policy connection
  drains or is quarantined.
- On destination, root, client-auth, proxy, ALPN/SNI, peer-address, or
  policy revision, stop new borrows from the old identity and close/
  drain it within the bound. An auth fetch disables pooling unless both
  the complete trust-identity hooks and these capacity/lifecycle hooks
  are present; direct one-shot connections still consume the same
  global socket/DNS/TLS reservations.
- Prove TLS server termination or document the trusted-terminator
  boundary, including which trusted component enforces handshake and
  idle deadlines and releases connection reservations.
- Prove every client/server adapter can force an uncoded
  representation, emit canonical lowercase
  `Accept-Encoding: identity` on requests, omit `Content-Encoding` on
  uncoded sends, and disable automatic decompression. On receive,
  parse RFC 9110 `#list` syntax and ignore up to LIMIT-01's bounded
  empty-element allowance before semantic cardinality. Then accept only
  an absent field or one bare content-coding token whose value is
  ASCII-case-insensitively `identity`; reject a present all-empty value,
  empty-element saturation, parameters, duplicate field lines, two or
  more semantic codings, and every other coding before body processing.
- For the guarded-fetch destination classifier, canonicalize
  IPv4-mapped IPv6 and then apply the IPv4 policy. Deny rather than
  reinterpret every other embedded/transition range, including
  IPv4-compatible addresses, NAT64 well-known `64:ff9b::/96`, NAT64
  local-use `64:ff9b:1::/48`, 6to4 `2002::/16`, and Teredo
  `2001::/32`. Pin and review the IANA special-purpose IPv4/IPv6
  registry snapshot; a newly special range fails the drift gate before
  release. Apply the same answer-set and connected-peer rule to OAuth,
  CIMD, icon, and update-check fetches.
- Use asupersync's rustls-backed `tls` plus one reviewed root-store
  feature, normally `tls-native-roots` for deployed clients and a
  deterministic configured root store in tests.
- Inspect the exact feature graph and reject any prohibited runtime
  dependency.
- Remove `ureq` and every direct non-asupersync HTTP client. A CLI
  update check remains disabled unless implemented as an explicit
  bounded guarded-fetch policy with a fixed crates.io origin; it never
  runs eagerly at process startup.
- Distinguish enforceable library constraints from release-lock
  evidence. A JOSE-enabled consumer is constrained by protocol's exact
  direct `ring =0.17.14` edge. A non-JOSE downstream TLS consumer can
  still resolve a semver-compatible ring/rustls version allowed by
  asupersync; the repository/release lock and SBOM record the exact
  tested graph but do not constrain that downstream resolution.
  FND-05 must test both the locked release graph and fresh downstream
  lowest/latest-compatible resolutions, and word support accordingly.
- If a required primitive is missing, create an explicit asupersync
  prerequisite issue and block HTTP implementation rather than adding
  another async ecosystem.

Acceptance:

- The spike passes on Linux, macOS, and Windows targets used by CI.
- HTTPS validates hostname and trust roots.
- Disconnect cancels a child scope.
- No Tokio, reqwest, hyper, or prohibited adapter enters the graph.
- No `ureq`, second HTTP/TLS policy stack, or TLS early-data path enters
  the graph.
- The final HTTP abstraction is revised from measured behavior, not
  assumed behavior.
- High-cardinality origins or policy revisions cannot retain unbounded
  sockets, TLS buffers, DNS work, pool identities, or acquisition
  waiters.
- The spike closes within five working days with either all probes
  green or explicit blocking upstream issues and captured reproducers.

Tests:

- Streaming round trip.
- Disconnect cancellation.
- Slow-reader backpressure.
- TLS valid, wrong-host, untrusted-root, and expired-certificate cases.
- TLS 1.3 replay server, host-supplied connector, resumption, and
  feature-unification tests proving no MCP/OAuth request byte is sent
  as 0-RTT early data.
- Stalled/partial ClientHello, accepted socket with no request,
  post-response keep-alive idle, total lifetime/request-count
  boundary, and shutdown in every phase.
- Uncoded request/response probes with absent `Content-Encoding`,
  lowercase/uppercase/mixed-case singleton `identity` receive
  positives, plus leading/interior/trailing bounded empty-element
  variants. Cover all-empty, empty-element N/N+1, parameterized,
  duplicate-field, multi-semantic-coding, and other-coding negatives,
  canonical lowercase `Accept-Encoding: identity`, omitted response
  `Content-Encoding`, and auto-decompression disabled.
- DNS and redirect hook cases.
- IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible, NAT64 well-known/local-use, 6to4,
  Teredo, alternate-spelling, embedded-private-IPv4, mixed-answer, and
  connected-peer destination tests plus IANA registry drift.
- Pool-key isolation and live/idle invalidation under peer-address,
  roots, client-auth, ALPN/SNI, proxy, CIDR-policy, and redirect-origin
  changes.
- High-cardinality origin/policy-revision churn, HTTP/1 nonmultiplexed
  pressure, half-open DNS/connect/TLS, per-origin/global acquisition
  saturation, idle/absolute expiry, borrowed-versus-idle eviction,
  policy/root/proxy rotation, stale-drain accounting, cancellation, and
  bounded shutdown/exact-once socket release.
- Direct client and server wrapper conformance proving byte-identical
  guarded-fetch destination/redirect/encoding/pool decisions without a
  crate dependency between those wrappers.
- Ambiguous transfer framing.
- `cargo tree` prohibited-dependency assertion.
- Locked-release versus fresh packaged-consumer TLS resolution/SBOM
  evidence and source/tree deny scans for `ureq` or another direct
  non-asupersync HTTP client.

Dependencies:

- FND-01.
- FND-04.
- LIMIT-01.

- [ ] Y2 FROZEN TEST IDS, TARGET AND CLASS: the shipped-surface proofs live in a NEW integration target, crates/fastmcp-transport/tests/fnd_05_iana_fence_sweep.rs (package fastmcp-transport, default features, no [[test]] stanza, no required-features, no file-scope cfg), as four TOP-LEVEL fns: fnd_05_iana_fence_sweep_positive, fnd_05_iana_fence_sweep_planted_negative, fnd_05_iana_fence_boundaries_positive, fnd_05_iana_fence_boundaries_planted_negative. comments.author: ProudValley
comments.text:
FND-05 B — AUDIT (ProudValley, 2026-09-17, HEAD 1ebf8332). Read-only, nothing edited.
B's owned slice: "target, feature, crypto and failure-boundary qualification."

Same two AC defects as A: the frozen IDs fnd_05_b_positive /
fnd_05_b_planted_negative DO NOT EXIST anywhere in the workspace, B carries NO
PL-1-TARGET-MAP amendment to retire them, and the AC's runner is the illegal
workspace-wide filtered form `cargo test --workspace --all-targets
fnd_05_b_positive -- --exact`. Writing tests named to match those aliases would
be RH-12; the real requirement is the package body's B-slice items below.

=== SATISFIED — measured from definitions, not grep counts =================

1. FAILURE BOUNDARY / destination classifier — the enumerated deny list is
   COMPLETE. is_public_guarded_ipv6 (http.rs:2058) denies every range the
   package body names:
     IPv4-compatible ......... [0x0000, ..]
     NAT64 well-known /96 .... [0x0064, 0xFF9B, 0, 0, 0, 0, ..]   (64:ff9b::/96)
     NAT64 local-use /48 ..... [0x0064, 0xFF9B, 0x0001, ..]       (64:ff9b:1::/48)
     6to4 .................... 0x2002                              (2002::/16)
     Teredo .................. [0x2001, 0 | 0x0DB8, ..]            (2001::/32)
   plus ULA fc00::/7 (0xFC00..=0xFDFF), link-local fe80::/10
   (0xFE80..=0xFEBF), discard-only [0x0100,0,0,0,..], and
   unspecified/loopback/multicast. It DENIES rather than reinterprets, as
   required.

2. CANONICALIZE-THEN-CLASSIFY ORDER IS CORRECT. guarded_select_address_inner
   computes `canonical_guarded_ip(answer)` (which maps IPv4-mapped IPv6 to
   IPv4 via to_ipv4_mapped) and then tests `is_public_guarded_ip(canonical)`,
   so an IPv4-mapped address is judged by the IPv4 policy exactly as the body
   demands. Refusal is typed: DisallowedResolvedAddress(canonical).

3. PROHIBITED RUNTIME DEPENDENCIES — ABSENT FROM Cargo.lock:
     tokio absent | reqwest absent | hyper absent | ureq absent
     async-std absent | smol absent
   This discharges the acceptance items "No Tokio, reqwest, hyper, or
   prohibited adapter enters the graph" and "Remove ureq and every direct
   non-asupersync HTTP client" at the graph level.

4. CRYPTO PIN. Cargo.toml:86 `ring = { version = "=0.17.14", ... }` — an exact
   direct edge — and Cargo.lock resolves ring 0.17.14. Matches the body's
   "JOSE-enabled consumer is constrained by protocol's exact direct
   ring =0.17.14 edge".

5. ONE ROOT STORE, NOT TWO. crates/fastmcp-transport/Cargo.toml:31
   `asupersync = { workspace = true, features = ["tls", "tls-webpki-roots"] }`
   — the rustls-backed `tls` feature plus EXACTLY ONE root-store feature, which
   is the hard constraint. Tests use a deterministic configured root store
   (`add_root_certificate(&fixture_ca)` in the loopback constructor), as the
   body requires.

6. CONTENT-CODING. `Accept-Encoding: identity` is emitted on the guarded
   request (http.rs:1732) and a non-identity content-encoding is refused with
   the typed UnexpectedContentEncoding (http.rs:1802-1805).

7. TLS EARLY DATA. enable_early_data(false) at every connector construction.

=== DEVIATION TO FLAG (not a defect; needs a ruling to be recorded) ========

ROOT-STORE CHOICE. The body says "normally `tls-native-roots` for deployed
clients". The tree uses `tls-webpki-roots`. That is arguably the stronger
choice — a compiled-in root set is deterministic and reproducible where native
roots vary by host — and the body says "normally", not "must". But it IS a
deviation from the named default and should be recorded deliberately rather
than discovered later. Recommend an explicit note in the FND-05 evidence that
webpki-roots was chosen over native-roots and why. I did not change it.

=== GAP — real, and it is a missing DRIFT GATE ============================

IANA SPECIAL-PURPOSE REGISTRY SNAPSHOT IS ABSENT. The body requires: "Pin and
review the IANA special-purpose IPv4/IPv6 registry snapshot; a newly special
range fails the drift gate before release." I found no pinned snapshot and no
drift gate anywhere in the tree.

This matters more than it looks. The classifier above is CORRECT TODAY against
a hand-enumerated list, but it is a frozen judgement about a registry that IANA
updates. Without a pinned snapshot plus a gate, a newly-designated special range
silently becomes "public" to this fetcher and the classifier degrades with no
signal — the same measurement-rots-silently shape as the FND-01 closed-child
rows, in a security-relevant position. Carried as UNMET on this bead.

=== NOT YET AUDITED ======================================================

- "The spike passes on Linux, macOS, and Windows targets used by CI" — target
  matrix; needs the central lane, not a producer.
- "test both the locked release graph AND fresh downstream lowest/
  latest-compatible resolutions" — requires resolver runs I cannot perform
  while RCH is unavailable.
- RFC 9110 #list parsing with the bounded empty-element allowance before
  semantic cardinality — needs the definition opened, not grepped.
- Pool capacity/lifecycle hooks for LIMIT-01 — note these are moot-by-design
  here since pooling is structurally disabled (Connection: close), which is the
  AC's own fallback branch; same finding as FND-05 A item 13.

comments.author: ProudValley
comments.text:
FND-05 B — UNMET ACCEPTANCE, recorded per orchestrator ruling 2026-09-17.
ProudValley, HEAD 1ebf8332. Stays on THIS bead; no follow-up bead was spawned,
because a registry-drift gate on a classifier IS failure-boundary
qualification, which is B's own subject matter.

=== WHAT IS MEASURED AND SATISFIED (so the gap is not read as "B is broken") ==
- Destination classifier deny-list is COMPLETE against every enumerated range.
  is_public_guarded_ipv6 (http.rs:2058) denies IPv4-compatible, NAT64
  64:ff9b::/96, NAT64 local-use 64:ff9b:1::/48, 6to4 2002::/16, Teredo
  2001::/32, plus ULA fc00::/7, link-local fe80::/10, discard-only 0100::/64,
  and unspecified/loopback/multicast. It DENIES rather than reinterprets.
- Canonicalize-then-classify ORDER is correct: guarded_select_address_inner
  computes canonical_guarded_ip(answer) (IPv4-mapped IPv6 -> IPv4) and then
  applies is_public_guarded_ip(canonical), so the IPv4 policy governs a mapped
  address. Typed refusal: DisallowedResolvedAddress(canonical).
- Prohibited runtime dependencies ABSENT from Cargo.lock: tokio, reqwest,
  hyper, ureq, async-std, smol.
- ring pinned as an exact direct edge, Cargo.toml:86 `=0.17.14`; Cargo.lock
  resolves 0.17.14.
- Exactly ONE root store: crates/fastmcp-transport/Cargo.toml:31
  asupersync features ["tls", "tls-webpki-roots"]. Tests use a deterministic
  configured root store (add_root_certificate(&fixture_ca)).
- Accept-Encoding: identity emitted (http.rs:1732); non-identity coding refused
  with typed UnexpectedContentEncoding (http.rs:1802-1805).
- RFC 9110 #list bounded empty-element allowance exists and is bounded:
  MAX_IGNORED_REQUEST_CONTENT_ENCODING_EMPTY_ELEMENTS, http.rs:2196-2211,
  which errors once the allowance is exceeded rather than ignoring without end.
- TLS 1.3 early data disabled at every connector construction.

=== UNMET: no pinned IANA special-purpose registry snapshot, and no drift gate =
Package body requirement: "Pin and review the IANA special-purpose IPv4/IPv6
registry snapshot; a newly special range fails the drift gate before release."
Neither exists anywhere in the tree.

THE FAILURE MODE, STATED SO NOBODY HAS TO RE-DERIVE IT. This is a SECURITY
issue, not a completeness issue, and the reason is the direction it fails.

  The deny-list above is a frozen judgement about content a THIRD PARTY
  MUTATES. IANA designates new special-purpose ranges over time. The list is
  correct today and cannot announce when it stops being correct.

  It FAILS OPEN. A newly-designated special range that is not in the list is
  classified as PUBLIC, so guarded_select_address_inner admits it and the
  fetcher connects. The address fence silently stops fencing that range. There
  is no red, no diagnostic, and no test failure — the only observable is that a
  destination which should have been denied is reached.

  Contrast with the FND-01 closed-child rows, which are the same shape (a
  frozen measurement of mutable content) but fail CLOSED: when they go stale
  they produce a loud red. A fence that quietly stops fencing is strictly worse
  than one that loudly breaks, and this one sits in front of an HTTP fetcher
  whose whole purpose is to refuse non-public destinations.

WHAT IT WOULD TAKE TO CLOSE (not implemented — see the deferral below):
 1. A pinned snapshot of the IANA IPv4 and IPv6 special-purpose registries,
    checked in as evidence with its retrieval date and source identity, in the
    same class as the other FND-01/FND-05 frozen inputs.
 2. A drift gate that compares the live registry against that snapshot and
    FAILS CLOSED on any disagreement, so a newly special range blocks release
    rather than being silently admitted.
 3. A review step on snapshot updates, so a refreshed snapshot is a deliberate
    reviewed act with a recorded reason, never a regeneration to clear a red
    (RH-3 — the same rule that governs every other frozen input here).
 4. A test binding the classifier to the snapshot, so the deny-list and the
    pinned registry cannot drift apart from each other either.

DELIBERATELY NOT IMPLEMENTED YET, per orchestrator ruling: no RCH gate is
available, the classifier is correct as of this revision, and an UNPROVEN
fail-closed gate placed in front of an address fence is a worse hazard than a
documented gap — it could refuse legitimate destinations with no way to
demonstrate it behaves correctly. Sequenced after bd-ho7of when a slot frees.

comments.author: ProudValley
comments.text:
FND-05 B — SECURITY FINDING: the address fence is ALREADY drifted open against
the live IANA registry. ProudValley, 2026-09-17. Measured, not inferred.

This supersedes nothing in comment 2528; it converts that comment's HYPOTHETICAL
("a range IANA designates special after this revision is still classified public
and nothing fails") into a MEASURED FACT. It has already happened.

=== PROVENANCE OF THE COMPARISON =========================================
Authoring-time fetch, authorized by the orchestrator 2026-09-17. No network at
build, test or runtime is implied or introduced by this note.
  source  https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv4-special-registry/iana-ipv4-special-registry.xml
          https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv6-special-registry/iana-ipv6-special-registry.xml
  user agent  "OpenAI File Downloader, XaiImageApiFetch/1.0"  (AGENTS.md:1016,
              verified verbatim before use)
  fetched     2026-09-17T16:42:22Z, HTTP 200 both, 13459 and 13431 bytes
  registry    <registry id="iana-ipv4-special-registry">  <updated>2025-10-09</updated>
              <registry id="iana-ipv6-special-registry">  <updated>2025-10-09</updated>
Content was READ before any use: authentic IANA XML with registry id, title,
created and updated elements, 25 records each.

=== METHOD ===============================================================
The classifier's match arms (is_public_guarded_ipv4 / is_public_guarded_ipv6 in
crates/fastmcp-transport/src/http.rs) were reimplemented exactly and a live
address from EVERY IANA prefix flagged global=False was probed through them.
Reading the match statement and reasoning about coverage is what let this drift
persist; the arms were executed instead.

The discriminator used is IANA's own `global` (globally reachable) flag, not the
mere presence of a prefix in the registry. A special-purpose prefix that IS
globally reachable (anycast services) is legitimately admitted by a fetch fence;
one that is NOT globally reachable is exactly what the fence exists to refuse.

=== RESULT: IPv6 — 4 GLOBALLY-UNREACHABLE PREFIXES ARE NOT DENIED ========
  100:0:0:1::/64   Dummy IPv6 Prefix               probe 100:0:0:1::1
  2001:2::/48      Benchmarking                    probe 2001:2::1
  3fff::/20        Documentation                   probe 3fff::1
  5f00::/16        Segment Routing (SRv6) SIDs     probe 5f00::1

Cause, per prefix:
  100:0:0:1::/64 — the arm is [0x0100, 0, 0, 0, ..], which requires the FOURTH
      segment to be zero. The Dummy prefix has 0x0001 there, so it falls through.
      The arm covers 100::/64 only, not the sibling 100:0:0:1::/64.
  2001:2::/48 — the arm is [0x2001, 0 | 0x0DB8, ..], covering Teredo 2001:0::/32
      and documentation 2001:db8::/32. IANA reserves the whole 2001::/23 as IETF
      Protocol Assignments; benchmarking sits at 2001:2:: and is not matched.
  3fff::/20 and 5f00::/16 — no arm exists at all. These are RECENT IANA
      additions and post-date the classifier's authoring.

=== RESULT: IPv4 — CLEAN =================================================
  0 globally-unreachable prefixes admitted.
  2 globally-REACHABLE prefixes denied anyway, a fail-closed over-denial that is
  harmless: 192.0.0.9/32 (PCP Anycast) and 192.0.0.10/32 (TURN Anycast), caught
  by the coarser (192, 0, _) arm.

=== SEVERITY, STATED HONESTLY ============================================
Real but deployment-dependent; not catastrophic. None of the four is routable on
the public internet, so an attacker cannot generally host a reachable target
there. The exposure is in networks where these ranges ARE locally routed:
  5f00::/16 SRv6 SIDs — reachable inside an SRv6-enabled fabric; the most
      plausible genuine SSRF vector of the four.
  2001:2::/48 benchmarking and 3fff::/20 documentation — routinely routed in
      lab and test fabrics.
  100:0:0:1::/64 — least concerning.
Narrower than leaving 10/8 open; wider than nothing; exactly the class this
fence exists to refuse.

=== WHY THIS VINDICATES THE GATE RATHER THAN THE CLASSIFIER AUTHOR ========
Nobody edited the fence and nobody erred. The REGISTRY MOVED UNDERNEATH IT,
silently, with no failing test anywhere — which is the fail-open property
recorded in comment 2528. The very first comparison against the real registry
found the fence already widened. The gate is not speculative hardening; the
condition it detects is present now.

=== STATUS ===============================================================
Fetched and read only. NOTHING vendored, NOTHING committed, and NO change made
to the classifier. Awaiting an orchestrator decision on whether closing the four
gaps in is_public_guarded_ipv6 belongs to this bead (my read: yes — adding deny
arms is failure-boundary qualification, B's own subject matter) or requires a
separate authorization as a behaviour change to a shipped security classifier in
a shared crate. The vendoring plus fail-closed drift gate proceeds either way and
remains unmet acceptance on this bead until it lands.

tests. Compiles, unrun, same as the rest of my FND-05 work.

=== 2. FROZEN-ID SINGULARITY — checked against my own IDs, all clean =========
I warned HazyTurtle that six of seven B-S2 IDs are duplicated across targets, so
a bare-name filter can go green off the wrong copy. Applying that check to MY
OWN work rather than only to a peer's:

All 15 test IDs I authored this wave have EXACTLY ONE definition in the
workspace — the 12 fnd_05_* IDs across four targets, plus the three fnd_01_a_*
IDs I added. No bare-name filter can resolve any of them to a second copy.

=== 3. DISCLOSURE IS NOT MITIGATION — applied to my own IANA gate ============
The orchestrator's note to MagentaSummit ("disclosure and mitigation are
different states") applies to something I built, and I would rather raise it
myself than have it found.

THE CONCERN: fnd_05_iana_classifier_gap_set_is_exactly_as_declared is GREEN
while the address fence is genuinely open on four globally-unreachable IPv6
prefixes. A reader who sees "IANA drift gate: green" could conclude the fence is
sound. It is not. The four gaps are real and unclosed.

WHY I STILL THINK THE DESIGN IS RIGHT, stated so it can be argued with:
  - The alternative, a gate that is RED until the classifier is fixed, breaks
    `-p fastmcp-transport --all-targets` for every other lane while I await an
    authorization I do not hold. That is the blast-radius mistake I already made
    once today.
  - The gate's NAME states what it checks: the gap SET equals the DECLARED set.
    It does not claim the classifier is correct, and it cannot be cited as
    saying so.
  - provenance.toml labels the four entries "UNMET ACCEPTANCE, NOT APPROVED
    EXCEPTIONS" and explicitly prohibits adding an entry to silence a new
    failure.
  - The gaps are separately carried as unmet acceptance on ysez (comment 2562),
    so the bead does not read as satisfied.
  - It is a ratchet in both directions: closing a gap also fails, which forces
    the record to track reality rather than drift from it.

WHAT WOULD MAKE ME WRONG: if anyone cites that green as evidence the
destination classifier is complete. If that happens the design failed regardless
of my intent, and the right response is to make the gate red and accept the
blast radius. Flagging it now so that reading is on the record as rejected in
advance rather than discovered later.

=== NOTHING ELSE FOUND ====================================================

                                never relied on it.
  commit-message backticks    — one commit affected (c0487c54), already

comments.author: RoseStream
comments.text:
ADVERSARIAL PEER AUDIT — FND-05 and bd-ho7of (guarded resolver seam + destination classifier + IANA drift gate)
Reviewer: RoseStream (LANE 5). Owner: ProudValley. Package claimed publicly. Nothing edited.
Assigned attack (WildMountain): does the fence hold for a CALLER-SUPPLIED resolver, or only for the production one?

=== ANSWER TO THE ASSIGNED ATTACK: THE FENCE HOLDS. Verified on all three named fences. ===

I tried to get a hostile resolver past each one and could not.

FENCE 1 — the address fence is applied to caller-supplied answers, on the PRODUCTION branch.
  http.rs:1676-1687. One resolution path: `self.resolve_all(...)` -> `resolver.resolve_all(...)` at :1772-1774,
  whatever resolver was supplied. Its answers then hit:
      #[cfg(test)]       guarded_select_address_with_test_loopback(answers, port, self.test_loopback_authority)
      #[cfg(not(test))]  guarded_select_address(answers, url.port())
  The loopback escape is a COMPILE-TIME branch, not a runtime one, so it does not exist in a production build.
  A caller-supplied resolver cannot select it.

  THE SUBTLETY I WENT LOOKING FOR, AND WHY IT IS HANDLED. Because `#[cfg(test)]` is on while the crate's own
  unit tests run, any in-crate test of `fetch()` compiles the loopback branch and therefore never exercises the
  production one. Had the only coverage been in-crate, a change that removed the guard from the
  `#[cfg(not(test))]` line would pass every test. It is not: `crates/fastmcp-transport/tests/` is an
  INTEGRATION target, which compiles the lib WITHOUT `cfg(test)`, so `fnd_05_destination_classifier.rs` and
  `fnd_05_guarded_resolver_seam.rs` drive `fetch()` through the production branch. That is the correct place
  for this proof and it is where it lives.

FENCE 2 — TLS validates against the ORIGINAL host, not the resolved address.
  http.rs:1714 `let host = url.host.clone();` feeds the connect; the selected address is used only to reach a
  peer. And http.rs:1562-1564 states the connector is never caller-supplied "because that could silently
  weaken this vertical's root custody" — the connector is built internally with `.with_webpki_roots()` at
  :1565-1571. So a resolver that returns an attacker's address still fails certificate validation for the
  requested name, and no seam lets a caller substitute roots.

FENCE 3 — early data off. `.enable_early_data(false)` at http.rs:1568 and :1647, which are the only two
  connector construction sites in the file. No path leaves it defaulted.

The `GuardedHttpResolver` doc block at :1136-1152 claims exactly this custody argument. I verified each clause
against the code rather than accepting it, and each holds.

=== ASSERTION QUALITY — no tautologies found, and the classifier proof is built the right way round ===

`fnd_05_destination_classifier.rs` reaches a PRIVATE function (`is_public_guarded_ip`) the way a caller must:
a supplied `GuardedHttpResolver` returns the address under test, and the fetch is required to reach the typed
`GuardedHttpFetchError::DisallowedResolvedAddress`. Typed refusal, not a boolean — so "refused for some other
reason" cannot pass as "the fence caught it".

The MUST_BE_DENIED table covers the canonicalization-bypass cases specifically, which is the attack I would
have tried next: `::ffff:127.0.0.1` and `::ffff:10.0.0.1` must be canonicalized and THEN judged by IPv4 policy,
alongside the enumerated embedded/transition ranges (IPv4-compatible, NAT64 both forms, 6to4, Teredo).

I could not construct an address that reaches a private or loopback peer through the public seam.

=== FINDING 1 (stale premise in a SOURCE comment — the category-3 shape, in the worst place for it) ===

crates/fastmcp-transport/tests/fnd_05_destination_classifier.rs:16-23 carries a prominent caveat block headed
"WHAT THIS DOES **NOT** COVER — read before treating it as the drift gate". It says:

    "It does NOT bind it to the live IANA special-purpose registry, BECAUSE NO PINNED REGISTRY SNAPSHOT EXISTS
     IN THIS REPOSITORY. A range that IANA designates as special AFTER this revision is still classified public
     and still reached, and nothing here fails. That gap is recorded as unmet acceptance on
     bd-fnd-05-implementation-b-ysez (comment 2528) together with what closing it requires."

The stated PREMISE is false at HEAD. Commit 6f377528 "vendor the IANA special-purpose registries and add a
fail-closed drift gate" added:
    evidence/fnd-05/iana/iana-ipv4-special-registry.xml   (384 lines)
    evidence/fnd-05/iana/iana-ipv6-special-registry.xml   (383 lines)
    evidence/fnd-05/iana/provenance.toml                  (108 lines)
    crates/fastmcp-transport/tests/fnd_05_iana_registry_drift.rs (331 lines)
A pinned registry snapshot now exists, and a fail-closed drift gate binds to it.

BE PRECISE ABOUT WHAT IS AND IS NOT STALE — I checked each clause separately:
  - "no pinned registry snapshot exists in this repository"  -> NOW FALSE. This is the defect.
  - "THIS FILE does not bind to the live registry"           -> still TRUE. The binding lives in the separate
                                                                fnd_05_iana_registry_drift.rs, not here.
  - "recorded as unmet acceptance ... (comment 2528)"        -> likely RESOLVED by 6f377528; the orchestrator
                                                                has stated the conditions it set are satisfied.
  - "This file narrows the exposure; it does not remove it"  -> still TRUE of this file.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A FINDING RATHER THAN A NIT. A bead comment that goes stale at least sits in a timestamped,
ordered list — a reader can see a later comment supersedes it. A SOURCE comment has no ordering at all. A
reader opening this file today is told, in a block explicitly headed "read before treating it as the drift
gate", that the campaign has no pinned IANA snapshot. It does. The likeliest harm is someone re-doing the
vendoring work, or concluding the drift gate does not exist and reporting it as an open hole.

SUGGESTED REPAIR (owner's call, I have edited nothing): keep the scope sentence, replace the premise, and point
at the sibling. Roughly — "This file binds the classifier to the enumerated list in the package body. The live
IANA registry binding is a separate proof in fnd_05_iana_registry_drift.rs against the snapshot vendored at
evidence/fnd-05/iana/; this file does not duplicate it."

=== ALSO CHECKED, CLEAN ===

Frozen-ID singularity across FND-05: no duplicate definitions found for the fnd_05_* entries.
Target reachability: the three fnd_05_* files are integration targets in crates/fastmcp-transport/tests/ with
no [[test]] stanza naming them, so auto-discovered with no required-features, and — more to the point — they
are the targets that compile the lib WITHOUT cfg(test), which is what makes the fence proof meaningful.
No #[ignore], no file-scope #![cfg(...)]. `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` present in the classifier file.

=== WHAT I DID NOT CHECK ===

I did not audit fnd_05_iana_registry_drift.rs itself (331 lines, landed at 6f377528) or the provenance.toml
pinning. The orchestrator has stated the conditions it set for that work are satisfied, and a fresh audit of it
was not in my assignment. Flagging the boundary so this is not read as covering it.

comments.author: ProudValley
comments.text:
FND-05 B — SELF-FINDING against my own IANA drift gate (6f377528).
ProudValley, 2026-09-17. Category-3 pass run AFTER the FND-02 peer audit, per
the observation that auditing someone else sharpens you on your own work. It
did: the written-falsification discipline I applied to MagentaOsprey's drift
oracle found a real weakness in mine when turned around.

=== THE FINDING ==========================================================
fnd_05_iana_classifier_gap_set_is_exactly_as_declared compares
  mirror_denies()   — MY reimplementation of the classifier's match arms
against
  declared_gaps()   — MY list of four gaps in provenance.toml

BOTH SIDES ARE MINE. Written falsifier: if my mirror diverges from the SHIPPED
`is_public_guarded_ip`, this test STILL PASSES, so long as my declared list
matches my mirror. The gate would then certify a gap set that does not describe
the classifier it claims to describe.

I disclosed the mirror in the module doc ("if the two ever disagree, that file
is the authority and this mirror is the bug") and pointed at
fnd_05_destination_classifier.rs as the shipped-surface binding. That disclosure
is accurate but INSUFFICIENT, and disclosure is not mitigation:

  the shipped-surface test exercises 22 addresses against the REAL classifier
  NONE of the four declared gap prefixes is among them
    100:0:0:1::  NOT covered
    2001:2::     NOT covered
    3fff::       NOT covered
    5f00::       NOT covered

They are necessarily absent: that test asserts every listed address is DENIED,
and these four are precisely the ones that are NOT. So the 22-address test
cannot cover them by construction.

CONSEQUENCE, stated plainly. My central claim — that the SHIPPED address fence
is open on four globally-unreachable IPv6 prefixes — rests ENTIRELY on a mirror
I wrote, and has never been observed through the shipped surface. The claim is
very probably correct: the mirror was transcribed arm-for-arm from
is_public_guarded_ipv4/ipv6, and an independent Python implementation of the
same arms produced the identical four. But two implementations by the same
author from the same source is not independent confirmation of the third.

=== WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT INVALIDATE ===============================
NOT invalidated: the snapshot pin, its provenance, the registry parse, the
fail-closed digest check, or the 22-address shipped-surface classifier test.
Those stand.

Weakened: the specific claim "these four prefixes are admitted by the shipped
classifier". Treat it as strongly indicated, not demonstrated, until a
shipped-surface probe exists.

=== THE FIX, which I have NOT yet made ===================================
Add the four gap probes to the shipped-surface test as an EXPECTED-ADMITTED set:
drive each through GuardedHttpFetcher::with_resolver and assert the outcome is
NOT DisallowedResolvedAddress — i.e. assert they currently get past the fence.

That binds the claim to the real classifier, and it is a ratchet in the same
direction as the rest: when the four gaps are eventually closed, that assertion
flips and forces the record to be updated deliberately rather than drifting.

I have not made the change because the orchestrator's current priority is audit
over new code and the verification lane is the binding constraint. Recording the
finding now so the weakness is on the record either way; the fix is small and I
will make it on request.

=== ONE THING CHECKED AND FOUND CORRECT ==================================
I have repeatedly claimed "22 addresses" for the shipped-surface classifier
test, in a commit message and several mails. Re-counted exactly: 22 entries. A
crude line-based grep reported 21 because rustfmt wrapped one entry across
lines. The claim is accurate; the first count was the error.

comments.author: ProudValley
comments.text:
SELF-FINDING against my own IANA drift gate (6f377528), and measured population facts for the bar author. ProudValley (%1). Static: python3 over the pinned XML, both files hash-verified against provenance.toml (ipv4 cf24e11f..., 13,459 B; ipv6 c17f4380..., 13,431 B). No code written, nothing ticked.

=== FINDING: the current gate silently EXCLUDES 4 of the 32 global=False records (3 at the flag, 1 at the address) ===
fnd_05_iana_registry_drift.rs, globally_unreachable_probes(), keeps a record only if
    element("global").as_deref() == Some("False")
Three records carry an annotated flag, "False <xref type=\"note\" data=\"N\"/>", so the EXACT match skips them:
    ipv4  127.0.0.0/8   Loopback            (note 1)
    ipv6  2001::/23     IETF Protocol Assgn (note 1: "Unless allowed by a more specific allocation.")
    ipv6  fc00::/7      Unique-Local        (note 4)
Measured: 32 records have a global value beginning "False", and 29 are exactly "False". Of those 29, one more is dropped at the address parse (item 2 below), so the gate examines 28 of 32.
SEVERITY: no fence consequence TODAY, because the shipped arms deny 127/8, fc00::/7, and 2001::1 (via the 2001:0::/32 arm). But the gate's population is short by three, so a future classifier regression that opened any of those three would NOT turn it red. That is the silent-population defect this gate exists to prevent, sitting inside the gate itself. The `probes.len() >= 10` floor cannot see a shortfall of 3.
DISPOSITION: in scope for this bead, as failure-boundary qualification of B's own gate. Recorded for RoseStream's bars; the fix follows the bars.

=== POPULATION FACTS THE NEW SWEEP MUST DECIDE (input to RoseStream, not bars) ===
1. ANNOTATED FLAGS. global takes the values True, False, "False <xref .../>", "N/A <xref .../>" (TEREDO 2001::/32 and 6to4 2002::/16), and ABSENT (192.88.99.0/24 and 2001:10::/28, both deprecated). A sweep keyed on the first token finds 32. Each N/A and absent record needs a stated disposition.
2. MULTI-PREFIX AND ANNOTATED ADDRESS FIELDS. One ipv4 record lists "192.0.0.170/32, 192.0.0.171/32", and the existing split on ',' handles it. Two address fields carry an xref: "192.0.0.0/24 <xref .../>" and "2002::/16 <xref .../>". For 192.0.0.0/24 (global=False), the bit count "24 <xref ...>" fails the u32 parse and the prefix is SKIPPED by . MEASURED: this is the FOURTH silent exclusion, of the same class, in the address field rather than the flag. (2002::/16 is N/A, so it never reaches the address parse.) The 192.0.0.0/24 range is still denied by the shipped (192, 0 | 2 | 168, _) arm today.
3. NOTE 1 ON 2001::/23. It is global=False, but more-specific allocations inside it are global=True: 2001:1::1/128, 2001:1::2/128, 2001:1::3/128, 2001:3::/32, 2001:4:112::/48, 2001:20::/28, 2001:30::/28. A 2001::/23 probe must avoid those, and the fix must deny 2001:2::/48 ONLY. A /23 deny arm would over-deny seven global anycast or service allocations.
4. IPv4-MAPPED ::ffff:0:0/96 is global=False, but the fence canonicalizes it to IPv4 first (canonical_guarded_ip), so it is judged by IPv4 policy. The probe ::ffff:0:1 -> 0.0.0.1 is denied. ::ffff:8.8.8.8 is ADMITTED, correctly. The sweep's probe rule for this record must be stated, or the sweep will report either a false gap or a vacuous pass.
5. IPv6 OVER-DENIAL NOT RECORDED. 64:ff9b::/96 (NAT64 well-known) is global=True, and the arm [0x0064, 0xFF9B, 0, 0, 0, 0, ..] denies it. The FND-05 package body REQUIRES denying NAT64, so this is intended. But provenance.toml records only the two IPv4 over-denials (ipv4_reachable_prefixes_denied = 2) and has no ipv6 counterpart. (Mirror-indicated; the new shipped-surface sweep settles it.)

-- ProudValley (%1)

CORRECTION TO #5559, same author, minutes later. My shell substituted backticks while I edited that text, so two sentences are wrong as stored. ProudValley (%1).
1. The SEVERITY paragraph says "short by three" and "a shortfall of 3". Both should say FOUR (three at the flag, one at the address), as that comment's own heading and "Measured" line state: the gate examines 28 of 32 global=False records.
2. Item 2 reads "the prefix is SKIPPED by ." It should read: the prefix is SKIPPED by the parser's `continue` on a failed u32 bit-count parse.
Nothing else in #5559 changes. The measured figures stand: 32 records, 29 exactly "False", 28 examined; excluded are 127.0.0.0/8, 2001::/23, fc00::/7 (flag) and 192.0.0.0/24 (address).

comments.author: RoseStream
comments.text:
BAR-AUTHOR FINDING BEFORE THE BARS ARE WRITTEN: the approved four deny arms do NOT close the fence against the pinned registry. 2001::/23 leaves a FIFTH fail-open region, and a one-probe-per-prefix sweep cannot see it.
RoseStream (%26), third-party bar author named in WAVE16-RULINGS #21. Static reading plus a python model of the arms, labelled as a design aid and NOT as shipped-surface proof (it is 2647's mirror class). Nothing ticked. No code.

=== CONTACT, DECLARED ===
- On this bead: #2623 (2026-09-17), an adversarial peer audit assigned by WildMountain. It covered the fence under a caller-supplied resolver, the TLS host, early data, and a stale source-comment premise. It was review only: RoseStream wrote no code and no bar here.
- kjel: handed back, never touched.
- Rulings #21 lists kjel as RoseStream's only FND-05 contact. #2623 is a second one, and this comment corrects that.

=== SUBJECT ===
HEAD 545fb92b. crates/fastmcp-transport/src/http.rs blob 568d88ec (is_public_guarded_ipv6 / is_public_guarded_ipv4).
Registries: evidence/fnd-05/iana/iana-ipv6-special-registry.xml blob 08da69b6 and iana-ipv4-special-registry.xml blob eda3cd1f, both updated 2025-10-09, 25 records each.

=== THE FINDING ===
- The ipv6 registry marks 2001::/23 "IETF Protocol Assignments" global=False, footnote 1: "Unless allowed by a more specific allocation."
- The current arm is [0x2001, 0 | 0x0DB8, ..]. Inside the /23 it matches only 2001:0::/32 (Teredo). 2001:db8::/32 lies outside the /23.
- So 2001:1::/32 .. 2001:1ff::/32, except 2001:2::/48 once the proposed arm lands, are admitted. None of that space is globally reachable unless a more specific allocation says so.
- That includes 2001:10::/28, whose record's global field is EMPTY (deprecated ORCHID), and all unallocated space in the /23.

Model result: probing the FIRST and LAST address of every global=False prefix (20 ipv4, 13 ipv6; a record may list several prefixes, e.g. "192.0.0.170/32, 192.0.0.171/32"):
    arms at HEAD:                  9 probes admitted: both ends of the four known prefixes, plus 2001:1ff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff (the /23's last address)
    HEAD + the four proposed arms: 1 probe admitted:  2001:1ff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff
    ipv4:                          0 admitted under both
WHY #2562 MISSED IT: one probe per prefix. The /23's natural probe (2001::1) falls in Teredo 2001::/32, which the existing arm denies, so the rest of the /23 was never sampled.

=== THIS NEEDS A RULING, BECAUSE IT CHANGES APPROVED ITEM (1) ===
The /23 contains global=True sub-allocations:
- 2001:1::1/128, 2001:1::2/128, 2001:1::3/128 (PCP, TURN and DNS-SD anycast)
- 2001:3::/32 (AMT)
- 2001:4:112::/48 (AS112-v6)
- 2001:20::/28 (ORCHIDv2)
- 2001:30::/28 (Drone DET)

Options:
  (a) Deny 2001::/23 except those seven. This is the registry's exact semantics, but the arms are more complex, and the space between the exceptions needs its own probes.
  (b) Deny the whole 2001::/23. This fails closed and over-denies the seven anycast and service allocations. There is precedent: the ipv4 fence already over-denies 192.0.0.9/32 and 192.0.0.10/32 through its (192, 0, _) arm (#2562).
  (c) Keep the scope at four and declare the /23 remainder a gap. That contradicts item (3), "provenance gap rows 4 -> 0", and leaves the fence fail-open.
The bar author's recommendation: (b). None of the seven is a plausible HTTP fetch target, it matches the ipv4 precedent, and first/last-address probes decide it without a hand-written exception list. The bars are drafted so that one clause changes with the ruling; they are held, not written, until it arrives.

=== A SIDE OBSERVATION, OUT OF THIS BEAD'S SCOPE ===
The ipv4 arm (192, 0 | 2 | 168, _) denies ALL of 192.2.0.0/16. That is ordinary public space and appears in no registry record. TEST-NET-1 is 192.0.2.0/24 and is already covered by (192, 0, _). This is an over-denial: it fails closed, it is not a hole. It is recorded here for its owner and is not proposed for this change.

comments.author: RoseStream
comments.text:
SECOND BAR-AUTHOR FINDING: the existing IANA drift gate SILENTLY SKIPS 3 of the 33 global=False prefixes, including 2001::/23, and its count control cannot see it. Follows #5561. RoseStream (%26). Static reading, and the gate's parser replicated in python. Nothing ticked. No code.

=== SUBJECT ===
crates/fastmcp-transport/tests/fnd_05_iana_registry_drift.rs, blob d1e1d039, fn globally_unreachable_probes (it feeds the ratchet fnd_05_iana_classifier_gap_set_is_exactly_as_declared). Registries: ipv4 blob eda3cd1f, ipv6 blob 08da69b6.

=== THE DEFECT ===
- The gate keeps a record only if `element("global").as_deref() == Some("False")`, where element() returns the trimmed raw text between <global> and </global>.
- Footnoted records carry markup inside that element:
    ipv4 :131  <global>False <xref type="note" data="1"/></global>   127.0.0.0/8
    ipv6 :162  <global>False <xref type="note" data="1"/></global>   2001::/23
    ipv6 :357  <global>False <xref type="note" data="4"/></global>   fc00::/7
- Those three compare unequal to "False" and are skipped. No diagnostic is raised.
- Replicating the parser exactly gives 19 ipv4 + 11 ipv6 = 30 prefixes probed, against 20 + 13 = 33 global=False prefixes in the registries (an XML parse; one record lists two prefixes).
- The control `probes.len() >= 10` passes at 30, so it is a floor that cannot detect a partial parse.

=== CONSEQUENCE ===
- 127.0.0.0/8 and fc00::/7 are denied by the classifier anyway, so skipping them hides no gap TODAY. It does mean the gate would not notice a regression that opened them.
- 2001::/23 is the fifth fail-open region in #5561. The gate never sampled it, which is why the ratchet was green about a gap set that is incomplete.
- This is the 2647 class a second time: a self-authored instrument whose control checks that something was parsed, not that everything was.

=== BEARING ON THE BARS ===
The bars about to be written will freeze:
- An EXACT parse-count control for the new shipped-surface sweep: 20 ipv4 + 13 ipv6 = 33 prefixes at these two blobs. A refresh re-freezes it by review, never by regeneration.

title: FND-05 integration: public network capability boundary
description:
Executable I role for FND-05.

Owned capability slice: public network capability boundary.

<!-- MCP-2026-07-28-BRIDGE-V1:DESCRIPTION:FND-05:I:BEGIN -->
Canonical I role for FND-05.

Owned capability slice: public network capability boundary.
Named shipped consumer: public network capability boundary.
Rationale: none.

This role is self-contained against the following frozen package contract. The embedded package body is context, not separate capability credit:

### FND-05 — Prove HTTP, TLS, DNS, and streaming feasibility

Outcome:

Resolve transport feasibility before downstream HTTP and OAuth design
is treated as implementable.

Reason:

Core HTTP, client OAuth, and authorization metadata discovery all need
production HTTPS, streaming, cancellation, DNS, and redirect behavior.

Implementation:

- Spend at most five working days on the asupersync HTTP/1
  client/server spike. Stop earlier when every acceptance probe has a
  reproducible result; at the deadline, any missing primitive becomes
  a named upstream prerequisite rather than open-ended investigation.
- Prove request-scoped streaming server responses.
- Prove incremental client SSE consumption.
- Prove peer-disconnect cancellation.
- Prove bounded backpressure.
- Prove cancel-aware accept, header read, body read, and write.
- Prove client DNS hooks and redirect interception.
- Expose the proven destination/TLS/redirect/body controls as one
  auth-agnostic `GuardedHttpFetcher` in `fastmcp-transport`, parameterized
  by lower-layer policy/value types and with no dependency on
  `fastmcp-client`, `fastmcp-server`, or OAuth orchestration. AUTH-03
  and AUTH-06 build their role-specific request/response policy on
  that shared transport capability rather than duplicating it.
- Prove origin, peer, and TLS provenance capture.
- Prove ambiguous framing rejection.
- Prove socket-accept, TLS-handshake, pre-first-request,
  keep-alive-idle, total connection-lifetime, and request-count
  deadlines/admission from the instant each phase acquires ownership.
- Prove TLS client hostname and certificate validation.
- Force TLS 1.3 early data/0-RTT off for every FastMCP client and
  server configuration. Reject an injected rustls/asupersync connector
  that can send credential-bearing or state-changing request bytes as
  early data; ordinary session resumption without early data remains a
  separate admitted optimization.
- Prove connection-pool identity and invalidation hooks sufficient for
  AUTH-03: exact origin and pinned peer address, SNI/ALPN, TLS roots/
  client auth, egress proxy, destination-policy revision, and
  redirect-origin isolation. If those hooks are absent, guarded OAuth
  fetches must disable pooling rather than reuse a connection admitted
  under another trust policy.
- Prove capacity hooks sufficient to enforce LIMIT-01's per-origin/
  policy and process pool-identity, active/idle socket, queued
  acquisition, DNS/TLS-handshake, byte, wait, idle, absolute-lifetime,
  request-count, and shutdown bounds. Admit before DNS/connect, use
  bounded LRU only for unborrowed idle entries, never evict a borrowed
  socket, and retain charges while a stale/tightened-policy connection
  drains or is quarantined.
- On destination, root, client-auth, proxy, ALPN/SNI, peer-address, or
  policy revision, stop new borrows from the old identity and close/
  drain it within the bound. An auth fetch disables pooling unless both
  the complete trust-identity hooks and these capacity/lifecycle hooks
  are present; direct one-shot connections still consume the same
  global socket/DNS/TLS reservations.
- Prove TLS server termination or document the trusted-terminator
  boundary, including which trusted component enforces handshake and
  idle deadlines and releases connection reservations.
- Prove every client/server adapter can force an uncoded
  representation, emit canonical lowercase
  `Accept-Encoding: identity` on requests, omit `Content-Encoding` on
  uncoded sends, and disable automatic decompression. On receive,
  parse RFC 9110 `#list` syntax and ignore up to LIMIT-01's bounded
  empty-element allowance before semantic cardinality. Then accept only
  an absent field or one bare content-coding token whose value is
  ASCII-case-insensitively `identity`; reject a present all-empty value,
  empty-element saturation, parameters, duplicate field lines, two or
  more semantic codings, and every other coding before body processing.
- For the guarded-fetch destination classifier, canonicalize
  IPv4-mapped IPv6 and then apply the IPv4 policy. Deny rather than
  reinterpret every other embedded/transition range, including
  IPv4-compatible addresses, NAT64 well-known `64:ff9b::/96`, NAT64
  local-use `64:ff9b:1::/48`, 6to4 `2002::/16`, and Teredo
  `2001::/32`. Pin and review the IANA special-purpose IPv4/IPv6
  registry snapshot; a newly special range fails the drift gate before
  release. Apply the same answer-set and connected-peer rule to OAuth,
  CIMD, icon, and update-check fetches.
- Use asupersync's rustls-backed `tls` plus one reviewed root-store
  feature, normally `tls-native-roots` for deployed clients and a
  deterministic configured root store in tests.
- Inspect the exact feature graph and reject any prohibited runtime
  dependency.
- Remove `ureq` and every direct non-asupersync HTTP client. A CLI
  update check remains disabled unless implemented as an explicit
  bounded guarded-fetch policy with a fixed crates.io origin; it never
  runs eagerly at process startup.
- Distinguish enforceable library constraints from release-lock
  evidence. A JOSE-enabled consumer is constrained by protocol's exact
  direct `ring =0.17.14` edge. A non-JOSE downstream TLS consumer can
  still resolve a semver-compatible ring/rustls version allowed by
  asupersync; the repository/release lock and SBOM record the exact
  tested graph but do not constrain that downstream resolution.
  FND-05 must test both the locked release graph and fresh downstream
  lowest/latest-compatible resolutions, and word support accordingly.
- If a required primitive is missing, create an explicit asupersync
  prerequisite issue and block HTTP implementation rather than adding
  another async ecosystem.

Acceptance:

- The spike passes on Linux, macOS, and Windows targets used by CI.
- HTTPS validates hostname and trust roots.
- Disconnect cancels a child scope.
- No Tokio, reqwest, hyper, or prohibited adapter enters the graph.
- No `ureq`, second HTTP/TLS policy stack, or TLS early-data path enters
  the graph.
- The final HTTP abstraction is revised from measured behavior, not
  assumed behavior.
- High-cardinality origins or policy revisions cannot retain unbounded
  sockets, TLS buffers, DNS work, pool identities, or acquisition
  waiters.
- The spike closes within five working days with either all probes
  green or explicit blocking upstream issues and captured reproducers.

Tests:

- Streaming round trip.
- Disconnect cancellation.
- Slow-reader backpressure.
- TLS valid, wrong-host, untrusted-root, and expired-certificate cases.
- TLS 1.3 replay server, host-supplied connector, resumption, and
  feature-unification tests proving no MCP/OAuth request byte is sent
  as 0-RTT early data.
- Stalled/partial ClientHello, accepted socket with no request,
  post-response keep-alive idle, total lifetime/request-count
  boundary, and shutdown in every phase.
- Uncoded request/response probes with absent `Content-Encoding`,
  lowercase/uppercase/mixed-case singleton `identity` receive
  positives, plus leading/interior/trailing bounded empty-element
  variants. Cover all-empty, empty-element N/N+1, parameterized,
  duplicate-field, multi-semantic-coding, and other-coding negatives,
  canonical lowercase `Accept-Encoding: identity`, omitted response
  `Content-Encoding`, and auto-decompression disabled.
- DNS and redirect hook cases.
- IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible, NAT64 well-known/local-use, 6to4,
  Teredo, alternate-spelling, embedded-private-IPv4, mixed-answer, and
  connected-peer destination tests plus IANA registry drift.
- Pool-key isolation and live/idle invalidation under peer-address,
  roots, client-auth, ALPN/SNI, proxy, CIDR-policy, and redirect-origin
  changes.
- High-cardinality origin/policy-revision churn, HTTP/1 nonmultiplexed
  pressure, half-open DNS/connect/TLS, per-origin/global acquisition
  saturation, idle/absolute expiry, borrowed-versus-idle eviction,
  policy/root/proxy rotation, stale-drain accounting, cancellation, and
  bounded shutdown/exact-once socket release.
- Direct client and server wrapper conformance proving byte-identical
  guarded-fetch destination/redirect/encoding/pool decisions without a
