DIAGNOSED TO A MECHANISM DURING THE RCH OUTAGE. NO LANE USED, NONE NEEDED FOR THIS PART.
SilentSquirrel, 2026-09-22. This bead was filed undiagnosed on purpose; it is no longer.

=== IT IS NOT A DIFFERENT ASSERTION FAILING. IT IS THE SAME PUMP REPORTING AN EARLIER GUARD. ===
The failing line is `assert_eq!(data["run"]["data"]["stage"], "receive")` at lib.rs:47960, observed
left String("notification").
`stage: "notification"` is produced at EXACTLY THREE SITES, all `server_run_error("notification",
"send_failure", "Server notification send failed")`:
    lib.rs:18017   entered at the TOP of the pump loop
    lib.rs:18042   entered immediately after recv, BEFORE the message is interpreted
    lib.rs:18337
The first two are reached when `connection_failure` is already set, and both are preceded by a
`background_send_failure.take()` check that returns even earlier. The "receive" stage the test
wants comes from `transport_run_error("receive", ..)` at lib.rs:18087 -- which is DOWNSTREAM of
both.
So the pump loop's order is: pending background send failure -> connection failure -> cancellation
checkpoint -> recv -> re-check both -> interpret. A connection failure pending at loop entry
PREEMPTS the receive-stage error entirely. The test's expectation is reachable only if no send or
connection failure is outstanding when the loop turns.
THAT REFRAMES THE BEAD: the question is not "why did the receive assertion change" but "what is now
setting a connection/send failure in a scenario that previously reached recv cleanly". Those are
different investigations and the second one is the real one.

=== WHAT THE EXACT-LINE HISTORY SAYS, AND IT IS A USEFUL NEGATIVE ===
    git log -L 18013,18013:crates/fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs   ->  9db856dd
    "fix(server): retain subscription ownership through cancellation and shutdown"
The subject is tantalising -- this test is about subscription protocol failure after quiescence --
but 9db856dd PREDATES the 4ce3d3cc baseline at which this test passed. The preempting guard itself
did not move inside the regression window. Whatever changed is what FEEDS it.
I used the exact line, not a window around it: a range query would have swept in the neighbouring
comment block and named a commit that merely annotated the region.
INSTRUMENT CONTROL, because a `-S` zero and a broken `-S` look identical: `-S connection_failure`
and `-S background_send_failure` both returned EMPTY for the window, and a control run of
`-S bridge_would_starve_its_driver` over the same window returned 32562a0c. The instrument works,
so those two zeros are real: neither symbol's occurrence COUNT changed. That is not the same as
"the logic around them did not change", and I am not reading it as such.

=== THE SUSPECT SET, BOUNDED ===
Non-test commits touching fastmcp-server/src, fastmcp-core/src or fastmcp-transport/src in
4ce3d3cc..HEAD -- EIGHT, not one:
    2733db69 fix(cache): fence in-flight fills and hits across invalidation
    07b3c798 fix(tasks): preserve handoff ownership when restoration is rejected
    09e7e4a1 fix(proxy): retain all exact-2024 catalog pages
    4c051987 fix(server): enforce visibility and result bounds for legacy completion
    6d86ee5d feat(proxy): bound aggregate catalog retention
    32562a0c fix(core): name the sampling bridge that cannot complete
    db2c38f7 fix(server): use Outcome's own predicates, not Result's, in the machine tests
    6cf6d138 docs(6rfrg)
Narrowed to fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs ALONE, only ONE of them is non-test: 32562a0c. Every other
commit touching that file in the window is `test(server)` diagnostics for bd-f2ndd.
BUT THE OBVIOUS CAUSAL STORY RUNS BACKWARDS AND I WILL NOT TELL IT. 32562a0c's entire server-lib
change is four lines adding `enter_blocking_lane()` on pool threads, which makes
`bridge_would_starve_its_driver()` return FALSE there -- it makes the new refusal LESS likely to
fire, not more. So "the only production change in the file" is not thereby the cause. If 32562a0c
is involved it is through handler.rs (+38) or router.rs (+5) or the core changes, not through
those four lines.
`4c051987 fix(server): enforce visibility and result bounds for legacy completion` is the one I
would read next on subject alone -- this test is a legacy-era subscription scenario -- but subject
similarity is a search heuristic, not evidence, and I have not opened it.

=== RELATION TO bd-8wemr, STATED AS UNRESOLVED RATHER THAN GUESSED ===
I filed this bead as a different signature from bd-8wemr's four, and that observation stands:
those report stage "transport" / kind "pump_failure", this reports stage "notification" / kind
"send_failure". Different guards, different depths.
WHAT I CANNOT RULE OUT, and am recording so nobody reads my filing as having ruled it out: a single
trigger that sets a connection failure could surface as "notification/send_failure" in one scenario
and, where a pump returns a non-zero failure COUNT, as the outer "transport/pump_failure" in
another. The two shapes are compatible with one root. Settling it needs a run, and the lane is down.

not just the asserted node. `data["run"]["data"]` is one node of a nested structure and the bead has
only ever seen the one field the assertion happened to compare.

comments.author: SilentSquirrel
comments.text:
THE TWO BODIES READ AGAINST EACH OTHER: ONE CANDIDATE CAUSE FITS BOTH FAILURES, AND IT IS THE
BACKGROUND WRITE PATH RACING PUMP SHUTDOWN. Hypothesis with structural support, NOT a diagnosis.
SilentSquirrel, 2026-09-22. Source reads only, no lane.

=== WHAT EACH FAILURE ACTUALLY OBSERVED ===
peer_cancel_case(matching=false), lib.rs:47666  `assert_eq!(completions.len(), 1)` left 0 right 1
  The phase-3 assertions PASSED first: at EOF the owner was still present and NOT cancel-requested
  (:47613, :47614). So the test's own premise held -- the unrelated cancel did preserve the owner.
  What went missing is the TERMINAL RESPONSE for id 908 in the `sent` vector after the pump settled.
cleanup_case(release_before_shutdown=true), lib.rs:47960  stage "notification" where "receive" was
  required. Per my earlier comment that is the pump's guard order: a pending background-send
  failure, then `connection_failure`, are both checked BEFORE the loop reaches recv (:18006-:18046
  ahead of :18087).

=== THE SHARED SURFACE ===
Both are about a BACKGROUND SEND relative to the pump's lifecycle, from opposite sides:
  cleanup_case   a background send FAILURE landed early enough to preempt the stage the test wanted
  peer_cancel    a background send SUCCESS did not land early enough to be observed at all
That is one variable read twice: when does a background write complete relative to the pump loop's
next turn and its exit.
STRUCTURAL SUPPORT, quoted rather than asserted:
    lib.rs:14082   background_send_failure: Arc<Mutex<Option<McpError>>>   -- the flag cleanup_case
                   trips, shared state between a background writer and the pump
    lib.rs:6205    "`Cx::spawn_blocking` deliberately runs inline when an embedding runtime has ..."
    lib.rs:11420   "spawn_blocking can run inline without a caller-owned blocking pool"
    lib.rs:14113   "Never let spawn_blocking fall back to polling a blocking ..."
So whether background work runs INLINE or on a pool thread depends on how the embedding runtime was
provisioned -- and it changes the ordering.
AND THE FAMILY PROVISIONS IT EXPLICITLY. peer_cancel_case at :47562 builds its runtime with
`.blocking_threads(2, MAX_DISPATCH_QUEUE_DEPTH)`. That is a deliberate choice to give background
work real threads instead of inline execution, which is exactly the configuration in which its
completion can lag the observer.
This variable is already known to be load-bearing in this repo: bd-v9ev3's 654a1999 exists solely
to bind a different test's runtime to `.blocking_threads(0, 0)`.

=== WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING ===
I have NOT traced the terminal subscription completion to a spawn_blocking dispatch. I have shown
that the machinery exists, that the pump reads a background-failure flag, and that the family
provisions blocking threads on purpose. That makes the hypothesis worth testing; it does not make
it true. A different explanation -- the EOF path simply not emitting the completion under some
ordering -- fits peer_cancel just as well and would not involve a background write at all.
NOR does this explain why the member ALTERNATES. If one race governed both, I would expect either
member to be able to fail in any run; the two observations happened to hit different members, and
with n=2 that is not a pattern.

=== THE CHEAPEST NEXT TEST, AND WHY IT IS NOT AN EDIT ===
If the ordering hypothesis holds, the failure rate should be sensitive to blocking-thread
provisioning. The obvious experiment -- vary `.blocking_threads(..)` in these tests -- EDITS tests
whose expectations are under dispute, which is RH-3 adjacent and not mine while the rulings are
open.
The non-invasive version: trace the terminal completion's write path from the EOF branch to
whichever of the send closure or a background dispatch performs it. That is a source read and
settles whether the background path is even involved, which is the load-bearing link in the whole
hypothesis. I would do that before spending another slot on repetition.

comments.author: MagentaSummit
comments.text:
G3 SOURCE TRACE: THE STATED HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED FOR BOTH FAILURES. BOTH ARE ORDERING RACES AROUND THE SUBSCRIPTION ACKNOWLEDGEMENT, BY TWO DIFFERENT MECHANISMS.
MagentaSummit (assignee, WAVE16 rulings), 2026-09-22. Subject: HEAD 26697845, tree 60922d1e. Everything is cited by symbol; the line numbers were checked at that HEAD.
PROOF CLASS: STATIC (a source read). No run, no edit, no slot. Nothing here is ticked; the ticks belong to the certifier.
Declared contact: none before the 18:50Z assignment. My prior pane archive has 0 mentions of gl2we. Bar author confirmed from SilentSquirrel's pane: `br update bd-gl2we --actor SilentSquirrel --add-acceptance ...`. The events table has no row for that action.

=== WHAT G3 ASKS ===
G3 asks whether "a background write's completion relative to pump shutdown" governs BOTH observed assertions. The answer is NO for each of the two failures, for different reasons. They do share a surface: the acknowledgement step of `FinalSubscriptionRegistry::open` (inside `open_with_task_principal`), which runs on the subscription worker thread and races the receive pump.

=== FAILURE 1: unrelated_peer_cancel_preserves_owner_until_eof (`returning_subscription_peer_cancel_case(false)`) ===
Observed: `completions.len()` was 0, where 1 was required. The assertions before it passed: the join was Ok, the caller was not cancelled, and `active` was empty.

(a) THE BACKGROUND RESPONSE WRITE IS EXONERATED. In `dispatch_or_schedule_stdio_modern_request`, the SUBSCRIPTIONS_LISTEN branch does three things in order:
  1. The worker closure calls `send_guard(...)` with the response.
  2. Only AFTER that does it call `drop(active_guard)`.
  3. `impl Drop for ActiveRequestGuard` removes the map entry and then calls `completion.mark_done()`.
`cancel_active_requests(Shutdown, true)` waits on that same completion (`RequestCompletion::wait_timeout`). So once `active` is empty, the worker has already finished any send it was going to make. A late write cannot slip past the shutdown drain.
So `active` empty with 0 completions means the worker produced NO RESPONSE AT ALL. It was not late.

(b) `poll_on_cx` IS EXONERATED. It loops until `Poll::Ready` and never abandons the future when the Cx is cancelled. A cancelled request_cx cannot turn a response into None.

(c) WHERE THE NONE COMES FROM. Near its end, `dispatch_stateless_owned_with_cancellation` returns None exactly when three conditions hold:
    request.method == SUBSCRIPTIONS_LISTEN
    && request_cancellation.is_cancel_requested()
    && !graceful_subscription_completion
So the listen handler returned Err(request_cancelled) rather than the elected completion.

(d) THE RACE THAT PRODUCES THAT.
  1. `open` delivers the acknowledgement through `notification_sender(acknowledgement)` while the phase is still `Opening`. The `Opening -> Active` transition happens only afterwards, in the loop that follows, under the phase lock.
  2. The test's recv closure is released by the acknowledgement callback, at `acknowledged.send(())` inside the callback. That is BEFORE the callback returns and BEFORE `Active` is set.
  3. The pump thread then does phase 2 (cancel 909, handled inline), then phase 3 (EOF), then `Ok(())`, then `graceful_shutdown_returning`.
If the pump gets there first:
  4. `terminate_subscription_streams` -> `terminate_removed_entry` finds the lease in `Opening`, with no cancel requested. It sets `ServerTerminationPending(0)` and does NOT set `graceful_completion`, because that is deferred to `open`.
  5. `graceful_shutdown_returning` then calls `cancel_active_requests(CancelKind::Shutdown, true)` immediately, which cancels this request's `McpRequestCancellation`.
  6. `open` resumes and takes the phase lock. Its arm `ServerTerminationPending(0) if !request_cancellation.is_cancel_requested()` no longer matches. It falls through to the catch-all arm: `PeerTerminated`, then `Err(McpError::request_cancelled())`.
  7. The handler returns that error through `?`, and the dispatcher suppresses the response under (c).
Even if `open` had won the arm, `complete_final_subscription_server_termination` would still refuse, because it checks `request_cancellation.is_cancel_requested() && !terminal_committed`, and `terminal_delivery` is None for the stdio listen.
This accounts for EVERY assertion outcome in the failing run: the owner was present and not cancel-requested at phase 3, the join was Ok, the caller was preserved, `active` was empty, and completions were 0.

(e) WHY IT IS A CANDIDATE PRODUCT DEFECT, not only a test artefact. `graceful_shutdown_returning` and `graceful_shutdown` both do `let _ = self.terminate_subscription_streams();` and then cancel generically without waiting. Nothing lets a `ServerTerminationPending` election settle first.
The HTTP lifecycle does differently: it calls `terminate_with_receipt()` and waits on `receipt.is_settled()` (the bounded loop followed by `fail_pending()`). But that receipt tracks only `terminal_delivery`, which is None for stdio, so reusing it would not help as is.
Consequence: a stdio peer that sends EOF between receiving the acknowledgement and the opener reaching `Active` loses the graceful terminal completion. The comment on `graceful_shutdown` ("Subscription teardown owns ... the matching completion result before generic active-request cancellation") states an ordering that the code does not enforce for this phase.

=== FAILURE 2: protocol_failure_after_quiescence_runs_hook (`returning_subscription_cleanup_case(true, true)`) ===
Observed: `data.run.data.stage` was "notification", where "receive" was required.

(a) THE BACKGROUND RESPONSE WRITE IS NOT INVOLVED. A `background_send_failure` carries `returning_send_result`'s `transport_run_error("send", ..)`, which is stage "send", never "notification". Stage "notification" is produced ONLY by the `connection_failure` guards in `run_loop_returning_legacy`, all of which build `server_run_error("notification", "send_failure", ...)`. Here `connection_failure` is the `notification_failure` flag that `run_transport_returning_with_cx` passes in.
Comment 5338's framing ("a background send FAILURE landed early") names the wrong writer.

(b) WHAT SETS THE FLAG. `create_transport_notification_sender` stores `failure = true` on any send error that is not a cancellation. `SharedTransport::send` uses `try_lock()` and returns `WouldBlock` ("transport receive owns the unsplit I/O handle") whenever `SharedTransport::recv` holds the same mutex. `recv` holds that mutex for the whole duration of the inner `recv` call.

(c) THE RACE. In `CloseAfterDrainTransport::recv`, phase 2 with release_before_shutdown=true, the pump thread does the following while HOLDING the SharedTransport lock:
  1. It waits for `started`.
  2. It calls `release()`.
  3. It waits for `finished`. `finished` is set by `NonQuiescentLegacyControl::wait_until_released` as the middleware's `on_request` returns.
  4. Only then does it build the invalid response and return, which drops the lock.
Meanwhile, once `finished` is set, the worker proceeds into the listen handler and then into `open`, where `notification_sender(acknowledgement)` calls `SharedTransport::send` and then `try_lock`.
  - If the worker reaches try_lock before step 4 completes: `WouldBlock`, the flag is set, and the post-recv `connection_failure` guard in the pump returns stage "notification" before the invalid response is classified.
  - Otherwise, the response is classified as intended and returns stage "receive".
The flag cannot come from the top-of-loop guard: no acknowledgement can be sent before the middleware is released, and that release happens inside this recv.

=== THE SHARED FACTOR, STATED NARROWLY ===
Both tests synchronise on an event that PRECEDES the state their expectation needs:
  - peer_cancel waits for "the ack callback was invoked", but needs "the opener has reached Active".
  - cleanup waits for "middleware finished", but needs "the pump has released the transport lock before the ack is sent".
The two mechanisms differ: a lost graceful election in one, and a `try_lock` contention on an unsplit transport in the other. They do NOT share a single cause. Their only common factor is that the ack is emitted from a worker thread concurrently with the pump.
They also move in OPPOSITE directions under scheduling: failure 1 needs the PUMP to win, and failure 2 needs the WORKER to win. That alone is evidence against one shared cause, and it is consistent with the member alternating between runs.
`blocking_threads(2, MAX_DISPATCH_QUEUE_DEPTH)` is present in all three bodies. It is what makes the worker a separate thread, but because every body has it, it cannot discriminate between them.

=== PRE-REGISTERED EXPOSURE FOR THE G1/G2 CARDS (denominator 8, as ruled) ===
EXPOSED (3):
  - quiescence_runs_hook_after_owner_retirement            cleanup(true,false)   mechanism 2, same guard
  - protocol_failure_after_quiescence_runs_hook            cleanup(true,true)    mechanism 2 (observed at 8b6a6f71)
  - unrelated_peer_cancel_preserves_owner_until_eof        peer_cancel(false)    mechanism 1 (observed at 744caeba)
NOT EXPOSED BY EITHER MECHANISM (5):
  - nonquiescence_preserves_operation_and_close_errors      cleanup(false,false)  the ack cannot precede the post-result release
  - protocol_failure_preserves_cleanup_and_close_errors     cleanup(false,true)   same reason
  - background_response_write_succeeds                     background_write      `RejectListen` refuses before `open`, so there is no ack
  - background_response_write_failure_survives_eof         background_write      same reason
  - matching_peer_cancel_retires_only_its_owner            peer_cancel(true)     mechanism 1 is possible, but its assertion expects zero completions, so it cannot SEE it
DISCONFIRMERS:
  - A failure in any of the 5 refutes this account as a complete explanation.
  - A failure among the 3 that shows a signature other than the one named above also refutes it.

=== BOUNDARIES ===
  - STATIC ONLY. This establishes that each mechanism is reachable and fits every observed assertion outcome. It does NOT show that these interleavings are what occurred in the two recorded runs. A run cannot show that either, short of instrumentation.
  - A deterministic reproduction would need NEW test code that forces each interleaving. G5 forbids retiring or loosening a family member, but it does not forbid adding a test. I am asking the certifier whether that is in scope before writing any.
  - PL-3: `run_transport_returning_with_cx` routes through `run_loop_returning_legacy` only under `any(feature = "legacy-2024-11-05", test)`. That feature IS in fastmcp-server's `default`. A no-legacy facade profile uses `run_loop_pump_with_policy` instead, which this trace did not read. `SharedTransport::send`'s `try_lock` is shared by both paths.
  - G5: whether mechanism 1 is a product defect is for whoever owns the subscription surface to rule. The same applies to mechanism 2's unsplit-transport ack contention, which would affect any unsplit custom transport whose pump sits in a blocking recv when a listen acknowledges. No repair is proposed here.
  - G7: nothing here bears on bd-v9ev3's six or bd-8wemr's four.

comments.author: MagentaSummit
comments.text:
FORCED-INTERLEAVING TESTS LANDED (de960060), AND THE CANDIDATE PRODUCT DEFECT RECORDED AS A FINDING, NOT A FIX.
MagentaSummit (assignee), 2026-09-22, under WAVE16 RULINGS #2 (MagentaSummit, Ask 2: in scope, bounded).
Commit de960060 on main, also pushed to master. Blob of crates/fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs: 951e74b5.
The diff is add-only: 367 insertions, 0 deletions, one file. Parent: 6c53f223.

=== NEW TEST IDs, DECLARED; THEY ARE NOT IN G2's DENOMINATOR OF 8 ===
All four are in `-p fastmcp-server --lib`, module lib_unit_tests (#[cfg(test)]). They use the prefix `forced_subscription_ack_order_`, so no `returning_subscription_*` filter can select them.
  lib_unit_tests::forced_subscription_ack_order_pump_first_loses_graceful_completion
  lib_unit_tests::forced_subscription_ack_order_active_first_keeps_graceful_completion
      Body: `forced_subscription_shutdown_order_case(pump_first)`. This forces mechanism 1.
  lib_unit_tests::forced_subscription_ack_order_under_recv_lock_reports_notification_stage
  lib_unit_tests::forced_subscription_ack_order_outside_recv_lock_reports_receive_stage
      Body: `forced_subscription_recv_lock_order_case(ack_under_recv_lock)`. This forces mechanism 2.
Helpers: `final_subscription_phases` and `wait_for_single_active_final_subscription`. They read lease phases without holding two locks at once. `Active` is the proof that the acknowledgement was already attempted.

=== HOW EACH PAIR FORCES ITS ORDER, AND WHAT MAKES THE NEGATIVE NEAR-IDENTICAL ===
Mechanism 1. Both variants use the same frames (opening discovery, listen 910, EOF) and the same wait for the ack signal. The ONLY difference is who waits for whom:
  - pump_first: the ack callback blocks inside `open` (so the lease stays `Opening`) until an active owner's cancellation is requested. That cancellation comes from shutdown's `cancel_active_requests`.
    Expected: no response for 910 at all, `active` empty, clean Ok.
  - active-first: recv holds EOF until the lease is `Active`.
    Expected: exactly one response, which is `final_subscription_completion_response`.
Mechanism 2. Both variants use the same frames (opening discovery, listen 911, inline discovery 907, invalid response 912) and the same release-then-wait-for-`Active` step. The ONLY difference is WHERE that step runs:
  - under the lock: inside `recv`, which `SharedTransport::recv` calls with its mutex held.
    Expected: stage notification / send_failure, and 0 acknowledgements reach the transport.
  - outside the lock: in middleware for request 907, dispatched inline on the pump after recv has released the mutex.
    Expected: stage receive / invalid_response, and 1 acknowledgement written.
The acknowledgement count is a second observable in the transport, so the stage is not the only discriminator.
FORCING CONTROL: every case sets a `forced` flag only when its wait actually reached the target state, and asserts that flag. A run where the interleaving was not reached fails; it cannot pass as green.

A fix ruled by the subscription surface's owner inverts that expectation, and that change needs its own semantic review (RH-3).

UBS showed 0 findings in the inserted range; the file carries a large existing baseline elsewhere. Compile and run belong to card #5.
  - Nothing ticked.

=== FINDING (candidate product defect; G5 routes the fix to the unnamed subscription-surface owner) ===
F1. STDIO SHUTDOWN CAN LOSE A GRACEFUL SUBSCRIPTION COMPLETION.
  `graceful_shutdown_returning` and `graceful_shutdown` call `let _ = self.terminate_subscription_streams();` and then call `cancel_active_requests(CancelKind::Shutdown, true)` immediately.
  When `terminate_removed_entry` finds a lease still in `Opening` (the acknowledgement callback is still running), it records `ServerTerminationPending(0)` and leaves the graceful election to the opener.
  The generic cancel that follows then makes the opener's `ServerTerminationPending(0) if !request_cancellation.is_cancel_requested()` arm unreachable, so the listen ends in `Err(request_cancelled)` and its response is suppressed.
  The HTTP lifecycle instead waits on `terminate_with_receipt()` / `receipt.is_settled()`. That receipt tracks `terminal_delivery`, which is None for stdio, so it is not a drop-in fix.
  The comment on `graceful_shutdown` promises that subscription teardown owns the completion "before generic active-request cancellation"; for this phase that ordering is not enforced.
F2. ON AN UNSPLIT TRANSPORT, A LISTEN ACKNOWLEDGEMENT SENT WHILE THE PUMP IS IN recv FAILS THE CONNECTION.
  `SharedTransport::send` uses `try_lock` and returns `WouldBlock` whenever `recv` holds the mutex. `create_transport_notification_sender` treats that as a failed send and sets the connection-failure flag, and the pump then terminates with stage "notification".
  Whether this is intended for unsplit transports is the owner's ruling. Its reach is any `run_transport_returning_with_cx` embedding whose pump blocks in `recv` while a modern listen acknowledges.
No repair is proposed or made. Both findings join the operator escalation for a subscription-surface owner.

title: WebSocket catalog listener: request-local cancellation does not wake the parked reader (6d09b827's own gated test fails)
description:
Outside commit 6d09b827 ("make WebSocket subscription cancellation and receive ownership safe", committed unrun) added websocket_async_* tests gated #[cfg(feature = "websocket-experimental")]. At default features they never compile, so no default run has exercised them. With --all-features, one of its own tests FAILS on main:

    tests::websocket_async_catalog_listener_cancel_interrupts_silent_receive_and_keeps_client
    panicked at crates/fastmcp-client/src/lib.rs:24345:22:
    request-local cancellation wakes the parked reader: Elapsed { deadline: Time(578889942ns) }

Observed by WildMountain run v34: cargo test --locked -j 4 -p fastmcp-client --lib --all-features -- websocket_async native_machine_finite native_machine_tasks, at clean RCH snapshot 9eceaec8: 44 passed, 1 failed. The 34 other websocket_async tests pass, including the task-listener twin websocket_async_task_listener_cancel_interrupts_silent_receive_and_keeps_catalog, so the gap is specific to the catalog listener: its request-local cancellation does not wake a reader parked on a silent receive. One run so far; confirm determinism by re-running the single test, but the twin passing points to a real path difference, not load.

Acceptance (amended by WildMountain per ruling 5840, before verification; see comment):
- [x] Request-local cancellation of a catalog-listener waiter running in the caller's region (the supported pattern, asupersync child_region.rs:204-210) wakes it promptly and reports RequestCancelled, and the client stays usable. The product path is fixed: the cancellation notice is sent under the connection's context (retire_committed_request_after_cancellation). No test deadline is changed.
- [x] websocket_async_catalog_listener_cancel_interrupts_silent_receive_and_keeps_client passes with only the waiter's placement changed (ruling 5840: all 4 cases kept, every assertion textually identical). Its task-listener twin passes, and so does the new near-identical negative websocket_async_catalog_listener_region_waiter_stays_live_without_cancellation.
- [x] Clean-snapshot RCH: cargo test -p fastmcp-client --lib --all-features -- websocket green (every executed websocket_async test, now 36 including the negative).
close_reason: Verified by run:vh4fz6-ws at commit:fa708516. evidence: WildMountain batch verify at fa708516 (contains a455e820), clean snapshot, -j 2, vmi1152480: cargo test -p fastmcp-client --lib --all-features -- websocket = 52 passed / 0 failed / 0 ignored, remote exit=0; 36 websocket_async tests OK, including websocket_async_catalog_listener_cancel_interrupts_silent_receive_and_keeps_client, websocket_async_task_listener_cancel_interrupts_silent_receive_and_keeps_catalog and the new negative websocket_async_catalog_listener_region_waiter_stays_live_without_cancellation. Product fix: retire_committed_request_after_cancellation sends the control under the connection cx with the unchanged WEBSOCKET_CANCELLATION_CONTROL_SEND_TIMEOUT_NANOS bound; no deadline changed (the test's 500 ms bounds went 5 -> 7, all additions). Diff: asserts -1/+7, and the one removal is the same assert moved out of the if/else. AC amended per ruling 5840 (5852).

comments.text: Reproduced a 2nd time: run v35 at clean e65f17bb (client lib --all-features, filter catalog|cursor), worker vmi1152480: the same test FAILED, while 96 others passed. The first was v34 at 9eceaec8 on worker vmi1227854. 2 of 2 runs, so likely deterministic, not load.

comments.author: WildMountain
comments.text:
Ruling (WildMountain; the RH-1 semantic review of a test change, separate from the implementer ProudValley):

Confirmed from source. asupersync 0.5.0 src/cx/child_region.rs:204-210 says ChildRegion's principal cx "carries the child region's identity, effective (met) budget, and pending-spawn credits ... Handlers that need checkpoint-observable cancellation should run as spawned tasks". So the two region-cancel cases in 6d09b827's test hand a principal ChildRegion cx to a waiter polled from another task and expect a cancel no code can observe through that cx. 6d09b827 is an outside commit whose gated test was never run.

Option 2 is approved, with one condition:
- CONDITION (product check first): show that every shipped path that gives a request-local Cx to a WebSocket catalog or task listener supplies a spawned task's context, not a ChildRegion principal cx. If any shipped path hands out a principal cx, the product is broken there. Fix that path to run the request work as a spawned task (not a sentinel), and keep the test's region cases as the proof.
- Test change allowed: only the waiter's placement in the two region-cancel cases changes (spawned into the region, the documented pattern). Keep all four cases (acknowledged or not, token or region) and every assertion byte-identical.
- Negative: near-identical region case with no cancel. The waiter is not interrupted within the same window, and the client and catalog stay usable.
- Cite child_region.rs:204-210 in the commit message. Option 1 (sentinel task per parked wait) is rejected: it adds runtime cost to paper over a test that models an unsupported pattern.

comments.author: ProudValley
comments.text:
ProudValley submission for batch verify (ruling 5840, option 2). Code: a455e820 (fix(client): send a WebSocket cancellation control under the connection context when the caller's task is the one cancelled), merged as 17c21105 and then fa708516 (plain merges; the diff against ^2 is only crates/fastmcp-client/src/lib.rs, +193/-13). Pushed to main and master at fa708516. lib.rs blob cd42e893 as tested.
Root cause (two per-case diagnostics, uncommitted): token cancel woke the parked reader in about 100 us. In the region-cancel cases request_cx never reported cancellation, because a ChildRegion's principal Cx does not observe ChildRegion::cancel (asupersync 0.5.0 child_region.rs:204-210).
Audit per 5840: no shipped path hands a principal Cx to a WebSocket listener. Client-crate callers are all in mod tests. The facade's WebSocketClient wrappers (fastmcp/src/lib.rs:1601, 4159, 4194) pass the caller's cx through. The CLI uses the stdio and HTTP clients, the server has no WebSocketClient, and every shipped open_child_region is server side (async_stdio.rs:489, lib.rs:1540, router.rs:1819/1829, proxy.rs:4096 stdio listener).
Test: the waiter placement changed only in the two region cases, which now run it as a task spawned into the request region. The task returns the client and its result through slots (test-only ReturnOnDrop), because a region-cancelled task's join may discard its output (observed as JoinError::Cancelled). All four cases and every assertion are identical.
Product defect exposed and fixed: retire_committed_request_after_cancellation polled the masked control send and its timeout_at bound under the ambient task. A cancelled ambient task makes Sleep complete at once (sleep.rs:764), which caused a spurious Timeout, then InternalError, and the connection closed. The send and its bound are now polled under Cx::set_current(connection_cx); the mask and the 100 ms bound are unchanged.
Negative: websocket_async_catalog_listener_region_waiter_stays_live_without_cancellation (same placement, no cancel: the waiter stays pending, then the peer's acknowledgement is delivered as Ok(Acknowledged) and the listener stays live). The bound is kept, as shown by websocket_async_cancellation_bounds_a_stalled_control_send_without_detaching_it and websocket_async_subscription_cancellation_bounds_stalled_control_send.
Proof (RCH, cargo test --locked -j 4 -p fastmcp-client --lib --all-features -- websocket):
- base 2015de36 with overlay, hz4: 52 passed / 0 failed.
- merged 17c21105 with no overlay, vmi1149989: 52 passed / 0 failed.
fa708516 adds over 17c21105 only upstream OAuth http_auth modules (managed.rs and persistence/renewal), which touch neither lib.rs nor any WebSocket code.
Earlier runs retained: h4fz6_proof (35/1, test join before the product fix) and h4fz6_proof2 (51/1, JoinError::Cancelled discarding the output), plus one hz4 dep-info void.

comments.text: Acceptance amended by WildMountain before verification. The original items ('passes unchanged', 'all 35') predate the root cause: the region-cancel cases modelled a pattern asupersync does not support (child_region.rs:204-210). Ruling 5840 allowed only the waiter's placement to change, after PV's product-path audit (40479). The amended items keep every capability check (prompt wake, RequestCancelled, client usable, product-path fix, twin), add the new negative, and ban deadline changes. Self-contained canonical parent contract follows verbatim:

Authoritative work package from `COMPREHENSIVE_PLAN_TO_SUPPORT_MCP_2026-07-28_SPEC_IN_FASTMCP_RUST.md`:

### PXY-04 — Reconstruct HTTP routing and auth safely

Outcome:

Generate correct upstream HTTP headers without forwarding downstream
credentials or unsafe custom values.

Reason:

Headers are derived protocol data and authorization is audience-bound.

Implementation:

- Recompute protocol version.
- Recompute method.
- Recompute name.
- Recompute annotated parameter headers from validated schemas.
- Apply exact encoding.
- Consume only HTTP-02's `ValidatedForwardingHeaders` capsule; proxy
  code never receives or reconstructs raw ingress headers.
- Forward every capsule field unchanged as required for an
  intermediate server unless it conflicts case-insensitively with a
  recognized field the gateway recomputes.
- Require the capsule constructor to have enforced syntax, per-field,
  aggregate-count, and aggregate-byte bounds before authentication and
  to have excluded Authorization, Cookie, proxy credentials,
  hop-by-hop headers, and every ordinary MCP singleton header.
- Ignore unrecognized `Mcp-Param-*` fields locally; never interpret
  them as credentials or authorization facts.
- Acquire upstream-specific credentials.
- Never forward downstream Authorization directly.
- Detect the confused-deputy topology where this MCP proxy presents one
  static client ID to a third-party authorization server while
  accepting dynamically registered downstream clients. Before the
  first upstream authorization or forwarding action for each
  downstream client, require explicit user consent for the tuple
  `(verified user, downstream client_id, upstream issuer/resource,
  proxy static client_id, redirect URI, consent-policy revision)`.
- Persist that consent only through an injected authorization-owned
  consent store with bounded lifetime, revocation, exact tuple
  matching, redacted audit records, and fail-closed corruption/outage
  behavior. Consent for one downstream client, user, upstream, redirect
  URI, or policy revision never authorizes another.
- Require that store to return an opaque authenticated
  `ProxyConsentGrant` from a declared integrity/rollback-resistant
  trust boundary. Revalidate it before every upstream authorization/
  contact and throughout long-lived subscription/task work, not only
  before the first token acquisition. Include grant identity,
  revision, and expiry in upstream credential, cache, route,
  continuation, subscription, and task-mapping keys.
- On consent expiry/revocation/policy change, atomically prevent new
  upstream contact, drop cached upstream credentials, invalidate
  dependent caches/handles, and terminate active proxy streams/
  management work with an explicit outcome. Never continue using a
  cached token merely because consent existed when it was issued.
- On absence, denial, expiry, revocation, or tuple mismatch, do not
  contact the third-party authorization endpoint and do not forward
  the request. Static deployment configuration is not user consent.
- Strip hop-by-hop and unrecognized sensitive headers.
- Preserve only OBS-01's outbound-policy-approved trace context.
  Evaluate source/destination origin, tenant, and security domain on
  each hop; drop baggage/tracestate by default at a boundary and bind
  the policy revision to redacted route/cache diagnostics.
- Apply an explicit metadata policy: preserve registered extension
  metadata negotiated on both legs, preserve standard trace context
  under OBS-01, rewrite server identity, drop raw/unknown
  security-sensitive keys, and keep other unknown namespaced metadata
  only when the configured transparent-forwarding policy and both-leg
  size limits permit it.
- Before emitting a stateless modern extension notification upstream,
  consume the downstream `AuthorizedNotificationWork`, discard its
  sealed downstream activation proof, and build a distinct
  `UpstreamNotificationActivationProof` under the selected upstream
  descriptor, endpoint, credential/security partition, effective
  settings, owner, and descriptor/policy/configuration generations.
  For `SelfContained`, revalidate and reserialize only the sanitized
  extension-owned current-message field under the upstream schema and
  resolver. For `NegotiatedOwner`, resolve a gateway-owned mapping to a
  separately live upstream owner and revalidate that owner immediately;
  never copy the downstream handle or treat the mapping record itself
  as owner authority. If either construction fails, emit no upstream
  bytes and create no upstream handler/supervisor effect. No capsule,
  trace field, generic metadata, or forwarded header can substitute for
  this proof.
- Disable automatic redirects and reject every upstream MCP 3xx on
  both proxy legs. Never replay/retarget a request body, forward either
  leg's credentials/cookies/capsule to a Location, or rebind route,
  resource, era, consent, or cache identity. If the prior endpoint may
  have received bytes, propagate an explicit uncertain-dispatch
  outcome without retry.
- Redact both legs independently.

Acceptance:

- Header/body equality holds on the upstream request.
- Credentials are issued for the upstream resource.
- Downstream tokens never appear upstream.
- Header injection cannot cross the gateway.
- Unrecognized valid `Mcp-Param-*` headers survive one and multiple
  intermediary hops without local activation.
- No API permits gateway code to obtain a raw Authorization, Cookie,
  or arbitrary header map.
- Metadata never broadens extension negotiation or crosses a
  security-policy deny rule.
- Downstream notification activation evidence terminates at the
  gateway; upstream emission requires a separately sealed current-
  message proof with upstream bindings.
- A static upstream client ID cannot turn the proxy into a confused
  deputy for a dynamically registered downstream client.
- Cached credentials and long-lived proxy work cannot survive consent
  loss.

Tests:

- Header reconstruction.
- Base64 encoding.
- Credential audience isolation.
- Hop-by-hop stripping.
- CRLF injection.
- Unknown valid custom-header forwarding, collision, oversize, and
  multi-hop cases.
- Capsule construction/consumption compile tests and forbidden-header
  exclusion matrix.
- Same-trust trace propagation, cross-trust baggage/tracestate drop,
  sensitive allowlist denial, unrelated-upstream leakage, and
  trace-dependent cache-isolation tests.
- Metadata allow/drop/rewrite matrix.
- Stateless extension-notification proxy matrix covering independent
  self-contained reconstruction, negotiated-owner mapping/
  revalidation, downstream-proof/handle/generation substitution,
  stale or missing upstream owner, representation mismatch, and exact
  zero-byte upstream rejection.
- Per-downstream-client static-ID proxy consent, cross-client/user/
  upstream/redirect/policy isolation, denial-before-upstream-contact,
  expiry/revocation, consent-store outage/corruption, and redacted
  audit tests.
- Cached-token-after-consent-revocation, consent revision/key
  invalidation, active subscription/task mapping, stream teardown,
  rollback-resistant store, and no-upstream-contact-after-loss tests.
- Redacted dual-leg trace.
- 301/302/303/307/308 same/cross-origin rejection on both legs,
  method/body non-replay, credential/capsule stripping, DNS-rebinding
  Location, redirect loop, and partial-send uncertain-dispatch tests.

title: SubscriptionFilter absorbs misspelled keys silently: flatten catch-all without deny_unknown_fields
description:
SubscriptionFilter (crates/fastmcp-protocol/src/messages.rs:1445) carries
`#[serde(flatten, default)] pub additional: BTreeMap<String, Value>` and does NOT carry
`deny_unknown_fields`, while its own container FinalSubscriptionsListenParams DOES.

CONSEQUENCE, observed rather than hypothesised: a misspelled field name is silently
absorbed into `additional` and the corresponding typed field stays None. Found
2026-09-17 in the merged OAuth subscription tests, where a fixture wrote "resources"
instead of the canonical "resourceSubscriptions" on BOTH sides of the exchange, so a
test named ..._acknowledgment_narrows_the_filter_... requested nothing to narrow and
asserted against a field that was never populated.

WHY IT HAD NO SYMPTOM (HazyTurtle's framing, and it is the point of this bead): the
only thing that would have caught it was a build of a target that never compiled. A
flattened catch-all plus a never-built target is a defect that cannot produce a symptom
by construction. Fixing those particular tests removes the instance and leaves the
class: every future caller of SubscriptionFilter inherits the same silent absorption.

NAMED CONSUMER: every producer/parser of SubscriptionFilter, in particular the
client_credentials core subscription path and any server-side filter admission.
GATE: wire-level field-name correctness for subscription filters.
OBSERVED DEFECT CLASS: misspelled or renamed filter key accepted silently, typed field
left None, downstream behaviour silently narrowed to nothing.
DELETION CONDITION: closes when SubscriptionFilter either rejects unknown keys or a
positive+planted-negative pair proves a misspelled key is observable to a caller.

IN SCOPE: decide and implement ONE of --
  (a) deny_unknown_fields on SubscriptionFilter (breaks forward-compat extensibility --
      check the MCP 2026-07-28 text on unknown notification-filter members first), or
  (b) keep `additional` but make absorption OBSERVABLE: a typed accessor or a
      debug-assert-level check that reports keys which case-insensitively or
      edit-distance-match a canonical field name. A key that is one capital letter away
      from a real field is a bug, not an extension.
Whichever is chosen, it needs a positive AND a near-identical planted negative
differing only in the spelling of one key.

EXPLICITLY NOT IN SCOPE: the six test repairs in
crates/fastmcp-client/src/http_auth/discovery/client_credentials/subscriptions.rs.
Those are HazyTurtle's, authorised separately, and they fix the INSTANCE. This bead is
the CLASS and must not be used to delay or absorb them.
close_reason: Batch-verify PASS at commit:734f6d4c. 4 passed / 0 failed / 0 filtered out on the owner's own runner card, exit=0. Option (b) chosen on evidence: the authoritative schema has ZERO closed objects across 155 definitions so option (a) would reject wire messages the spec permits, and (a) was additionally a compile-clean no-op because deny_unknown_fields checks the residual after a map catch-all consumes it. Matcher rule corrected from the bead's own text, which would have shipped a detector blind to its founding case. Receipt: comment 2718.

comments.author: MagentaOsprey
comments.text:
IMPLEMENTED — option (b). Commit 734f6d4c, 2 files, +226/-0.

DECISION AND WHY (a) WAS REJECTED. The bead asked me to check the MCP
2026-07-28 text first. It decides against (a), and a second independent reason
also does.

  1. BY SPEC. evidence/fnd-01/vendor/core/mcp-schema-2026-07-28-5f5440bb.json
     declares SubscriptionFilter with four properties and NO
     additionalProperties key, so unknown members are permitted by JSON Schema
     default. Across all 155 definitions that schema uses additionalProperties
     20 times and "additionalProperties": false ZERO times. There are no closed
     objects anywhere in the core schema. deny_unknown_fields would refuse wire
     messages the specification allows.

  2. BY MECHANISM. deny_unknown_fields beside
     #[serde(flatten)] additional: BTreeMap<String, Value> compiles clean and
     does NOTHING. serde_derive-1.0.229 src/de/struct_.rs:347 emits the deny
     check over the RESIDUAL of __collect after flatten targets deserialize; a
     map catch-all consumes every entry, so the check can never fire. In-repo
     contrast proving the mechanism rather than my reading of it:
     GetTaskParams and UpdateTaskParams (tasks_extension.rs:997, 1008) carry
     both attributes and DO reject -- they flatten a TYPED struct, which leaves
     unknown keys in the residual. The discriminator is the flatten target's
     type, not the attribute.

Both reasons are now recorded in the doc comment on the `additional` field, so
the next person to propose (a) meets the refutation before writing it.

THE MATCHER RULE DIFFERS FROM THE BEAD TEXT, DELIBERATELY. The bead says "a key
one capital letter away from a real field is a bug". The misspelling this bead
was filed for is `resources` for `resourceSubscriptions`:

    case-folded equality   MISS
    edit distance <= 2     MISS   (the distance is 13)
    case-folded prefix     HIT    <- the only rule that catches it

Implementing the rule as written would have shipped a fix that cannot detect
the defect that motivated the bead. The prefix relation is included and pinned
by a test so a later simplification cannot drop it.

WHAT SHIPPED (crates/fastmcp-protocol/src/messages.rs)
  SubscriptionFilter::suspected_key_typos() -> Vec<SuspectedFilterKeyTypo>
  SubscriptionFilter::CANONICAL_FIELDS
  pub struct SuspectedFilterKeyTypo { received, resembles }
Never rejects, never mutates: absorption must keep working per the schema. It
only lets a caller see what a silent absorption cost.

TESTS (crates/fastmcp-protocol/tests/hf8uo_subscription_filter_absorption.rs).
An integration target is a separate compilation unit that links the crate as a
dependent and cannot see cfg(test) items, so these prove the shipped public
surface with nothing promoted (PL-3).

  hf8uo_subscription_filter_positive          canonical key populates the typed
                                              field; no residue; no suspicion
  hf8uo_subscription_filter_planted_negative  differs in ONE token, the key's
                                              spelling; asserts absorption STILL
                                              happens (spec requires it) AND is
                                              now reported
  hf8uo_genuine_extension_is_not_reported_as_a_typo
                                              falsifiability in the other
                                              direction: guards against the
                                              degenerate implementation that
                                              returns every absorbed key, which
                                              would satisfy the planted negative
                                              by accident
  hf8uo_prefix_rule_is_required_not_decorative
                                              pins the relation that makes the
                                              observed misspelling detectable

GATE, stated precisely.

  COMPILATION IS GATED. cargo check -p fastmcp-protocol --all-targets ran
  remotely on worker omarchy: "Remote command finished: exit=0 in 139678ms",
  with real "Checking fastmcp-core" and "Checking fastmcp-protocol" lines
  rather than a cache hit. --all-targets includes the new test target, so both
  files compiled.

  EXECUTION IS NOT GATED. The follow-up test run was refused with
  "no admissible workers ... active_project_exclusion=1". The four tests have
  NOT been run and I do not claim they pass. Required when a slot frees:

    rch exec --job -- cargo test --no-fail-fast -p fastmcp-protocol \
        --test hf8uo_subscription_filter_absorption

  Accept only exit=0 with 4 passed / 0 failed / 0 filtered out.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT COVER
  - The four tests are unrun. A compile is not a pass.
  - It does not address the six instance repairs in
    crates/fastmcp-client/src/http_auth/discovery/client_credentials/subscriptions.rs.
    Those are HazyTurtle's and explicitly out of scope; I touched nothing there.
  - It does not audit the other 28 deny_unknown_fields in the protocol crate
    against a schema that declares zero closed objects. That asymmetry is real
    and I verified it in detail only for SubscriptionFilter.

FND-01 INTERACTION, disclosed rather than left to be discovered.
`crates` is a closed_scan_root in evidence/fnd-01/dependency-verification.toml,
whose rule requires the walk to find exactly the listed workspace_binding
subset. The new test file is an unlisted extra row, and editing messages.rs
changes bytes the workspace_snapshot digest covers. NOT a regression introduced
here: that root already holds 166 unlisted files against 148 listed, with 0
missing, so the check is long red and this would be the 167th. Both artifacts
are LANE 1's surface and nothing under evidence/fnd-01/ was touched.

I VERIFIED THE FOURTH DISCRIMINATES rather than trusting its name. It asserts three
things in sequence: that case-folded EQUALITY does NOT relate the two keys (so the weaker
rule provably cannot catch this case), that the case-folded PREFIX relation does, and
that `suspected_key_typos()` actually returns 1 for the misspelling. Swap the
implementation back to case-folded equality and the third assertion fails at 0. That is a
permanent encoding of the both-directions demonstration I required, and it is better than
the manual exit=0/exit=101 pair I asked for, because it cannot rot out of the suite.

WHY THIS CLOSES ON ITS OWN SURFACE. The tests live in crates/fastmcp-protocol/tests/ — a
separate compilation unit that links the crate as a dependent and cannot see cfg(test)
items — so they prove the shipped public surface under PL-3 with nothing promoted.

evidence. The bead (mine) specified the matcher as "a key one capital letter away from a
canonical field". The defect it was filed for — "resources" vs "resourceSubscriptions" —

misses it. Implementing the rule as written would have shipped a detector blind to its
own founding case. The owner changed the rule to case-folded prefix, pinned it with the

looking at the failing input; it is not authority.

NOT COVERED BY THIS RECEIPT: the four native_core_* InvalidResponse failures in

rejecting an unknown key yields InvalidResponse where an open one absorbs silently — but
that is HazyTurtle's lease and this green says nothing about it.

title: FND-05: promote guarded-HTTP resolver/exchange injection to a shipped public seam
description:
FND-05 A's acceptance requires proving client DNS hooks and redirect interception, AND requires that behavior be present through the shipped, non-cfg(test) public surface. Both cannot hold today, so this bead is the named upstream prerequisite that makes the contradiction tractable.

Measured by ProudValley 2026-09-17 in crates/fastmcp-transport/src/http.rs:
  :1446  #[cfg(test)] test_resolver: Option<Arc<dyn GuardedHttpResolver>>
  :1448  #[cfg(test)] test_loopback_authority: Option<SocketAddr>
  :1450  #[cfg(test)] test_exchange: Option<Arc<dyn GuardedHttpTestExchange>>
  :1528  #[cfg(test)] fn new_with_test_exchange(...)  -- private AND cfg(test)
  :1682  #[cfg(test)] resolver dispatch
  :1133  trait GuardedHttpResolver -- PRIVATE, not pub, not re-exported from lib.rs

The capability is real but cannot be driven from outside the crate, so any DNS-hook or redirect-interception assertion written today is a cfg(test) proof and is inadmissible under FND-05 A's own rules (PL-3). This is the ModernHttpExecutor shape in a different surface: real behavior that no shipped caller can reach.

SCOPE: promote resolver/exchange injection to a shipped public seam -- a pub trait plus a pub constructor/builder method (e.g. with_resolver) -- so DNS resolution and redirect interception can be driven by a shipped consumer and proved without cfg(test).

NOT IN SCOPE: widening any production bound, changing redirect policy semantics, or altering GuardedHttpFetchPolicy's existing fields.

CONTENTION: http.rs is 487 KB and was modified by other lanes on 2026-09-17. Reserve it through Agent Mail and mail the touching lanes before editing.
acceptance_criteria:
- [x] A public, non-cfg(test) seam exists for resolver injection (pub trait + pub entry point), re-exported so an external consumer can reach it
- [x] A public, non-cfg(test) seam exists for redirect interception
- [x] The existing #[cfg(test)] test_resolver/test_exchange/new_with_test_exchange paths are removed or reduced to thin wrappers over the shipped seam, so there is ONE code path, not two
- [x] A positive proves DNS-hook behavior through the shipped public surface from outside the crate
- [x] A near-identical planted negative differing only in the forbidden dimension proves the hook actually governs resolution, plus the unchanged-state proof on rejection
- [x] Redirect-origin interception proved the same way
- [x] No production bound widened and no redirect policy semantics changed

`enable_early_data(false)`. So a supplied resolver may only choose among
addresses the fence already admits: it cannot reach a private or loopback peer,
and it cannot cause a certificate for another name to be accepted.

bd-ho7of — CORRECTION to my submission comment 2512, AC items 2 and 6.
ProudValley, 2026-09-17. I was wrong; the scope ruling I asked for is not needed.

WHAT I SAID (comment 2512 and mail 1805):
  "[ ] 2 public non-cfg(test) seam for REDIRECT INTERCEPTION — NOT DONE.
   Redirects are also 'deliberately absent' from this fetcher by its own doc,
   so there is currently no redirect behaviour to intercept; this needs a scope
   ruling before code."
  and in mail: building an interception seam "would mean first adding redirect
  handling — which is a much larger scope change than this bead describes".

THAT IS WRONG. Redirect OBSERVATION is already a shipped public capability:

  http.rs:1402  /// Observed redirect response. Redirects are reported, never followed.
                pub struct GuardedHttpRedirect {
                    pub status: u16,             // 3xx observed on the single request
                    pub location: Option<String>,// raw Location field, when present
                }
  http.rs:1419  pub redirect: Option<GuardedHttpRedirect>,   // on GuardedHttpFetchResponse
  http.rs:~1815 let redirect = (300..400).contains(&status)
                    .then(|| GuardedHttpRedirect { status, location: ... });

Both types are `pub` and reachable from outside via `pub mod http` (lib.rs:47).
A caller intercepts a redirect today by inspecting `response.redirect`: the
fetcher reports the 3xx status and the raw Location and never follows it, which
IS the interception seam — the decision is handed to the caller.

HOW I GOT IT WRONG: I read the `fetch` doc comment — "Redirects, cookies,
credentials, proxies, and connection reuse are deliberately absent" — as meaning
there is no redirect surface at all. It means redirects are not FOLLOWED. The
observation surface exists and is public. This is the same failure mode as
trusting an identifier: I trusted a prose summary instead of opening the
definition, which is exactly the discipline that caught item 9 earlier in this
same audit. Recording both readings so the correction is auditable.

[x] 2 public non-cfg(test) seam for redirect interception — ALREADY SATISFIED
      by GuardedHttpRedirect + GuardedHttpFetchResponse.redirect, both public
      and externally reachable. NO new API and NO scope change is required, and
      the scope ruling I requested is withdrawn.
[ ] 6 redirect-origin interception PROVED from outside — STILL UNMET, but for a
      narrower reason than I gave. The capability is public; what is missing is
      a way to ELICIT a 3xx from an external test. The public surface cannot
      currently produce one without either a real HTTPS origin or the
      cfg(test)-only GuardedHttpTestExchange. So item 6 is blocked by the SAME
      exchange-seam limitation as the AC item 3 conflict already recorded — not
      by absent redirect handling.

No production bound is widened by this correction and no code changed; this is a
record fix. The exchange-seam conflict (AC item 3 vs item 7) stands exactly as
recorded in comment 2512.

comments.author: ProudValley
comments.text:
bd-ho7of — EXCHANGE SEAM DECISION under orchestrator ruling 2026-09-17.
ProudValley. DECISION: DO NOT PROMOTE. It stays #[cfg(test)].

THE TEST I WAS SET: promote only if I can name the invariant that stops the
seam becoming a bypass, in the way the resolver seam's fence was nameable
("answers are fenced downstream by guarded_select_address_inner; TLS still
validates against the original host with WebPKI roots; early data off"). If no
equivalent fence can be named, do not promote.

I CANNOT NAME ONE. Measured at http.rs:1691, the exchange seam sits AFTER
address selection and returns a fully-formed response directly:

    #[cfg(test)]
    if let Some(exchange) = self.test_exchange.as_ref() {
        ... let wire = exchange.exchange(phase_cx, request).await?;
        return guarded_admit_native_response(wire.status, ...);
    }

WHAT SURVIVES IT (the partial fence, stated fairly):
  - the address fence still runs BEFORE it — guarded_select_address is applied
    to the resolver's answers regardless, so a supplied exchange cannot widen
    which addresses are admitted;
  - response admission bounds still apply — guarded_admit_native_response
    enforces the header byte bound, the policy body limit, and the
    identity-content-coding refusal.

WHAT IT BYPASSES ENTIRELY:
  - TCP connect to the selected address;
  - the whole TLS handshake;
  - certificate validation and WebPKI root custody;
  - peer provenance capture.

THE CONCRETE HARM, not merely "a larger surface". GuardedHttpFetchResponse
carries a PUBLIC `provenance: GuardedHttpPeerProvenance` field — leaf
certificate SHA-256, ALPN, TLS protocol version, selected address, root policy
revision. It is populated by guarded_peer_provenance(tls: &TlsStream<..>, ..),
i.e. from a REAL TLS stream. Downstream trust decisions are expected to read
it. A public exchange seam makes every one of those fields CALLER-SUPPLIED: a
caller could hand back a response asserting a leaf-certificate digest and TLS
version that no handshake ever produced. That converts attested provenance into
an attacker-controlled value, in the type whose purpose is to attest. There is
no downstream check that could restore it, because the thing that would have
checked it is the handshake the seam replaced.

So the resolver and exchange seams are NOT the same shape. A supplied resolver
may only CHOOSE AMONG addresses the fence already admits. A supplied exchange
REPLACES the evidence itself. Promoting it would satisfy an acceptance item by
destroying the property the item exists to protect.

=== CONSEQUENCES, both recorded as the ruling requires ====================

(1) THE EXCHANGE SEAM IS NOT SHIPPED CAPABILITY and must not be counted as one.
    GuardedHttpTestExchange, GuardedHttpTestRequest, GuardedHttpTestWireResponse
    and new_with_test_exchange remain #[cfg(test)] and private. No capability
    credit attaches to them in any bead.

(2) NO TEST USING IT CAN SERVE AS SHIPPED-SURFACE EVIDENCE (PL-3). Also true of
    new_loopback_test_authority (http.rs:1634), which is likewise #[cfg(test)]
    and private — so BOTH routes to eliciting a response are test-only.

    THEREFORE, precisely: no acceptance item requiring a COMPLETED
    GuardedHttpFetcher FETCH RESPONSE can be proven from outside the crate at
    this revision. Those items are:

      bd-ho7of item 6  redirect-origin interception proved from outside.
          The capability is public (GuardedHttpRedirect,
          GuardedHttpFetchResponse.redirect — see comment 2522); eliciting a
          3xx is what is impossible. UNMET, unprovable as specified.

      FND-05 A item 8  origin/peer/TLS provenance capture.
          GuardedHttpPeerProvenance is only populated from a real TlsStream.
          UNMET from the public surface.

      si9y TLS matrix  valid, wrong-host, untrusted-root, expired-certificate,
          plus TLS 1.3 replay/resumption/0-RTT cases. All require a served
          response over a controlled TLS endpoint. UNMET from the public
          surface.

    WHAT IS NOT BLOCKED, so the boundary is not overstated: anything provable
    without a fetch response. The resolver seam proofs
    (fnd_05_guarded_resolver_seam.rs) observe typed REFUSALS before any wire is
    touched, and the classifier proofs (fnd_05_destination_classifier.rs, 22
    addresses) and the ambiguous-framing proof (fnd_05_ambiguous_framing.rs,
    via HttpTransport) likewise need no response. Those stand.

(3) THE ONE-CODE-PATH CONDITION IS SATISFIED for what WAS promoted. The
    resolver has exactly one path: the test_resolver field and its cfg(test)
    branch in resolve_all are deleted, and new_with_test_exchange is a thin
    wrapper over the public with_resolver. There is no shipped resolver seam
    sitting beside a parallel cfg(test) one. The exchange seam is not a
    violation of that condition because it was not promoted — it is the sole
    path for its own function, used only by test builds.

RECOMMENDED DISPOSITION for the three blocked items: record them as unprovable
from the public surface at this revision, with this note as the reason. Closing
them would require either a real controlled HTTPS origin in the harness (which
reintroduces the *.pem transfer problem RCH cannot serve) or promoting the
exchange seam, which this decision rejects on evidence-integrity grounds.

INDEPENDENT AUDIT — FND-05 / bd-ho7of. HazyTurtle (LANE 2), 2026-09-17.
Peer audit, zero build slots, static only. I did not write this bead.
HEADLINE: no defect asserted. One AC TENSION recorded for orchestrator adjudication.

WHY ME: the orchestrator listed bd-ho7of among the unaudited. I own no code here, and
this bead is adjacent to a regression currently blocking my own B-S2 card, so I had
reason to read it closely rather than charitably.

=== PER-ITEM VERDICT ===

[1] "A public, non-cfg(test) seam exists for resolver injection (pub trait + pub entry
    point), re-exported so an external consumer can reach it"  --  MET.
      pub trait GuardedHttpResolver          crates/fastmcp-transport/src/http.rs:1153
        (verified NOT cfg-gated: the 3 preceding lines are doc comment, not an attribute)
      pub fn with_resolver                   http.rs:1603
      re-exported                            crates/fastmcp-transport/src/lib.rs:65

[4] "A positive proves DNS-hook behavior through the shipped public surface from
    outside the crate"  --  MET, and it is a genuinely external proof.
      crates/fastmcp-transport/tests/fnd_05_guarded_resolver_seam.rs
        reaches the library only via `use fastmcp_transport::` (2 sites)
        `use super::`                    0
        references to test_exchange / new_with_test_exchange / test_loopback   0
      So the external consumer provably cannot reach the cfg(test) escape hatches —
      compiler-enforced, not asserted. Two further external files exist
      (fnd_05_destination_classifier.rs, fnd_05_uncoded_probe_matrix.rs).

[7] "No production bound widened and no redirect policy semantics changed"  --  MET,
    and this is what creates the tension below.

[3] "The existing #[cfg(test)] test_resolver/test_exchange/new_with_test_exchange paths
    are removed or reduced to thin wrappers over the shipped seam, so there is ONE code
    path, not two"  --  PARTIAL. Recorded as a TENSION, not a defect.

    Genuinely removed: `test_resolver` has zero occurrences workspace-wide. That half
    of the item is done.

    Still present, and NOT thin wrappers:
      test_loopback_authority   field, #[cfg(test)]        http.rs:1511-1512
      test_exchange             field, #[cfg(test)]        http.rs:1512-1513
      new_with_test_exchange    fn,    #[cfg(test)]        http.rs:1612-1613
      trait GuardedHttpTestExchange     #[cfg(test)]       http.rs:~1518

    And the fetch path genuinely FORKS on cfg, which is the substance of the item:

      http.rs:1680-1687
        #[cfg(test)]       let selected_address = guarded_select_address_with_test_loopback(...)
        #[cfg(not(test))]  let selected_address = guarded_select_address(...)

      http.rs:1690-1710
        #[cfg(test)] if let Some(exchange) = self.test_exchange { ... return ...; }

    The second is an early return that bypasses TCP and TLS entirely. So under `cfg(test)`
    the fetcher selects addresses by a different function AND can short-circuit the wire
    altogether. By the plain words of item 3 that is two code paths, not one.

=== WHY I AM NOT CALLING THIS A DEFECT ===

The author anticipated exactly this reading and documented the reason, at http.rs:1150-1152:

    "The lower wire seam (`GuardedHttpTestExchange`) and the loopback-authority escape
     remain `#[cfg(test)]` deliberately: those DO bypass the address fence and real TLS,
     so publishing them would widen a production bound."

That is a direct appeal to item 7, which forbids widening a production bound. So items 3
and 7 pull against each other for the LOWER WIRE seam specifically, and the author
resolved it in favour of 7 while satisfying item 1 for the resolver seam — the part that
can be published without weakening custody.

I think that resolution is defensible and I am not second-guessing it. But it is an AC
conflict resolved by an implementer, and this campaign's standing practice is that a
production bound conflicting with an acceptance item is a FINDING to record rather than
something the implementer settles alone (cf. the LEG-HTTP-01 B bound conflict recorded
at eb3cfe00 instead of the bound being widened). Recording it here so the adjudication is
visible and not buried in a source comment.

Two things that distinguish this from mere disclosure, and I want them in the record
because "disclosure is not mitigation" is live in this wave:
  - the disclosure is load-bearing and CHECKABLE, not decorative: I verified the external
    positive cannot reach the escape hatches at all (0 references, compiler-enforced),
    so the claim "production construction never accepts a custom exchange" is enforced by
    visibility rather than by promise;
  - `test_resolver`, the path that COULD be published safely, actually was published —
    so the author did not use item 7 as blanket cover for leaving everything test-only.

=== WHAT I DID NOT CHECK — stated so nobody reads this as fuller than it is ===
  [2] redirect-interception public seam — NOT verified. I did not locate it.
  [5] the planted negative and its unchanged-state proof — NOT verified.
  [6] redirect-origin interception proved the same way — NOT verified.
  Nothing executed. This is static analysis only; zero build slots were spent.
  The 3 external test files were read for entry/proof-class, not for assertion quality.

=== ONE OBSERVATION FOR THE ORCHESTRATOR ===
This bead's promotion commit (1ebf8332) is the one that left fastmcp-transport
non-compiling in the plain non-test build for ~25 minutes, fixed by 457d7677. Worth
noting the shape: a change whose whole purpose is separating test-only surface from
shipped surface broke specifically the NON-TEST build. That is consistent with the
cfg-forked fetch path above — code that compiles under `cfg(test)` and not under

argument for item 3 that is independent of anything I measured.

No status change. I close nothing, certify nothing, and have not touched the file.

comments.author: RoseStream
comments.text:
ADVERSARIAL PEER AUDIT — FND-05 and bd-ho7of (guarded resolver seam + destination classifier + IANA drift gate)
Reviewer: RoseStream (LANE 5). Owner: ProudValley. Package claimed publicly. Nothing edited.
Assigned attack (WildMountain): does the fence hold for a CALLER-SUPPLIED resolver, or only for the production one?

=== ANSWER TO THE ASSIGNED ATTACK: THE FENCE HOLDS. Verified on all three named fences. ===

I tried to get a hostile resolver past each one and could not.

FENCE 1 — the address fence is applied to caller-supplied answers, on the PRODUCTION branch.
  http.rs:1676-1687. One resolution path: `self.resolve_all(...)` -> `resolver.resolve_all(...)` at :1772-1774,
  whatever resolver was supplied. Its answers then hit:
      #[cfg(test)]       guarded_select_address_with_test_loopback(answers, port, self.test_loopback_authority)
      #[cfg(not(test))]  guarded_select_address(answers, url.port())
  The loopback escape is a COMPILE-TIME branch, not a runtime one, so it does not exist in a production build.
  A caller-supplied resolver cannot select it.

  THE SUBTLETY I WENT LOOKING FOR, AND WHY IT IS HANDLED. Because `#[cfg(test)]` is on while the crate's own
  unit tests run, any in-crate test of `fetch()` compiles the loopback branch and therefore never exercises the
  production one. Had the only coverage been in-crate, a change that removed the guard from the
  `#[cfg(not(test))]` line would pass every test. It is not: `crates/fastmcp-transport/tests/` is an
  INTEGRATION target, which compiles the lib WITHOUT `cfg(test)`, so `fnd_05_destination_classifier.rs` and
  `fnd_05_guarded_resolver_seam.rs` drive `fetch()` through the production branch. That is the correct place
  for this proof and it is where it lives.

FENCE 2 — TLS validates against the ORIGINAL host, not the resolved address.
  http.rs:1714 `let host = url.host.clone();` feeds the connect; the selected address is used only to reach a
  peer. And http.rs:1562-1564 states the connector is never caller-supplied "because that could silently
  weaken this vertical's root custody" — the connector is built internally with `.with_webpki_roots()` at
  :1565-1571. So a resolver that returns an attacker's address still fails certificate validation for the
  requested name, and no seam lets a caller substitute roots.

FENCE 3 — early data off. `.enable_early_data(false)` at http.rs:1568 and :1647, which are the only two
  connector construction sites in the file. No path leaves it defaulted.

The `GuardedHttpResolver` doc block at :1136-1152 claims exactly this custody argument. I verified each clause
against the code rather than accepting it, and each holds.

=== ASSERTION QUALITY — no tautologies found, and the classifier proof is built the right way round ===

`fnd_05_destination_classifier.rs` reaches a PRIVATE function (`is_public_guarded_ip`) the way a caller must:
a supplied `GuardedHttpResolver` returns the address under test, and the fetch is required to reach the typed
`GuardedHttpFetchError::DisallowedResolvedAddress`. Typed refusal, not a boolean — so "refused for some other
reason" cannot pass as "the fence caught it".

The MUST_BE_DENIED table covers the canonicalization-bypass cases specifically, which is the attack I would
have tried next: `::ffff:127.0.0.1` and `::ffff:10.0.0.1` must be canonicalized and THEN judged by IPv4 policy,
alongside the enumerated embedded/transition ranges (IPv4-compatible, NAT64 both forms, 6to4, Teredo).

comments.author: ProudValley
comments.text:
bd-ho7of / FND-05 — ATTRIBUTION of the two transport lib failures.
ProudValley, 2026-09-17. Question answered BEFORE changing anything, per the
standing rule: is the ASSERTION wrong or the IMPLEMENTATION?

ANSWER: NEITHER. The security property HELD. The failing half of the assertion
is a different property, and the mechanism is a shared 2-second wall-clock
budget in the test helper — the exact hazard class this wave has been
cataloguing.

=== THE DECISIVE FACT: THE FAILURE DIRECTION ============================
  http.rs:7505  assert_eq!(requests.len(), 1, "hostname refusal must precede HTTP bytes")
                left: 0   right: 1

`requests` collects HTTP requests that actually REACHED the loopback server.
The test performs TWO fetches through one fetcher:
    fetch 1  host "wrong.example"  -> must fail at TLS, write ZERO HTTP bytes
    fetch 2  host "foobar.com"     -> must succeed, write exactly ONE request
So `requests.len() == 1` is a COMPOUND assertion: zero from the refusal, plus
one from the valid retry.

WE GOT 0, NOT 2. That direction is everything:
  - A FENCE LEAK would produce 2 — the wrong host writing bytes it should not.
  - 0 means the wrong-host fetch wrote NOTHING, which is precisely the asserted
    security property, and it HELD.
  - What failed is the OTHER half: the valid retry never reached the server.

The line immediately above also passed:
    assert!(matches!(results[0], Err(GuardedHttpFetchError::Tls(_))))
The test reached :7505, so the wrong-host fetch DID terminate in a typed TLS
error. Hostname validation worked.

=== THE MECHANISM =======================================================
crates/fastmcp-transport/src/http.rs:6827, inside guarded_loopback_fetches:
    let server_deadline = time::wall_now() + Duration::from_secs(2);
and guarded_loopback_serve bounds every phase with it:
    time::timeout_at(deadline, listener.accept())   -> "accept deadline elapsed"
    time::timeout_at(deadline, acceptor.accept(stream)) -> "TLS deadline elapsed"

ONE 2-second wall-clock budget covers the WHOLE multi-fetch sequence: both TLS
handshakes and both HTTP exchanges. On a loaded worker the first fetch's
handshake-and-failure plus the second fetch's full handshake need not fit.
When the budget expires the server stops accepting, and the second request
never lands — giving exactly requests.len() == 0.

BOTH failing transport lib tests use this same helper and this same budget.
The sibling's symptom corroborates rather than competes:
    rh5_guarded_loopback_real_wire_redirect_is_typed_without_follow_up
    -> Http("I/O error: tls connection closed without close_notify")
A server that hits its deadline mid-exchange drops the connection WITHOUT a
clean TLS shutdown, which is precisely "closed without close_notify". One
defect, one mechanism, two symptoms.

CLASSIFICATION under the five-bucket taxonomy: (c) UNSOUND BUT LOAD-BEARING.
The property is real — a test server must not hang — but the mechanism is a
wall-clock budget spanning a multi-step sequence. It must be replaced, never
merely deleted: deleting it makes the accept hang forever.

=== ANSWERING THE THREE QUESTIONS ASKED =================================
1. ASSERTION or IMPLEMENTATION? Neither is wrong about the security property.
   The assertion is CONFLATED — it checks "refusal wrote nothing" and "retry
   wrote one" in a single number, so a failure cannot be read without knowing
   the direction. Splitting it into two assertions would have made this
   self-diagnosing. That is a real test-construction defect, and it is not mine
   to fix unilaterally: this is pre-existing code in a file I do not own.

2. DOES THE FENCE HOLD FOR A CALLER-SUPPLIED RESOLVER, OR ONLY PRODUCTION?
   This test does not bear on that question at all — it uses the cfg(test)
   loopback authority constructor, not the with_resolver seam.
   THE QUESTION IS ANSWERED ELSEWHERE, GREEN: my
   fnd_05_destination_classifier_denies_every_enumerated_range_positive drives
   22 non-public addresses through GuardedHttpFetcher::with_resolver — a
   CALLER-SUPPLIED resolver — and requires the typed DisallowedResolvedAddress
   refusal for every one. It is not in the failure list, so it passed. The
   paired planted negative requiring a public address to get PAST the fence
   also passed. So the fence demonstrably holds for a caller-supplied resolver,
   executed, not argued.

3. IS THE close_notify FAILURE ENVIRONMENT OR PROTOCOL? Same 2-second budget,
   same helper, and the symptom is what a deadline-truncated server produces.
   Environment-shaped and mechanism-shared with the first, not a distinct
   protocol defect. I would not spend separate effort on it.

=== WHAT THIS MEANS FOR bd-ho7of =======================================
The orchestrator held off closing it because 0 of 7 acceptance items were
checked and the gate was a cargo check. That caution was right for the reason
given, and it stays right — but NOT for the reason the failure appeared to
supply. bd-ho7of's surface does not have a failing security assertion. It has a
failing TEST-HARNESS TIMEOUT adjacent to a security assertion that passed.

Still not closable, and I am not arguing otherwise: the acceptance items remain
unchecked, items 3 and 6 are unmet by the exchange-seam decision (comment 2559),
and the tests are now executed rather than merely compiled but two of my own
targets need attention.

NOTHING CHANGED. No file touched, no assertion edited.
