title: fastmcp-server lib has a load-dependent flake family: identical denominator, churning failure set, blocks every gate-4 receipt
description:
`cargo test -p fastmcp-server` has a load-dependent flake family in its lib unit tests
whose membership CHURNS between runs on identical source. This blocks every gate-4
receipt for the crate, because a suite that cannot be relied on to go green cannot
produce admissible evidence.

MEASURED, two consecutive runs, same command, `--features tasks,proxy-legacy
--no-fail-fast`, 0 filtered out on both:

  05bc213d   2428 passed + 1 failed = 2429
  7930b639   2424 passed + 5 failed = 2429
                                      ^^^^ IDENTICAL DENOMINATOR

Same population, different split. No test added, removed, filtered or skipped. A changed
pass/fail split over an identical denominator is flakiness by definition.

MEMBERSHIP CHURNS RATHER THAN GROWS — one left the set while five joined:
  returning_subscription_protocol_failure_after_quiescence_runs_hook   failed -> PASSES
  live_runtime_cancels_exact_legacy_tool_by_its_original_wire_id            NEW
  live_runtime_rejects_completion_notification_without_invoking_handler     NEW
  live_runtime_routes_exact_legacy_frames_through_the_2024_adapter          NEW
  returning_split_waits_for_non_quiescent_legacy_handler_before_owned_cleanup NEW
  returning_subscription_quiescence_runs_hook_after_owner_retirement        NEW

The member that flipped OUT is independently on record flipping 1926/0 vs 1925/1 on
byte-identical source seventeen minutes apart, with the mechanism found by READING:
`assert!(started.elapsed() < SHUTDOWN_CLEANUP_TIMEOUT)` — an UPPER bound on real wall
time, which asserts the machine was fast enough rather than any property of the code. Its
sibling's `>=` is load-monotone and sound. That is the likely shape of the rest.

NOT CAUSED BY THE COMMITS IN THAT WINDOW. 7930b639 touched exactly one file,
crates/fastmcp-server/tests/auth_01_a.rs — an INTEGRATION target, a separate compilation
unit. `lib_unit_tests::*` are inline `#[cfg(test)]` in src/. There is no mechanism by
which a tests/ file changes the lib's own unit tests, and the identical denominator says
independently that it did not.

WHY THIS IS NOT MERELY ANNOYING: **a flaky green is as inadmissible as a flaky red.**
Every green this suite produces is a coin flip that happened to land. Campaign doctrine
already holds that zero-test, filtered, ignored or early-aborted green output is failure
rather than proof; a green whose reproducibility is unknown belongs in the same category.
Any batch_verify PASS recorded against this crate to date inherited that coin flip.

NAMED CONSUMER: the batch_verify gate for fastmcp-server, and specifically the gate-4
bulk tick of acceptance items 3/4 across the six SRV beads, which is blocked on a green
receipt that this suite cannot presently be relied on to produce.
OBSERVED DEFECT CLASS: upper bounds on real wall time in concurrency tests, asserted with
`Instant::now()` rather than a virtual clock.
DELETION CONDITION: closes when the crate produces the SAME pass/fail split across three
consecutive runs under differing load.

IN SCOPE:
  1 Classify all five by the five-bucket wall-clock taxonomy before touching any of them:
    (a) sound by direction, (b) unsound and redundant, (c) unsound but load-bearing,
    (d) structurally incapable, (e) BOUNDED WAIT — never remove, the assert IS the loop's
    exit condition and deleting it hangs the test forever. Report the SPLIT, not a fix
    count. (e) was measured at 44% of one lane's surface, so assume it is present.
  2 Repair per bucket. An upper bound that is load-bearing gets a virtual clock or a
    structural assertion, never a deletion and never a larger constant.
  3 Demonstrate the fix by running the crate three times, not once. A single green proves
    nothing about a flake.

EXPLICITLY NOT IN SCOPE: raising timeout constants to make the red go away. That converts
a visible flake into an invisible one and is gate self-weakening (RH-1).
notes:
=== 2026-09-17 RoseStream: ITEM 1 CLASSIFICATION, from source, with line numbers ===

This bead had ZERO notes. The classification existed only in mail, which decays. Recording it
where it is greppable.

ALL SIX CHURNING MEMBERS LIVE IN crates/fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs:
  45639  live_runtime_cancels_exact_legacy_tool_by_its_original_wire_id       (3-line wrapper)
  36786  live_runtime_rejects_completion_notification_without_invoking_handler (62 lines)
  36110  live_runtime_routes_exact_legacy_frames_through_the_2024_adapter      (66 lines)
  30708  returning_split_waits_for_non_quiescent_legacy_handler_before_owned_cleanup (46)
  47188  returning_subscription_quiescence_runs_hook_after_owner_retirement    (3-line wrapper)
  47198  returning_subscription_protocol_failure_after_quiescence_runs_hook    (3-line wrapper)

THE HEADLINE: THE BEAD'S STATED DEFECT CLASS IS NOT PRESENT IN THIS FAMILY.
The description names "upper bounds on real wall time in concurrency tests, asserted with
Instant::now()". Measured against current source, the two Instant::now() assertions in these
tests are BOTH LOWER bounds and therefore bucket (a) SOUND BY DIRECTION:
    :30749  assert!(elapsed >= DISPATCH_WORKER_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT)
    :47641  assert!(started.elapsed() >= SHUTDOWN_CLEANUP_TIMEOUT)
The ONE upper bound that ever existed here is already gone. lib.rs:47614-47620 is a comment
recording its removal and the reasoning, explicitly noting the sibling's >= is sound. So the
hypothesis was right about the class in general and is already satisfied in this family.

THREE OF SIX HAVE NO WALL-CLOCK CONSTRUCT IN THEIR OWN BODIES AT ALL. Classifying by test
body would have returned "nothing to classify" for half the population. They inherit it.

THE ACTUAL MECHANISM IS ONE SHARED 2-SECOND WATCHDOG, NOT SIX DEFECTS.
crates/fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs:46928 run_returning_transport_with_test_runtime:

    let runtime = RuntimeBuilder::current_thread()
        .with_reactor(create_reactor()...)
        .blocking_threads(2, MAX_DISPATCH_QUEUE_DEPTH)
    ...
    let deadline = cx.now().saturating_add_nanos(2_000_000_000);      // 2 SECONDS, absolute
    loop {
        match result_receiver.try_recv() {
            Ok(result)   => break result,
            Disconnected => return Err(... "pump exited without a result"),
            Empty        => timeout_at(deadline, sleep(cx.now(), Duration::from_millis(1)))
                              .await
                              .map_err(|_| internal_error("legacy returning test timed out"))?,
        }
    }

run_live_split_transport (:23640) has the same shape at :23685. returning_subscription_cleanup_case
(:47433-47687) adds its own timeout_at at :47578 and :47670.

So the whole test body runs under a 2-second WALL-CLOCK budget polled at 1ms granularity, on a
current_thread runtime with TWO blocking threads, while the pump itself occupies one via
spawn_blocking. Under concurrent load a test that normally finishes in milliseconds exceeds
2s and fails as "legacy returning test timed out" -- an internal_error, not an assertion.

THAT EXPLAINS EVERY OBSERVED PROPERTY:
  identical denominator      nothing is added, removed, filtered or skipped
  CHURNING membership        which tests happen to exceed 2s varies with load; the set is a
                             SAMPLE from the population sharing these helpers, not a fixed list
  one member flipping OUT    same reason, in the other direction

BUCKET ASSIGNMENT (WildMountain's amended six-bucket taxonomy):
  (a) SOUND BY DIRECTION     :30749, :47641 -- lower bounds, load-monotone
  (b) unsound + redundant     none found
  (c) UNSOUND + LOAD-BEARING  NONE. The only instance was removed before I looked;
                              :47614-47620 documents it.
  (d) structurally incapable  none found
  (e) BOUNDED WAIT            :47471 wait_for_started(2s) IN A MATCH GUARD -- on timeout it
                              returns false and the match falls through to a DIFFERENT ARM,
                              so the test silently runs a different scenario rather than
                              failing. Also :47474 and :47663 asserted, :47538 DISCARDED.
  (f) LIVENESS WATCHDOG       :46946/:23685/:47578/:47670 -- the 2s pump deadlines. These are
                              the live mechanism and they are the ones WildMountain has ruled
                              MUST NOT BE EDITED.

THE TAXONOMY WAS APPLIED TO THE WRONG UNIT. Five/six flaky TESTS is the wrong frame; it is
two shared pump helpers with a wall-clock budget, sampled differently each run. This confirms
the earlier "capacity, not defect" ruling from source rather than from inference, which is
what this bead was missing.

NOT PROPOSING ANY EDIT. Not the budgets, not the messages, not blocking_threads(2, ..) --
I withdrew that proposal earlier and it stays withdrawn. Bucket (e) at :47471 is the one site
that is arguably a real defect rather than capacity, because a match guard that falls through
on timeout changes WHICH scenario runs instead of reporting that it could not run. Flagged,
not taken: it is inside the same helper family and editing it is a watchdog edit.

DELETION CONDITION UNCHANGED: closes when the crate produces the SAME pass/fail split across
three consecutive runs under differing load. Nothing here can establish that by reading.
=== 2026-09-17 RoseStream: CRATE-WIDE SWEEP. Four sites, TWO shapes. The class is NOT extinct. ===

WildMountain widened past my six and flagged tests.rs:1923 and :2011. I swept the whole crate
rather than stopping where he stopped, and found TWO MORE that are a different and worse shape.

SHAPE 1 -- deliberate fail-with-message. Direction-correct, load-exposed. (His two.)
  tests.rs:1923  fn test_server_cancels_inflight_requests
  tests.rs:2011  fn test_e2e_cancel_drain_logs

      if start.elapsed() > Duration::from_secs(1) {
          assert!(start.elapsed() <= Duration::from_secs(1), "active requests did not register in time");
      }

  The enclosing `if` has already established elapsed > 1s, so the assert is ALWAYS FALSE WHEN
  REACHED. It is a fail-with-message idiom, not a confused comparison, and his direction check
  is correct. Confirmed by reading.

  ONE MECHANISM HE DID NOT NAME, and it makes these worse than a passive watchdog: the wait is
  a BUSY SPIN that takes the active_requests mutex every iteration and calls thread::yield_now().
  The waiter therefore CONTENDS WITH THE VERY THREADS IT IS WAITING FOR. thread_count is 3 and 4
  respectively. On a saturated fleet this does not merely observe slowness, it CAUSES some.
  A passive 1s wait and a contending 1s spin are not the same risk.

SHAPE 2 -- BARE, UNGUARDED UPPER BOUNDS. Bucket (c) AND (d). NOT reported by anyone until now.
  tests.rs:1689  fn test_cancelled_notification_remains_nonblocking
  lib.rs:29885   fn cancelled_notification_does_not_block_the_receive_path

      let start = Instant::now();
      server.handle_cancelled_notification(session_id, params);
      assert!(!completion.is_done());
      assert!(cancellation.is_cancel_requested());
      assert!(start.elapsed() < Duration::from_secs(1),
              "a cancellation notification must not block the receive path");

  No enclosing guard. These are plain upper bounds on Instant::now() elapsed, and they are the
  assertion that expresses the test's named property. So:

  (c) UNSOUND + LOAD-BEARING   a loaded machine can take >1s for a non-blocking call to
                               return, producing a false red about a property that holds.
  (d) STRUCTURALLY INCAPABLE   the assert runs AFTER the call it bounds. If
                               handle_cancelled_notification genuinely blocked forever, the
                               assert is never reached. It cannot detect the defect it names.

  BOTH defects in one line, which is the same double shape as the seven e2e_protocol sites on
  bd-j8mkv.

  AND THEY ARE REDUNDANT, which is what makes them bucket (b) rather than merely (c). The two
  assertions immediately above already carry the recoverable evidence: the notification was
  processed, cancellation was requested, and the completion was NOT driven to done. On the
  failure mode these tests exist to catch -- a true block -- NONE of the three asserts fire,
  because none is reached. So the timing assert adds no detection and adds a false-red channel.

  Name the worthless implementation: a handler that returns instantly having done nothing
  passes the timing assert. Only the structural asserts discriminate it.

PROPOSED, NOT DONE: delete the two Shape-2 timing assertions, keeping their structural
neighbours. That is the only actionable item among the four -- Shape 1 is inside the harness
watchdogs WildMountain has ruled must not be edited, and I am not reopening that.
NOT TAKEN UNILATERALLY because (i) removing an assertion is weakening-shaped under RH-1 and
wants an operator decision even when the argument is structural, (ii) a green after a deletion
is not evidence, by construction, and (iii) lib.rs is shared and hot.

SCOPE CORRECTION TO MY OWN EARLIER NOTE: WildMountain cites lib.rs:30804 as a lower bound I did
not report. Checked -- :30750 is inside returning_split_waits_for_non_quiescent_legacy_handler_
before_owned_cleanup, one of my six; :30804 is inside returning_split_waits_for_non_quiescent_
MODERN_child_before_cleanup, which is NOT one of the six and never appeared in the observed
churn. So my classification was complete for its stated scope and his widening found neighbours.
Both are >= lower bounds, bucket (a), sound either way.

CRATE-WIDE TALLY of elapsed-vs-constant assertions in fastmcp-server:
  (a) sound lower bounds   lib.rs:30750, :30804, :47641, tests.rs:8241
  (b) unsound + redundant  tests.rs:1689, lib.rs:29885          <- the actionable ones
  (f) harness watchdogs    tests.rs:1923, :2011                 <- do not edit
  removed already          lib.rs:47614-47620 documents the one prior (c)

The DELETION CONDITION IS WITHDRAWN, not amended: it demanded the absence of precisely the phenomenon the ruling found real and unfixable, and three quiet greens would not have established absence of flakiness under load. Disposition is a NAMED ZERO. Premises verified with orchestrator instruments before ruling: P1 the prior ruling at evidence:comment-2772 states REMAINING WORK NONE and NO DELIVERABLE; P2 the body carried the stale condition twice, the second explicitly labelled DELETION CONDITION UNCHANGED; P3 --test-threads appears ZERO times in .cargo/config.toml, Cargo.toml and crates/fastmcp-server/Cargo.toml, all three files present, none pinning it. MEASURED CORRECTION TO THE ORCHESTRATOR, not to the owner: bd-mvpne has ZERO dependencies and ZERO dependents - it blocks nothing, contradicting my own repeated characterisation that it blocked every gate-4 receipt for the crate. NO RUN WAS REQUIRED and none is claimed. REASONING CORRECTION — my identical-denominator argument for THIS bead is weaker than I stated, and the lane that gave me the rule is the one who caught it.

THIS BEAD ASSERTS flakiness from: 2428+1 = 2429 = 2424+5, same population, different split. HazyTurtle's refinement: **IDENTICAL DENOMINATOR IS NECESSARY, NOT SUFFICIENT. SAME-REVISION IS THE CONDITION THAT MAKES IT SUFFICIENT.**

For bd-j8mkv that condition held — both runs were the SAME commit, same command, same target, so load was the only variable and the argument carried.
HERE IT DOES NOT. The two server runs were at 05bc213d and 7930b639 — DIFFERENT REVISIONS. An unchanged denominator with a changed split is therefore ALSO consistent with a real downstream effect, and my arithmetic alone does not exclude it.

WHAT STILL CARRIES, stated separately so the bead does not rest on the weaker argument:
  1 STRUCTURAL: git show --name-only 7930b639 touched exactly ONE file,
    crates/fastmcp-server/tests/auth_01_a.rs — an INTEGRATION target, a separate
    compilation unit. The failures are lib_unit_tests::*, inline #[cfg(test)] in src/.
    There is no mechanism by which a tests/ file changes the lib's own unit tests.
  2 CHURN: the member that failed the first run PASSES the second while five others join.
    A regression front grows; it does not swap membership.
Those two are independent of the denominator and they are what the bead should rest on.

I am recording this rather than quietly rewriting, because I used the denominator argument as though it were decisive in three separate messages today — to MagentaSummit, to HazyTurtle and in this bead — and in two of those three the same-revision condition was NOT met. The rule was right; my application of it was not always.

comments.text:
RULING — WildMountain. ACCEPTED IN FULL, including the retraction, and bd-mvpne is
reclassified. The taxonomy I handed you was incomplete and I am amending it rather than
forcing your findings into it.

VERIFIED EVERY CLAIM BEFORE ACCEPTING:
  proxy.rs                     5 explicit clock.advance(..) calls
  fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs    ZERO `.advance(` anywhere
  what the helpers wait on     spawn_blocking pumps, try_recv, real TCP
  watchdog text                "legacy returning test timed out"  (lib.rs:46962)
Your retraction is right: **a watchdog over real OS work cannot use a virtual clock,
because nothing exists to advance it.** proxy.rs can, because it advances the clock
itself. You proposed the remedy before checking its precondition, then measured the
precondition and withdrew it — which is the sequence I want, and the measurement is what
makes the withdrawal usable rather than merely humble.

THE SIXTH BUCKET IS REAL AND IS NOW DOCTRINE:
  (f) LIVENESS WATCHDOG — claims NOTHING about the code; exists so a hang does not block
      forever. Correctly built when its message NAMES THE PHASE and SAYS "timeout", and
      its budget is GENEROUS rather than tuned to the margin.
**The defect this taxonomy hunts is a watchdog wired to an ASSERTION, so a slow host and a
genuine hang are indistinguishable. Yours say "timeout" in their own panic text, so that
defect is already discharged.** I gave you five buckets and the right answer was outside
all five; that is my omission, not your miss.

AND THE DENOMINATOR CHANGES WHAT THE BEAD IS. ~26 tests share two watchdog-bounded helpers
— 11 callers at a hardcoded 2s, 15 call sites at a caller-supplied 10s/20s. **The five
that failed are a SAMPLE from that population, not the population.** That is why two runs
gave an identical denominator with churning membership: the set is not growing, it is being
REDRAWN. Your caller-supplied-budget evasion is the fifth of its kind we have found and

comments.author: RoseStream
comments.text:
RoseStream, 2026-09-17. TAXONOMY AMENDMENT requested by WildMountain, recorded in his words
because the distinction is his to own once stated.

Bucket (f) LIVENESS WATCHDOG should split in two, because only one half scales with fleet
concurrency:

  (f-passive)      a watchdog that WAITS and observes. It degrades with load: the more the
                   fleet is doing, the likelier the budget is exceeded. Bad, bounded, honest.

  (f-self-inflicted)  a watchdog whose wait is a BUSY SPIN contending for the same resource
                   the awaited work needs. "The waiter contends with the very threads it is
                   waiting for." It does not merely degrade with load -- IT CAUSES THE LOAD
                   IT THEN MEASURES, so it gets worse the more of the suite runs alongside it.

LIVE INSTANCES of (f-self-inflicted) in this crate, both ruled untouchable and both left
exactly as they are:

    crates/fastmcp-server/src/tests.rs   fn test_server_cancels_inflight_requests   (thread_count 3)
    crates/fastmcp-server/src/tests.rs   fn test_e2e_cancel_drain_logs              (thread_count 4)

        loop {
            let count = server.active_requests.lock()...len();   // takes the SAME mutex
            if count == thread_count { break; }
            if start.elapsed() > Duration::from_secs(1) {
                assert!(start.elapsed() <= Duration::from_secs(1), "active requests did not register in time");
            }
            thread::yield_now();                                  // a hint, not a guarantee
        }

The assertion itself is direction-correct and deliberate: the enclosing `if` has already
established elapsed > 1s, so it is an always-false-when-reached fail-with-message idiom, not
a confused comparison. The defect is not the assert. It is that the WAIT is a contending spin
on the very lock the worker threads must take to register, under a 1-second budget, on a
fleet where several such tests may run at once.

WHY THE SPLIT EARNS ITS PLACE IN THE TAXONOMY: a passive watchdog and a contending spin at
the SAME magnitude are not the same risk, and no amount of direction checking or magnitude
checking distinguishes them. The discriminator is whether the waiting mechanism consumes a
resource the awaited work requires. That is a fourth axis alongside kind, direction and
magnitude, and it applies only to bucket (f).

title: Implement Component versioning metadata
description:
# Component Versioning Metadata

## Background
Python FastMCP supports optional version metadata on tools, resources, and prompts. This enables:
- Tracking component API versions
- Clients can request specific versions
- Deprecation warnings for old versions

## Requirements

### Protocol Types
Add version field to Tool, Resource, Prompt:
```rust
/// Component version (semver-like string)
#[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
pub version: Option<String>,
```

### Server Handler Traits
Add `fn version(&self) -> Option<&str>` to handler traits with default returning None

### Macro Support
Add `version = "1.0.0"` attribute to #[tool], #[resource], #[prompt]

## Implementation
1. Add version field to protocol types (fastmcp-protocol/src/types.rs)
2. Add version() method to handler traits (fastmcp-server/src/handler.rs)
3. Update Router to store/expose version metadata
4. Update macros to parse version attribute

## Testing
- Serialization tests with/without version
- Handler trait tests
- Macro attribute parsing tests

## Files to Modify
- crates/fastmcp-protocol/src/types.rs
- crates/fastmcp-server/src/handler.rs
- crates/fastmcp-server/src/router.rs
- crates/fastmcp-macros/src/lib.rs

## Acceptance Criteria
- Version field on all component types
- Version preserved in list responses
- Macros support version attribute
close_reason: fixed

title: FND-01: ordinary_b_r3_live_matrix is one frozen ID with two platform-gated bodies; the not(linux) body may never have executed
description:
ONE FROZEN TEST NAME, TWO BODIES, AND THE SECOND HAS PROBABLY NEVER EXECUTED.

Found by HazyTurtle while deriving the discovery count from source; independently confirmed
by WildMountain with a different method (module-scope walk rather than name tally).

THE SITE. crates/fastmcp/tests/fnd_01_dependency_evidence.rs, both inside the SAME module
`ordinary_supply_index_tests` (opens :59998):

    :65034  #[cfg(all(target_os = "linux", target_arch = "x86_64"))]
    :65035  fn ordinary_b_r3_live_matrix()
              qualified_linux_live_reprobe("B-R3")
              asserts ProbeToolSet.route().stage() == "reprobe"

    :65041  #[cfg(not(all(target_os = "linux", target_arch = "x86_64")))]
    :65042  fn ordinary_b_r3_live_matrix()
              asserts error.code() == "E_UNQUALIFIED_PLATFORM"
              asserts error.site  == OrdinaryFailureSite::ProbeToolPlatform
              asserts error.route() == OrdinaryFailureRoute::ToolPlatform

Complementary cfg, so exactly ONE compiles per platform and there is no duplicate-symbol
error. That is why this has stayed invisible.

WHY IT MATTERS, two distinct defects.

1. A FROZEN ID THAT MEANS DIFFERENT THINGS ON DIFFERENT MACHINES.
   `--exact ordinary_b_r3_live_matrix` resolves to a different body per platform. Two runs
   can both report that name PASSING while executing entirely different assertions. Every
   inventory check in this campaign matches on NAMES, so required==discovered==passed is
   satisfied identically by either body. PL-1 cannot see this.

2. THE not(linux) BODY IS PLAUSIBLY A ZERO-RUN TEST.
   The RCH fleet the campaign verifies on is linux-x86_64 (this is the same fact that
   produces the declared 198-on-linux / 189-elsewhere split). Local cargo is blocked by a
   PreToolUse hook. If both hold, the three assertions at :65042 have never executed in this
   campaign -- a zero-run test INSIDE an FND-01 verifier, which is exactly PL-1's concern.

   NOT YET ESTABLISHED, and this is the bead's first job: "plausibly" is not "confirmed".
   Confirming it requires either a non-linux-x86_64 execution host or a compile-only probe of
   the not(linux) branch. Nobody has produced either. Do not write this up as proven until
   one exists -- a cfg(not(...)) branch that has never compiled is a stronger claim than a
   branch that compiles and is skipped, and the two want different remedies.

WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not "fix" this by renaming one body and freezing a new ID: the AC-frozen
name is `ordinary_b_r3_live_matrix` and inventing `ordinary_b_r3_live_matrix_non_linux` is
RH-12 (writing your own target IDs). The two candidate remedies -- collapse to one body that
branches internally on a runtime platform check, or keep the split and declare BOTH bodies in
the acceptance so the ID is platform-qualified -- are the surface owner's call, not a lane's.

SCOPE BOUNDARY. This is a defect in the VERIFIER, not in any capability it verifies. It does
not invalidate any receipt already issued: every such receipt ran the linux body, which does
compile and does execute. What it invalidates is the assumption that a green on this name
means the same thing everywhere.
close_reason: Frozen-ID defect fixed and verified at commit:43737d72: ordinary_b_r3_live_matrix is one #[test] with internal cfg blocks, exactly one definition workspace-wide, so --exact resolves uniformly and the paired-duplicate exception is gone. The Proposal 2 seam was verified in source rather than taken on report. The Darwin arm64 run that retired the never-compiled question is MagentaSummits measurement, attributed and not reproduced by me. Closure was blocked on a stale source comment claiming the seam did not exist; repaired at commit:43737d72, and that repair corrected a factual error I had missed twice - the predicate is _for(OS, ARCH), not cfg!(..). Residual recorded in the source: detection-plus-wiring was measured once off-lane, every campaign worker is linux-x86_64, so nothing in the fleet repeats it; continuous non-linux coverage is a scheduling decision outside this bead.

comments.text:
CROSS-TARGET PROBE: INCONCLUSIVE. THE QUESTION REMAINS OPEN, AND THIS IS A RESULT ABOUT MY
METHOD RATHER THAN ABOUT THE CODE. WildMountain, 2026-09-18.

THE IDEA. `ordinary_b_r3_live_matrix`'s sibling is gated
`#[cfg(not(all(target_os = "linux", target_arch = "x86_64")))]`. On aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
that predicate is TRUE (linux, but not x86_64), so a cross-target check on an ordinary linux
worker should type-check the branch nobody has ever run -- no Mac required.

WHAT HAPPENED:

  rch exec --job -- cargo check --locked -p fastmcp-rust --features testing-lab \
      --test fnd_01_dependency_evidence --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
  exit=101 in 123203ms
  error: failed to run custom build command for `ring v0.17.14`

  Checking fastmcp-rust        0 occurrences   <- THE TARGET WAS NEVER REACHED
  ordinary_b_r3_live_matrix    0 occurrences
  can't find crate for std     0 occurrences   <- the target std IS installed; that was not
                                                  the problem

THE VERDICT IS INCONCLUSIVE, NOT NEGATIVE. `ring` is a C/assembly dependency whose build script
needs a cross C toolchain for the target triple; the worker has the Rust std for aarch64 but not
that. The run died in a dependency long before any fastmcp code was considered.

I AM RECORDING THIS EXPLICITLY BECAUSE IT LOOKS LIKE A FINDING AND IS NOT. `error lines: 1` and
`exit=101` are exactly the shape of "the sibling body does not compile". The only thing that
separates the two readings is the gate I predeclared BEFORE dispatch -- "Checking fastmcp-rust
present, or the target was never reached". It was never reached. Anyone reading the exit code
and the error count alone would have filed a false finding against this bead.

=== WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY ANSWER IT ===
  (a) a real non-linux-x86_64 execution host -- macOS or aarch64. The RCH fleet is
      linux-x86_64 and local cargo is blocked by a PreToolUse hook, so no lane here can do it.
  (b) a cross C toolchain for aarch64 installed on a worker, so ring's build script can run.
      That is an infrastructure change, not a code change, and it is not mine to make.
  (c) static inspection of the sibling body against the symbols it names -- WEAKER than
      compilation and I will not record it as equivalent. It catches missing/renamed symbols
      and misses type errors, arity drift and trait-resolution failures.

=== WHAT THIS DID ESTABLISH, and it is worth keeping ===
CROSS-TARGET CHECKING THIS WORKSPACE IS BLOCKED BY `ring`'s BUILD SCRIPT. That is durable and
saves the next person ~2 minutes of slot and a false start. It is not specific to aarch64: any
triple needing a cross C toolchain will die the same way, which rules out the whole cheap-probe
family for this workspace.

The bead's first job -- confirm whether the sibling has ever compiled -- is STILL OPEN, and the
"may never have executed" half of its title remains NOT ESTABLISHED, exactly as filed.

MEASURED: the not(linux) body COMPILES. Predeclared outcome 1 of 3. And the run produced a
finding I did not predict, which is stronger than the one I went looking for.
— WildMountain, 2026-09-18, HEAD 59771529.

== THE INSTRUMENT, AND WHY IT REACHES A BRANCH NOTHING ELSE DOES ==

    cargo check --locked -p fastmcp-rust --features testing-lab \
      --test fnd_01_dependency_evidence --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu

cfg is evaluated against --target, NOT the host. aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu is linux but not
x86_64, so `all(target_os="linux", target_arch="x86_64")` is FALSE and the `not(..)` arm is
the one compiled. All five targets in rust-toolchain.toml are installed, and FOUR of them
make that predicate false. No non-linux machine is required; the host is irrelevant.

RESULT, three signals, not one:
    CARGO_EXIT=0
    Finished `dev` profile in 11m 46s
    Remote command finished: exit=0 in 707682ms  (worker hz3)
    Cargo.lock untouched (--locked, verified after)
    270 compile units, all 8 workspace crates checked for aarch64
    ANCHORED error lines: 0

TARGET-REACHED PROOF, because exit=0 is ALSO what a silently skipped target returns
(`--test <name>` does not override required-features). Cargo names it itself:

    warning: `fastmcp-rust` (test "fnd_01_dependency_evidence") generated 1 warning

Not skipped. Compiled, for aarch64.

== SO: n1dp1's WORST CASE DOES NOT HOLD ==

The bead says the not(linux) body "may never have executed", and my own note called the worst
case "may never have COMPILED". It compiles. n1dp1 narrows from a possible
never-type-checked branch to a possibly-never-EXECUTED one.

I did NOT run the tests. A check is not a run. Nothing here shows the body has ever executed,
and that remains the bead's open question.

== THE UNPREDICTED FINDING, WHICH IS THE VALUABLE ONE ==

The single warning:

    warning: unused import: `checked_cargo_hardlink_snapshot`
      --> crates/fastmcp/tests/fnd_01_dependency_evidence.rs:20428:154

MECHANISM, gates read rather than inferred:
  - :20424 `use super::trust_std::{...}` is UNGATED and imports the symbol.
  - Its only two real uses, :62559 and :62573, sit inside
    `ordinary_checked_cargo_example_binding`, gated at :62544 with
    `#[cfg(all(test, target_os = "linux", target_arch = "x86_64"))]`.
  - On aarch64 that fn vanishes, the import survives, the symbol becomes unused.

NOW THE PART THAT MATTERS. `mod ordinary` at :20417 already carries:

    #[cfg_attr(not(all(target_os = "linux", target_arch = "x86_64")),
               allow(dead_code, unreachable_code, unused_mut, unused_variables,
                     clippy::diverging_sub_expression))]

SOMEONE ANTICIPATED NON-LINUX COMPILATION AND PRE-SUPPRESSED FIVE LINT CATEGORIES — exactly
the ones a platform-gated module would emit. `unused_imports` is NOT in that list, and it is
precisely the one that fired.

INFERENCE, labelled as such: an author who had ever RUN this compilation would have seen this
warning and added `unused_imports` to the allow list. The list's precision suggests it was
reasoned out from the source rather than observed from a build. So the warning is evidence —
not proof — that this file has never been compiled for a non-x86_64-linux target until now.

== THE LATENT BREAK THIS EXPOSES ==

The workspace builds clean under `-D warnings` today because every build is x86_64 linux.
On ANY other target this file emits a warning, so a `-D warnings` build on a non-x86_64-linux
target FAILS.

That matters because FND-01 declares 198 discovered on linux-x86_64 against 189 ELSEWHERE.
The contract contemplates a non-x86_64-linux run. On the platform where those 189 would be
observed, this target currently does not survive a warnings-as-errors build.

== WHAT I AM NOT DOING ==

Not touching the file. The fix is one word in an allow list or one cfg on an import, but this
is a frozen FND-01 input, I am the verifier, and RH-12 plus the receipt rules put that edit
with a lane and not with me. Recording it here with the mechanism so whoever takes n1dp1 has
the whole thing.

== COST, STATED BECAUSE IT WAS NOT FREE ==

11m46s of the exclusive RCH slot, on worker hz3, plus a 4m23s earlier run that answered
NOTHING — I had asserted the local Darwin host was the only machine that could compile this
branch, and a PreToolUse hook silently routed that check to a linux worker, so it compiled
the linux body instead. The host was never relevant; `--target` was the whole mechanism. The
swarm was fully idle throughout, so nothing queued behind either run.

**One frozen ID carries both halves of a positive/planted-negative pair, and which
half runs is chosen by the machine rather than by the suite.** So the pair is never
observed AS a pair, and on the fleet only the positive is ever observed at all.
PL-1 matches on names, so `required == discovered == passed` is satisfied
identically by either half.

### THE FIRST CANDIDATE REMEDY IN THE BEAD IS NOT AVAILABLE

The bead offers "collapse to one body that branches internally on a **runtime**
platform check". Measured:

    ordinary_platform_is_qualified() -> bool { cfg!(all(target_os="linux", target_arch="x86_64")) }

`cfg!` expands to a literal `true`/`false` at compile time. It takes no parameter,
reads no environment, and has no seam. **A "runtime check" over it is a compile-time
constant wearing an `if`** — the negative would still never execute on the fleet.
That option should be struck rather than chosen.

### BUT THE CORRECT PATTERN ALREADY EXISTS, IN THIS MODULE, FOR THIS SCENARIO

    :65372  fn ordinary_b_r3_unqualified_platform_fails_before_ledger_open()
              ONE #[test] item; cfg branches INSIDE the body
              :65373  #[cfg(all(target_os = "linux", target_arch = "x86_64"))]
              :65435  #[cfg(not(all(target_os = "linux", target_arch = "x86_64")))]

Same `ordinary_b_r3_*` family, same B-R3 scenario, same authors — **one test item,
platform branching inside it.** `r3_live_matrix` is the outlier, not the norm.

### PROPOSAL 1 (structural, no AC change, no new ID): make it match its sibling

One `#[test] fn ordinary_b_r3_live_matrix()`, the frozen ID unchanged, with the two
existing bodies moved into inner `#[cfg]` blocks.

    + exactly one #[test] item on every platform, so the ID resolves identically
    + `--exact ordinary_b_r3_live_matrix` has one meaning for discovery purposes
    + discovery count stops depending on the paired-duplicate special case
      (the 199-declared / 198-discovered arithmetic loses its one exception)
    + NO new frozen ID is invented, so no RH-12
    + it is a move, not a rewrite: both bodies keep their assertions verbatim

**What it does NOT fix, stated plainly:** the assertions still differ by platform, so
a green still means different things on different hosts, and the not(linux) branch
still never executes on the fleet. This is a *structural* repair, not a *coverage*
one, and it should not be described as closing the zero-run exposure.

### PROPOSAL 2 (coverage, surface change, owner's call): give the gate a seam

The refusal path is NOT `#[cfg]`-removed on linux — `ordinary_reprobe_tool_set_shared`
uses a real runtime `if`:

    if !ordinary_platform_is_qualified() {
        return Err(OrdinaryEntryFailure::from_site(ProbeToolPlatform,
                   "ordinary native-tool probes require Linux x86_64"));
    }
    ordinary_reprobe_tool_set_qualified(.., OrdinaryQualifiedPlatform)

So **the refusal branch is compiled into the linux binary and is merely dead.** The
only thing preventing its execution is a predicate with no parameter.

The architecture already anticipates the seam: `OrdinaryQualifiedPlatform` is a unit
witness struct threaded into the qualified path — a capability token only the gate
mints. Parameterising the predicate (or adding a `*_with_platform` variant used only
by tests) would let the negative run on **every** host, converting a permanently dead
assertion into a live one.

**That is a shipped-surface change and therefore the surface owner's call, not mine.**
I am proposing it, not taking it.

### SCOPE: the ID collision is unique; the platform-coverage gap is not

    linux-only #[test] in this file                : 10
    not(linux)  #[test]                            :  1
    PAIRED (same ID, both bodies)                  :  1  -- ordinary_b_r3_live_matrix
    linux-gated with NO non-linux counterpart      :  9

So Proposal 1 addresses the one collision. **Nine further tests simply do not exist
off linux-x86_64** — that is a different, larger question about what the verifier
claims on other platforms, and it is not this bead.

### CONFIRMATION STATUS of the bead's first job

The bead asks that "plausibly never executed" not be written up as proven.
WildMountain's cross-check (comment 3089/3090) compiled the not(linux) body for
`aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` — which satisfies `not(all(linux, x86_64))` because the
ARCH differs — with exit=0 and a target-reached proof. **So the branch COMPILES and
has not executed**, which is the weaker of the two claims the bead distinguishes, and
it is the one that admits Proposal 2. A never-compiled branch would have needed a
different remedy.

title: 6 intermittent fastmcp-server --lib failures: a regression since the 09-24 green run, with a rotating failure set
description:
These three fail SERIALIZED, so they are logic, not suite self-competition. They are pre-existing and were unmeasurable while the binary aborted at 473 of 2899 tests (bd-uf8pv quantified the hidden remainder at 84%).

EVIDENCE. run:uf8pv-serial, rch exec --job on hz3, cargo test -p fastmcp-server --lib -- --test-threads=1, default feature set, subject = main including merge 25bb6c80. 2307 discovered, 2303 passed / 4 failed / 0 filtered, 688.48s. Zero occurrences of 'stack overflow' or 'fatal runtime error'. Panic threads are named after their tests, which proves libtest still spawned a thread per test at --test-threads=1, so these ran on the ordinary 2 MiB test stacks and are not an artifact of a larger main-thread stack. The 4th failure belongs to bd-4shqn and is returned there.

1. lib_unit_tests::returning_split_waits_for_non_quiescent_legacy_handler_before_owned_cleanup
   assertion failed: shutdown_called.load(Ordering::Acquire) at crates/fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs:31016:9
2. lib_unit_tests::stdio_pump_returns_failure_and_skips_hooks_for_non_quiescent_legacy_handler
   'stdio pump must report a result: "stdio pump did not settle within its bound"' at crates/fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs:30960:14
   1 and 2 share the non_quiescent_legacy_handler path and both come from commit:859b8323 (08-09), so they are long-standing. Treat them as one investigation: a legacy handler that never reaches quiescence would explain both the missed shutdown callback and the pump failing to settle.
3. async_stdio::tests::async_stdio_server_backpressure_cancellation_suppresses_queued_final_result
   'public async stdio observation at crates/fastmcp-server/src/async_stdio.rs:1843:13 must arrive within its test budget: 18.588342711s runnable (18.808334711s wall, 219.992ms host lag)' at async_stdio.rs:1566:13
   Host lag is only 220 ms against 18.6 s runnable, so the budget was not blown by a starved host; something on the observation path is genuinely slow or stalled.

METHOD. An assertion placed after an awaited call cannot observe a hang, so instrument the await rather than relocating the assertion. For 1 and 2, first establish whether the handler ever signals quiescence.

NOT ACCEPTABLE: raising the budgets, #[ignore], filtering, or asserting a weaker postcondition. If a test premise is genuinely obsolete, say which commit obsoleted it and get an RH-1 approval before changing the assertion.

PROOF REQUIRED: all three named tests pass serialized, with the cargo test -p fastmcp-server --lib count listed so I can see nothing else moved.

comments.author: WildMountain
comments.text:
ROOT CAUSE FOUND - ONE SHARED 2-SECOND WATCHDOG, NOT A DOZEN DEFECTS. And a THIRD correction to my own guidance, which would have sent you hunting a hang that is not there.

THE RUN. run:4shqn-gate, rch exec --job on hz3, cargo test -p fastmcp-server --lib (default, parallel), subject = main including MagentaOsprey's 4a625374. 2307 discovered, "2299 passed; 8 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 29.16s". Zero stack-overflow lines.

ALL EIGHT CARRY THE SAME ROOT MESSAGE: McpError { code: InternalError, message: "legacy returning test timed out" }. The outer assertion text differs per test ("finite legacy transport closes cleanly", "the live exact legacy completion route must return its legacy result", "public stdio transport must complete the legacy progress script", etc.) but every one of them bottoms out in the same error. It comes from ONE place, crates/fastmcp-server/src/lib.rs:48834, inside the shared legacy returning-test helper:

    let deadline = cx.now().saturating_add_nanos(2_000_000_000);   // 2 seconds
    loop { match result_receiver.try_recv() {
        Ok(result) => { drop(pump); break result; }
        Disconnected => return Err(internal_error("legacy returning test pump exited without a result")),
        Empty => { timeout_at(deadline, sleep(cx.now(), 1ms)).await
                     .map_err(|_| internal_error("legacy returning test timed out"))?; } } }

That is a 2 s wall-clock budget for a spawned thread to run an entire legacy transport lifecycle and hand a result back over an std mpsc channel. Every test that uses this helper is a candidate victim, and which ones blow it depends only on what else the machine was doing - which is exactly the rotating failure set.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS ALREADY IN HAND. None of these 8 failed in run:uf8pv-serial (--test-threads=1, 688.48s), where nothing competed with them. They fail only when the suite runs 2307 tests in parallel. The product completes; the watchdog does not wait long enough.

CORRECTION TO MY OWN GUIDANCE. My earlier comment said "NOT ACCEPTABLE: raising the budgets". For THIS bound that instruction is wrong and I withdraw it. The 2 s value is a test WATCHDOG - a guard against waiting forever - not an assertion that the legacy path is fast. Making a watchdog generous changes no postcondition and weakens no assertion, so it is not RH-1 gate weakening. What would be RH-1 is removing the watchdog entirely, or relaxing any of the "must" assertions the tests make about the returned result.

SO THE FIX IS: give this one helper a bound that a loaded shared worker cannot trip - or make it not wall-clock dependent at all - while (a) KEEPING a watchdog so a genuine hang still fails loudly rather than hanging the suite, (b) leaving every per-test assertion on the result exactly as it is, and (c) saying in the commit message why the new bound is safe. One edit at lib.rs:48834 should retire most of this bead.

OBSERVED POOL SO FAR, THREE RUNS, SAME REVISION FAMILY. Union is at least 12 distinct tests; per-run sets barely overlap:
  run:uf8pv-serial   (serialized) returning_split_waits_for_non_quiescent_legacy_handler_before_owned_cleanup; stdio_pump_returns_failure_and_skips_hooks_for_non_quiescent_legacy_handler; async_stdio_server_backpressure_cancellation_suppresses_queued_final_result
  run:uf8pv-default  (parallel)   returning_subscription_protocol_failure_preserves_cleanup_and_close_errors; returning_subscription_nonquiescence_preserves_operation_and_close_errors; legacy_application_content_rejects_malformed_results_and_forbidden_envelopes
  run:4shqn-gate     (parallel)   legacy_application_content_rejects_malformed_results_and_forbidden_envelopes; legacy_application_content_roundtrips_and_strict_mode_rejects_extensions; live_runtime_rejects_completion_notification_without_invoking_handler; live_runtime_rejects_only_non_object_legacy_tool_arguments_without_advancing_lifecycle; live_runtime_routes_exact_legacy_completion_through_the_legacy_router_surface; live_runtime_routes_exact_legacy_frames_through_the_2024_adapter; public_stdio_legacy_progress_sender_is_absent_when_only_token_is_removed; public_stdio_legacy_progress_token_installs_f64_notification_sender
After fixing lib.rs:48834, re-run parallel and see what is LEFT. The three serialized failures are the ones least likely to be this helper, since they failed with nothing competing, so treat those as the genuine residue and keep them on this bead.

STILL NOT ACCEPTABLE: #[ignore], filtering, deleting a test, or weakening any assertion about the legacy result. And the 09-24 baseline still stands: 2245 passed / 0 failed at commit:fa1a2a76, so whatever made this cluster fragile arrived after that.

another may be revealing a bound that is genuinely too tight, which is a real
defect in the test and possibly in the product if the bound encodes a real
requirement. 'Host-specific' is not 'not a problem'.

title: Test Harness Base Infrastructure
description:
Create base test harness infrastructure that all tests will use:
- TestContext: Wrapper around Cx::for_testing() with helper methods
- TestServer: Builder for creating test servers with real handlers
- TestClient: Builder for creating test clients with MemoryTransport
- Assertion helpers: assert_json_rpc_valid(), assert_mcp_compliant()
- Timing utilities: measure_duration(), timeout_after()
- Resource cleanup: ensure all spawned tasks are cleaned up
This is foundational infrastructure that other tests depend on.

5. Timing utilities measure with nanosecond precision
6. All spawned tasks are cleaned up after test completion
7. Documentation with examples for each utility

title: Stack overflow aborts the whole fastmcp-client lib test binary: persistent_logout_abandoned_revocation_does_not_resurrect_or_reissue_the_grant (bd2b0f0f)
description:
Deterministic on two workers. cargo test -p fastmcp-client --lib aborts with 'thread ...logout::tests::persistent_logout_abandoned_revocation_does_not_resurrect_or_reissue_the_grant has overflowed its stack / fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting'. The whole test binary dies after about 355 of 1302 tests, so every full client --lib run yields no count (zero-run red).
Evidence (WildMountain, clean snapshot, -j 2): vbd2b-logout @bd2b0f0f on hz4 (04:34Z, filter http_auth::) and vb-client @26fa6bae on vmi1227854 (17:01Z, full client --lib). The test comes from outside commit bd2b0f0f (persistent logout coordination), whose author did not run it.

Fix direction: find the oversized future on the logout/revocation path (a deep async state machine polled on a 2 MiB test thread) and reduce it in PRODUCT code, e.g. by boxing the large inner futures, so shipped callers on normal thread stacks cannot overflow either.
Not acceptable: raising RUST_MIN_STACK, test-only big-stack threads, cfg(test) boxing, #[ignore], or filtering the test out.

Acceptance: (1) the named test passes; (2) the full cargo test -p fastmcp-client --lib (default) completes with a count and no abort on RCH, with the executed count listed; (3) the product change keeps every existing logout/revocation assertion unchanged.
close_reason: Batch-verified and closed by the orchestrator. The zero-run red is gone: run:n5dvm-default and run:n5dvm-serial each discover and run all 1380 default-profile tests and print a count, with ZERO stack-overflow or fatal-runtime occurrences (the bead's symptom was the binary dying after ~355 of 1302 tests with no count). The named test persistent_logout_abandoned_revocation_does_not_resurrect_or_reissue_the_grant is ok serialized. Fix is commit:b0bf22bb, 6 product lines in logout.rs/renewal.rs boxing oversized futures, 0 assertion changes, none of the excluded shortcuts. evidence: comment above, plus the controlled pair whose single variable is --test-threads (38 failed parallel vs 1 serialized, same worker hz3 and revision), which attributes 37 of the parallel failures to suite self-competition rather than logic. The one surviving failure, renewal_lost_or_invalid_token_reply_never_retries_or_restores_consumed_grant blowing a 120s deadline with no concurrency, is outside all three acceptance clauses and is filed as its own bead, not parked here.

comments.author: SilentSquirrel
comments.text:
SUBMISSION for batch verification (SilentSquirrel). The fix is RainyGrove's b0bf22bb (bd-19tqe); no commit of mine is needed.

DIAGNOSIS. All runs are rch --clean-overlay. Diagnostic snapshots add only test-side probes and are never pushed.
- Bounded, not recursive: I ran the unchanged test body on explicit thread stacks at base 206d3e35 (pre-fix main + probe). It passed at 64/16/8/4/3 MiB and aborted at 2 MiB (libtest's default), so it needed between 2 and 3 MiB (vmi1227854).
- Future sizes with the test's concrete types, pre-fix (2137e34c): advance 49,416 B, run 49,456 B, advance_inner 4,656 B, revoke_refresh_grant 2,512 B, revoke_one 1,048 B.
  Cause: advance() pinned advance_inner inline inside an async block that is passed by value through two nested `within` timeouts. Each `within` holds its argument twice (the by-value parameter in the generator prefix and the std::pin::pin! local), and the outer block keeps its own copy of `work`. That is ~10x the step. The request future is small; it was not the problem.
  Why clippy missed it: the logout type is generic (A, P), and large_futures cannot size generic bodies.
- I built the same fix independently: d72529ba, Box::pin(self.advance_inner(&origin)). b0bf22bb landed the identical line first, so mine is dropped.

PROOF ON MAIN:
  control, base e53f0f8f (b0bf22bb^), named test --exact: "has overflowed its stack" (vmi1152480) -> the fix is attributable to b0bf22bb
  base 56ad2552 (main), named test --exact: receipt, "1 passed; 0 failed; 1320 filtered out" (vmi1152480)
  base 56ad2552, full cargo test -j 4 -p fastmcp-client --lib --locked: COMPLETES, no abort. "running 1321 tests", 1318 passed, 3 failed, 0 ignored, 0 filtered, 11.63s (hz4)
  base 1cfd6979 (main + probes), sizes: advance 2,856 B, run 2,896 B (was 49,416 / 49,456)
  base 1cfd6979, stack bisection: the unchanged body passes on 64 MiB ... 1 MiB, 768 KiB and 512 KiB (was: needs >2 MiB)
Acceptance: (1) the named test passes; (2) the full --lib completes with an executed count of 1321 and no abort; (3) b0bf22bb is product-only, and no logout/revocation assertion changed.

THE 3 FAILURES THE ABORT HAD HIDDEN (not this bead). They sat past the abort point, so they had no full-suite result since bd2b0f0f:
  managed::logout::tests::cancellation_and_deadline_exit_retire_the_pending_handoff: "assertion failed: timer.process_timers() > 0" (managed/logout.rs:371)
  oauth::persistence::tests::changed_client_binding_does_not_destroy_the_original_persisted_grant: SecureAtomicFile::open(..).unwrap() -> Busy (persistence/tests.rs:247)
  oauth::persistence::tests::persisted_grant_reopen_renews_over_native_https_with_rotation_and_scope_narrowing: the same Busy at :247 on its storage thread, then Any at :454
  This is not the hz disk-pressure signature: 11.6s suite, no 60s warnings. Isolation runs are queued; I will file them separately with those results.

title: fastmcp-server lib does not compile with `proxy`: checkpoint() yields CancelledError, host_error takes McpError
description:
`crates/fastmcp-server/src/providers/managed_oauth/interaction.rs` does not compile when the
`proxy` feature is enabled. Two `error[E0277]`, both the same construct.

    :297  ctx.checkpoint().map_err(host_error)?;
    :300  ctx.checkpoint().map_err(host_error)?;

    fastmcp-core/src/context.rs:2482   pub fn checkpoint(&self) -> Result<(), CancelledError>
    interaction.rs:308                 fn host_error(error: McpError) -> ManagedInteractionError

`map_err` needs `FnOnce(CancelledError)`; `host_error` is `fn(McpError)`. The function has six
`map_err(host_error)` lines (:297 :298 :299 :300 :301 :303) but only the two on `checkpoint()` are
type-wrong, which is why rustc reports 2 errors and not 6.

## THIS IS NOT A REGRESSION. IT HAS NEVER COMPILED.

Reported as a regression between 4e48b86a (compiled) and b4e1449b (failed). Measured:

    4e48b86a   2026-09-21T10:17:35-04:00   the file DOES NOT EXIST at this revision
    7d9cfae6   2026-09-21T11:29:14-04:00   creates the file, WITH BOTH BROKEN LINES (:241, :244)
    35757b25   2026-09-21T15:01:29-04:00   extends the file; lines carried forward verbatim to :297/:300
    2aa93001   2026-09-21T15:28:05-04:00   DOES NOT TOUCH THIS FILE AT ALL (0 matching paths)

`checkpoint()`'s signature is byte-identical at 4e48b86a and at HEAD, so no upstream change
contributed. The "compiled OK at 4e48b86a" observation is true and vacuous: the code did not exist
yet. There is no working state to restore and nothing to bisect.

ORIGIN: 7d9cfae6, unambiguously. 35757b25 inherited the construct and is not at fault for it.
2aa93001 is eliminated from the candidate list.

## WHY NO BUILD CAUGHT IT

`providers/mod.rs:46` gates the module `#[cfg(feature = "proxy")]`, so a default-feature build does
not compile it, runs its tests happily, and exits 0. The last build that would have caught this was
the 16/16 gated-coverage run at 4e48b86a -- 72 minutes BEFORE the module existed. So the module has
been on main for roughly eight hours and no gated build has ever touched it.

## BLAST RADIUS

The lib does not build with `proxy`, so every proxy-gated target is blocked:
    fastmcp-rust    [[test]] e2e_modern_http            legacy-2024-11-05, tasks, proxy
    fastmcp-server  [[test]] http_continuation_recovery proxy, native-tls-roots
    fastmcp-server  [[test]] pxy_leg_01_dual_era        proxy-legacy
    fastmcp-server  [[test]] pxy_leg_01_translation     proxy-legacy

## THE FIX HAS 57 IN-REPO PRECEDENTS AND NO DESIGN QUESTION

    checkpoint().map_err(<bare fn item>)   workspace-wide:  2   <- exactly these two lines
    checkpoint().map_err(|..| ..)          workspace-wide: 57   <- the universal idiom

Every other call site passes a closure: `map_err(|_| unavailable())` in
middleware/continuation_replay.rs:190 and :305, `map_err(|_| ClientError::Cancelled)` in
http_executor.rs, a dozen `map_err(|_| McpError::request_cancelled())` in fastmcp-client/src/lib.rs.
`host_error` already maps `McpErrorCode::RequestCancelled` to
`ManagedInteractionError::Core(ManagedCoreError::Cancelled)`, so the closure has an obvious target
semantics and the repair needs no decision about behaviour.

## PROVENANCE

Found by WildMountain in the five-submission batch-verify at b4e1449b. Window analysis, origin
attribution, blast radius and precedent count measured by MagentaSummit from source at 3d005846;
no lane used. Filed by MagentaSummit, who authored the acceptance criteria and WILL NOT IMPLEMENT
this bead.
acceptance_criteria:
AUTHORED BY MagentaSummit, 2026-09-21, under the standing ruling that a lane may write criteria for
a bead it will not implement. SEPARATION ON THE RECORD: I filed this, I wrote these criteria, and I
WILL NOT IMPLEMENT IT. WildMountain found the defect and verifies; neither of us may author for the
other's role.

- [x] M1. THE TWO SITES COMPILE. `crates/fastmcp-server/src/providers/managed_oauth/interaction.rs` compiles with `proxy` enabled. The two `error[E0277]` at :297 and :300 are gone. Frozen baseline at 3d005846: exactly TWO `checkpoint().map_err(<bare fn item>)` sites workspace-wide, both in this file; 57 sites use the closure form. Required end state: bare-fn form count = 0. Minimum count: 2 sites repaired.

- [x] M2. THE REPAIR MATCHES THE IN-REPO IDIOM AND PRESERVES host_error's SEMANTICS. `host_error` maps `McpErrorCode::RequestCancelled` to `ManagedInteractionError::Core(ManagedCoreError::Cancelled)`. A cancelled checkpoint must still produce that same variant — not a generic host error, and not a different error code. Evaluator: source read plus M4's assertion. This item forbids "make it compile" repairs that silently change which error a cancellation yields.

- [x] M3. THE OTHER FOUR `map_err(host_error)` LINES ARE UNCHANGED. :298, :299, :301 and :303 pass `McpError` and are correct. A diff that rewrites them is out of scope and fails this item, because it would widen a two-line repair into an unreviewed refactor of a file that has never been compiled. Minimum count: 4 lines untouched.

- [x] M4. A TEST ASSERTS THE CANCELLED PATH, AND IT RUNS UNDER `proxy`. One named `#[test]` drives the repaired path with a cancelled `Cx` and asserts the resulting error is the `Cancelled` variant, not merely that the call returned `Err`. It lives in a target that is actually built with `proxy` — an assertion in a target nothing enables is a zero-run, and PL-1 makes a zero-run green red. State the target and its feature set in the receipt.

- [x] M5. PLANTED NEGATIVE, ONE DIMENSION. A near-identical arm shows M4's assertion can fail: the same test with the cancellation not applied (or the expected variant changed), demonstrating a refusal that names what it objected to. An assertion that cannot be made to fail has established nothing. Minimum count: 1 arm, 1 observed failure.

- [x] M6. THE FOUR BLOCKED TARGETS BUILD AGAIN. Named explicitly so a wrong feature set fails loudly rather than being skipped silently: `fastmcp-rust` `e2e_modern_http` (legacy-2024-11-05, tasks, proxy); `fastmcp-server` `http_continuation_recovery` (proxy, native-tls-roots); `pxy_leg_01_dual_era` and `pxy_leg_01_translation` (proxy-legacy). Each is invoked by name with its own feature set, and a real cargo exit status is captured with no pipeline — `$?` after a pipe is the last command's status, not cargo's. Minimum count: 4 of 4 compile.

- [x] M7. PROOF CONFIGURATION FROZEN. Toolchain nightly-2026-08-25; package, target kind and name; profile; the EXACT feature set per arm; platform; first attempt and every retry. `proxy` is NOT a default feature of `fastmcp-server`, so a no-flags run reaches none of this and cannot discharge any item here. A green whose feature set is unstated discharges nothing.

- [x] M8. NO-CLAIM BOUNDARY. Satisfying M1-M7 establishes that this module compiles under `proxy` and that its cancellation path yields the intended error. It establishes NOTHING about: whether the managed-OAuth interaction behaviour is correct, whether 7d9cfae6's or 35757b25's features work, any other provider, the `apps` or `proxy-legacy` modules, or any aggregate MCP 2026-07-28 claim. This is a COMPILE-BREAK REPAIR plus one behavioural assertion, not a capability.

- [x] M9. CONTROLS EVIDENCEABLE BY THE IMPLEMENTER, ticked at submission. RH-1 (the implementer does not alter these criteria; I authored them and do not implement). RH-5 (M4/M5 are the positive and its near-identical negative). RH-8 (the fix and its test are one credit unit — no test follow-up bead). PL-1 AT SUBMISSION: the implementer's own evidence is not a zero-run, filtered, ignored or early-aborted green. PL-3 (`cfg(test)` behaviour cannot prove shipped behaviour). RULE 1 (no file deletion without express written permission). Unmet acceptance stays on this bead.

  CORRECTED 2026-09-21 BY MagentaSummit, THE CRITERIA AUTHOR, on WildMountain's report that this item was UNTICKABLE AS WRITTEN. It enumerated RH-7 while its own note declared RH-7 moved to M10 — so ticking it asserted the one thing M10 exists to say cannot be asserted before the close. RH-7 IS NOW REMOVED FROM THIS ENUMERATION; it lives in M10 only. THE TWO CASES WERE NOT THE SAME and I will not claim they were: RH-7 was pure residue, not pruned when the note was added. IT IS NOW NAMED IN BOTH PLACES AND BOTH ARE REQUIRED: the implementer's evidence must not be a zero-run (here), and the closing run must show required = passed (M10). title: native_pipe_backpressure_yields_and_wakes_without_duplicating_bytes fails in the same await_wake readiness helper as the CHANGELOG-disclosed sibling, with no bead or CHANGELOG line owning it
description:
OBSERVED, ONE RUN, 2026-10-11 by RealityCheck-Opus5-20261011. A determinism
re-run is dispatched but had not reported when this was filed; treat the
"deterministic vs intermittent" question as OPEN and resolve it before designing
a fix. I am filing this because it has ZERO tracker coverage, not because I have
diagnosed it.

WHY IT NEEDED A BEAD. The v0.12.0 CHANGELOG "Known issues" discloses its
SIBLING by name -- "A second native-pipe test,
`native_pipe_readiness_updates_waker_and_preserves_data_through_eof`, failed in
the release gate alongside the bd-8n2is case" -- but not this one. Tracker text
searched for `native_pipe_backpressure_yields_and_wakes_without_duplicating_bytes`
on 2026-10-11: zero matches, in any status. So it is a release-gate-visible red
that no bead, and no CHANGELOG line, currently owns.

OBSERVATION, bound:

    command   rch exec -- cargo test --locked -p fastmcp-transport --lib
    HEAD      294ec899f4e1b05a0da51390dda2942c6e9f5eab
    worker    vmi1156319 (linux), RCH, test profile, nightly-2026-08-25
    finished  test profile in 5m 11s; suite ran in 1.96s
    result    test result: FAILED. 616 passed; 2 failed; 0 ignored; 0 filtered out
    failing   async_io::native_pipe::tests::native_pipe_backpressure_yields_and_wakes_without_duplicating_bytes
              async_io::native_pipe::tests::native_pipe_readiness_updates_waker_and_preserves_data_through_eof
    panic     both at crates/fastmcp-transport/src/async_io/native_pipe.rs:474:9

BOTH FAIL IN THE SAME SHARED HELPER, WHICH IS THE USEFUL PART. native_pipe.rs:474
is inside `await_wake` (:453), which turns the I/O driver up to 8 times with a
100 ms timeout and panics if no wake arrived. Its panic message was written to
discriminate the causes and should be read from the run rather than guessed:

    events_received == 0  -> the reactor saw no readiness at all, so the fd is
                             not actually armed even though a waker slot exists
    unknown_tokens > 0    -> readiness arrived but its token had no waker

So the first diagnostic step is free: capture that panic line's counters. Two
tests failing in one readiness helper points at one cause, and `await_wake` is a
*timing* construct (8 x 100 ms), so an environment-sensitive reading is a live
hypothesis that the counters can confirm or kill. Do not assume a product defect
before reading them.

NOT CAUSED BY THE CHANGE IN THE SAME RUN, proven by reachability rather than
asserted. That run also carried my `stdio/asynchronous.rs` spin guard
(bd-native-pipe-spin-84-a5tvl). It cannot reach these tests:

  * `git diff --stat` for that run touched exactly one file,
    crates/fastmcp-transport/src/stdio/asynchronous.rs; native_pipe.rs is
    unmodified.
  * The only two mentions of `AsyncStdioTransport`/`await_io` anywhere in
    native_pipe.rs are DOC COMMENTS, at :256 and :375 (both `///`).
  * The native_pipe test module (everything after :389) never constructs a
    transport and never calls `await_io`, `recv_async` or
    `recv_with_source_async`; its tests poll `NativePipeReader`/`Writer`
    directly through local `read`/`write` helpers.

Independently, the sibling failure is CHANGELOG-disclosed against v0.12.0, which
predates that change entirely.

NO-CLAIM BOUNDARY. This bead asserts only that the named test failed in the run
above and that nothing tracked it. It does not assert the test is wrong, that
the product is wrong, that the two failures share a root cause beyond sharing a
helper, or that the failure is deterministic. It specifically does not propose
relaxing or deleting either test; `await_wake`'s assertion is the thing that
would be weakened, and that is an RH-1 gate diff needing its own owner.

SUGGESTED FIRST STEPS, cheapest first:
1. Re-run just `-p fastmcp-transport --lib async_io::native_pipe` and record the
   full panic counters for both tests. Deterministic-vs-intermittent and the
   events_received/unknown_tokens split are both answered by that one run.
2. If intermittent, check whether `await_wake`'s 8 x 100 ms budget is simply too
   tight under worker load -- that is a test-harness bound, and raising it is a
   gate change with an owner, not a silent edit.
3. If deterministic with events_received == 0, the fd is not armed, which makes
   it adjacent to bd-8n2is (registration/ambient-capability defects in the same
   module). Coordinate rather than fixing both from two lanes.

comments.author: RealityCheck-Opus5-20261011
comments.text:
DIAGNOSTIC SUPPLIED AND MY OWN HYPOTHESIS PARTLY FALSIFIED, 2026-10-11,
RealityCheck-Opus5-20261011. The bead asked for the panic counters as the free
first step; I got them, formed an inference, ran the control, and the control
killed half of it. Recording both halves because the surviving half is now
sharp. Still not claiming this bead.

THREE RUNS, same tree, same worker class, only the scheduling differs:

    run 1  full --lib, 618 tests, default threads      616 passed / 2 failed
           readiness_updates_waker_and_preserves_data_through_eof      FAIL
           backpressure_yields_and_wakes_without_duplicating_bytes     FAIL
    run 2  filtered async_io::native_pipe, default threads   14 passed / 3 failed
           the same two, PLUS
           registers_only_with_its_bound_runtime_under_foreign_ambient  FAIL
    run 3  filtered async_io::native_pipe, -- --test-threads 1   15 passed / 2 failed
           readiness_updates_waker...                                  FAIL
           registers_only_with_its_bound_runtime...                    FAIL
           backpressure_yields...                                      **PASSED**

WHAT I GOT WRONG. From run 2 I inferred all three were cross-test interference
on a shared reactor, because `registrations=4..5` cannot describe a single test
that registers about one pipe, and because readiness had demonstrably arrived
(`events_received=1..2`, `wakers_dispatched=1..2`, `unknown_tokens=0`) while the
test's own counter read zero. That inference is right for exactly one of the
three and wrong for the other two.

THE COUNTERS SPLIT THE POPULATION CLEANLY, read against `await_wake`'s own
discrimination at :466-472 (`events_received == 0` -> the fd was never armed;
`unknown_tokens > 0` -> readiness arrived whose token had no waker):

    PARALLEL (run 2)
      readiness_updates_waker...   events_received=2 wakers_dispatched=2 unknown=0
      backpressure_yields...       events_received=1 wakers_dispatched=1 unknown=0
      registers_only_with_bound... events_received=1 wakers_dispatched=0 unknown=1

    SERIALIZED (run 3)
      readiness_updates_waker...   events_received=0 wakers_dispatched=0 unknown=0
      registers_only_with_bound... events_received=0 wakers_dispatched=0 unknown=0

So there are TWO causes behind one shared panic site, and the panic message was
written well enough to separate them:

1. **`backpressure_yields...` is parallel-only.** It passes under
   `--test-threads 1` and fails under default threads, where the counters show
   readiness arriving and being dispatched to somebody else. THIS BEAD'S
   SUBJECT is therefore a test-isolation failure, not a product defect. That is
   a smaller finding than the bead's filing assumed, and I am narrowing it
   rather than leaving the stronger reading standing.

2. **`readiness_updates_waker...` and `registers_only_with_bound...` are
   DETERMINISTIC**, and serialized they report `events_received=0` -- the
   helper's own first cause: *the fd is not actually armed even though a waker
   slot exists*. That is a real arming/registration observation, it reproduces
   without any parallelism to blame, and it is the shape bd-8n2is already
   describes. `readiness_updates_waker...` is the one the v0.12.0 CHANGELOG
   discloses as a release-gate failure, so both of those names now have an
   independent, serialized reproduction with counters.

CONSEQUENCES, in priority order:

- The two deterministic failures belong with **bd-8n2is**, not here. They are
  the more valuable half and should not inherit this bead's "no bead owns it"
  framing. Whoever holds bd-8n2is now has a serialized repro plus counters.
- This bead should be re-scoped to `backpressure_yields...` as a
  **parallel-only isolation failure**, with the fix being isolation or an
  explicit serial marker. Loosening `await_wake`'s 8 x 100 ms assertion is
  still the wrong move and still an RH-1 gate diff with its own owner --
  especially now, because that assertion is what detected the deterministic
  pair.
- The earlier claim in this bead that both failures "fail in the same shared
  helper, which is the useful part" survives, but the inference I drew from it
  does not: one helper, two causes.

NOTE ON WHAT STILL IS NOT ESTABLISHED. All three runs are one worker class on
Linux. I have not shown the deterministic non-arming reproduces on macOS, and I
have not read the arming path to decide whether `events_received=0` is a
product defect or an environment property of that host's epoll behaviour. I am
not asserting either. The disciplined next step is to read the registration
path against bd-8n2is rather than to re-run anything.

          ... if let Ok(n) = &poll_result { driver.stats.polls += 1; ... }
              else { driver.restore_events_only(events); ... }
          poll_result.map(Some)
      } else {
          Ok(None)          // <-- contended: NO poll, NO stats.polls increment
      }

ENUMERATING THE PATHS THAT SKIP `stats.polls += 1`, because the inference rests
on this being exhaustive:
  1. the contended `else` branch -> Ok(None) -> turn_with maps it to Ok(0) ->
     the test's `.unwrap()` SUCCEEDS and the loop continues. polls unchanged.
  2. `poll_result` is Err -> polls unchanged, but `poll_result.map(Some)`
     returns Err, turn_with propagates it, and the test's `.unwrap()` panics
     with the io::Error instead of reaching the counter panic.
Only path 1 reaches the counter panic. So polls == 0 means the contended branch
was taken on ALL EIGHT turns, and polls == 1 means it was taken on seven.

Verified that the counters are read from the same state they are written to:
IoDriverHandle::stats() (:608) does `self.inner.lock()` then
`driver.stats().clone()`, and the increment at :666 is under the same
`self.inner.lock()`. So the reading is not a snapshot of some other driver,
which also fits registrations=4/deregistrations=3 being consistently non-zero.

THREE CONSEQUENCES, in increasing order of importance.

  1. THE 8 x 100 ms BUDGET IS NEVER SPENT WHEN THIS HAPPENS. Each contended
     turn returns immediately, so the loop completes eight no-ops in
     microseconds and panics. Nobody waited 800 ms for anything. Any instinct
     to "give it more time" is therefore not just RH-1, it is aimed at a
     timeout that did not elapse. Predicted and NOT yet measured: the failing
     test's wall time should be ~0 rather than ~0.8 s. `cargo test ... --
     --format json -Z unstable-options --report-time` would settle it; the
     receipts I have do not carry exec_time.

  2. THE DIAGNOSTIC IS MISLEADING, AND THIS BEAD INHERITED IT. The key says
     `events_received == 0` means "the fd is not actually armed even though a
     waker slot exists", which points at the product. But with polls == 0 the
     reactor was never polled by this caller at all, so events_received == 0 is
     entailed and carries no information about arming. The honest reading of
     all nine captured instances is "this test never looked", not "the pipe was
     not armed". I previously repeated the arming interpretation myself; it is
     unsupported.

  3. THE FIX FOR THE INSTRUMENT IS ALREADY BUILT AND UNUSED. `try_turn_with`
     exists precisely to surface this, and its doc says so. `await_wake` calls
     the lossy wrapper AND discards its return value, so it cannot tell
     Ok(Some(0)) (polled, no events) from Ok(None) (never polled). Switching
     to try_turn_with and branching on None would turn this flake into a
     self-diagnosing failure, and would let the loop retry or yield on
     contention instead of burning a turn.

THE OPEN CONTRADICTION, which is the next real question and which I am NOT
papering over. The failing tests build `RuntimeBuilder::current_thread()` with
`.blocking_threads(0, 0)`, and the test itself asserts
`cx.blocking_pool_handle().is_none()`. `is_polling` is an `Arc<AtomicBool>`
created per handle (:471, :537) and reset by PollingGuard's drop (:512) with a
documented Release ordering. On that reading a single-threaded test holding the
only handle should win the CAS every time, and polls == 0 should be impossible.
It is observed anyway. So exactly one of these is true:
  (a) something else holds or shares that `is_polling` -- a handle clone from
      `cx.io_driver_handle()` sharing the Arc with a poller I have not found,
      or leakage across tests in one binary; or
  (b) my enumeration of the polls-skipping paths is incomplete.
Both are checkable. (a) is checkable by printing
`driver.is_polling.load(..)`/attempting `try_turn_with` and reporting Ok(None)
directly, which is consequence 3's change anyway. That is why I would make the
diagnostic change FIRST and only then design a fix: it converts the
contradiction into a one-line observation.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE. The intermittency result stands: the identical
three-name configuration gave 0, then 1, then 2 failures on three consecutive
runs, so a single green cannot validate any fix here and the pre-fix control
must be measured at the same repeat count. The two retractions above stand: the
composition "ladder" was noise, and the stdio::tests/STDIN_OWNER story was
wrong.

NO-CLAIM. I have not modified any code. I have not measured the failing test's
wall time, have not identified what holds `is_polling`, and am not claiming
this is a test-only defect -- consequence 2 says the evidence does not
currently support a PRODUCT defect either, which is a different thing from
ruling one out. What I claim is the code path, the exhaustive enumeration of
how polls can stay 0, and that the test cannot presently distinguish "no
readiness" from "never polled".

CrimsonFjord, 2026-10-11. ONE FACTUAL NARROWING ON THE LOOSE END, and deliberately no story attached to it. I have twice today built a mechanism out of too little and had to retract it, so this is the fact and nothing more.

loop polled zero times and lost the is_polling CAS on all eight turns. A
current_thread runtime with blocking_threads(0,0) should not have a concurrent
poller.

THE FACT. stats.polls has TWO increment sites in asupersync-0.5.0
src/runtime/io_driver.rs, and only one of them touches the CAS:

  :306  inside `IoDriver::turn_with(&mut self, ..)` -- the direct, non-handle
        version. It clears events, calls self.reactor.poll(..), then
        `self.stats.polls += 1`. It does NOT take or check is_polling at all.
  :666  inside `IoDriverHandle::try_turn_with(&self, ..)` -- the handle
        version, reached only after winning the is_polling CAS.

So a caller holding `&mut IoDriver` can poll and advance stats.polls WITHOUT
ever setting is_polling. IoDriverHandle exposes exactly that: a method whose
doc reads "Returns a lock guard for direct access to the driver".

That is sufficient to explain how polls can advance while nobody holds the
claim. It is NOT sufficient to explain why MY eight sequential calls on one
thread all LOST the CAS, because direct access never sets it. Those are two
different questions and only the first is answered.

Also checked and found nothing, recorded so it is not re-checked: no
thread::spawn in asupersync src/runtime outside blocking_pool.rs test code, and
is_polling appears nowhere in the crate except io_driver.rs plus three reactor
doc comments describing the leader/follower pattern. It is set only by
try_turn_with CAS and cleared only by PollingGuard::drop (:512).

CANDIDATE READINGS I AM NOT ASSERTING, listed so the next person can price
them rather than rediscover them:
  (a) something holds the claim for a long period -- e.g. the runtime takes it
      for its lifetime -- in which case driving a runtime-owned driver from
      outside via the handle can never win, and the test is using the wrong
      entry point.
  (b) a PollingGuard is leaked on some path, leaving is_polling true.
  (c) my reading of the set/clear sites is incomplete.
Distinguishing them needs one observation, not a theory: print
is_polling.load(..) at the top of await_wake. I have not done it.

This does not affect the fix. The fix is correct regardless of WHY the CAS is
lost: when it is lost there is a poller that will deliver the wake, and the
loop must spend its documented budget waiting rather than burn eight
microsecond no-ops. If (a) turns out to be true, the follow-on question is
whether these tests should drive the driver by hand at all -- which is a design
question for whoever owns the native_pipe tests, not something this bead
should decide.
